article_title: Effects of an automated corrective feedback-based peer assessment approach on students’ learning achievement, motivation, and self-regulated learning conceptions in foreign language pronunciation
citation: Chen-Chen Liu, Gwo-Jen Hwang, Peng Yu, Yun-Fang Tu, Youmei Wang. (2025). Effects of an automated corrective feedback-based peer assessment approach on students' learning achievement, motivation, and self-regulated learning conceptions in foreign language pronunciation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10484-z
title: The ACF-PA learning model: a four-stage foreign language speech learning cycle combining AI technology with corrective feedback
description: The article proposes a four-stage foreign language speech learning model based on the corrective feedback learning loop (Hattie & Timperley, 2007), comprising "acquisition, correction, reflection, and application." In the acquisition stage, learners receive lectures on pronunciation rules; in the correction stage, the AI tool "French Assistant" provides immediate automated corrective feedback using automatic speech recognition; in the reflection stage, peer assessment is adopted after courses using rubrics covering vowel, consonant, stress, intonation, and fluency; in the output stage, learners complete pronunciation exercises and peer assessment across five learning tasks. The model integrates AI technology with corrective feedback strategies to provide timely, personalized guidance.
requirements: An AI learning app with automatic speech recognition capability (French Assistant) that provides immediate automated corrective feedback on pronunciation
constraints: The study was conducted over only 5 weeks, which the authors note was not enough to form long-term learning habits
target_learners: College students learning foreign language pronunciation
target_learning_goals: French pronunciation accuracy
Self-regulated learning
Intrinsic motivation
examples: Students used the French Assistant app to search for French words, upload pronunciation audio, and receive immediate feedback with detailed information about wrongly pronounced syllables and scores

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Accountability as the reverse of explainability, with a three-layer accountability model
description: The article distinguishes the two central issues directionally: "Accountability is the reverse of explainability. Explainability flows through the system from inputs to output (decision) whereas accountability flows backwards, from a decision to the person taking responsibility for it." It presents Kroll's three-layer accountability model: a bottom recording layer tracking what the system does, a middle analytical layer matching records with output performance, and a top responsibility layer determining who made which change. Applied to the USA visa lottery this required only a .12% computational overhead, suggesting accountability mechanisms can be built in at design time.
requirements: Accountability mechanisms need to be built in during system design
Layers must reconcile accountability with protecting commercially confidential algorithms or trained model weights
constraints: When machine learning systems must operate very quickly, immediate accountability is impractical and post-facto accountability is what remains
target_learners: teachers held accountable for learning achievements
target_learning_goals: responsible and traceable deployment of machine learning in education
key_sources: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2

article_title: Learning during a pandemic: an Activity Theory analysis of the challenges experienced by Aotearoa/New Zealand university students
citation: Dilani Gedera · Dianne Forbes · Cheryl Brown · Maggie Hartnett · Ashwini Datt. (2023). Learning during a pandemic: an Activity Theory analysis of the challenges experienced by Aotearoa/New Zealand university students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10284-3
title: Activity Theory as an analytical framework for online learning challenges, with revised terminology and four levels of contradictions
description: The article applies Engeström's Activity Theory, in which "Engeström's (1987) expanded Activity Theory comprises elements forming an activity system" — subject/participant, tools, objective, rules, community, roles and outcome. It adopts revised terminology (e.g., participant instead of subject, objective instead of object) to avoid confusion in educational contexts, and uses contradictions — imbalances within, between elements of, or between activity systems — as the analytical lens, classifying them as primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary. Contradictions manifest as obstacles, interruptions, conflicts, tensions and gaps but are treated as a driving force for change and development.
requirements: The activity system is used as the minimal meaningful unit of analysis, with Activity Theory elements serving as coding buckets for qualitative data.
constraints: Engeström's original terminology does not easily translate to educational contexts, requiring the revised terms adopted in this article.
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving students' online learning experiences during disrupted teaching
key_sources: Dilani Gedera · Dianne Forbes · Cheryl Brown · Maggie Hartnett · Ashwini Datt. (2023). Learning during a pandemic: an Activity Theory analysis of the challenges experienced by Aotearoa/New Zealand university students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10284-3

article_title: Open educational resources: undertheorized research and untapped potential
citation: David A. Wiley. (2021). Open educational resources: undertheorized research and untapped potential. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09907-w
title: The access hypothesis of OER benefits
description: The access hypothesis, named by Grimaldi, Basu Mallick, Waters, and Baraniuk (2019), is an explanatory mechanism for OER effects: "OER benefits learning by providing access to critical course materials, and therefore predicts that OER should only benefit students who would not otherwise have access to the materials." It reframes OER outcome questions as questions about the impact of the price of required course materials, since many OER are available at no or low cost. The commentary presents it as a current direction toward stronger theorization of OER research.
requirements: Researchers must account for students who would have had access to required course materials even had they been expensive when estimating OER effects
constraints: Predicts benefits only for students who would not otherwise have access to the materials
target_learners: higher education students, including Pell-eligible and other cost-burdened students
target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes such as final grades and success metrics through affordable access to course materials
examples: Grimaldi et al. (2019) used simulation analysis to show that failing to account for students with prior access likely prevents detecting any OER effect
key_sources: David A. Wiley. (2021). Open educational resources: undertheorized research and untapped potential. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09907-w

article_title: Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms
citation: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2
title: Activity Theory six-element framework framing automarker-mediated formative learning
description: The article uses Activity Theory as the pedagogical lens aligning the automarker with DSA coursework. "AT extends the three elements of the Vygotskian triangle (1934–1987) into six elements that together realize the final outcomes": subject (instructor), tool (automarker), object(ives) (building algorithmic reasoning and programming skills), learning community (instructor and students), rules and regulations (prescribed coursework), and division of labour (teacher and learner roles). Ongoing interactions among the six elements transfer into final outcomes such as programming practice and instructor workaround strategies.
requirements: The core of AT is the proposed learning activity, emphasizing how ongoing interactions take place between the six elements
Community members have clearly defined responsibilities specific to their role and must comply with set rules and regulations
constraints: The framework is applied to one DSA course context at a tertiary institution
target_learning_goals: know-what, know-how and know-why competencies in programming
examples: Figure 1 (A) and (B) maps the AT elements to this study's context, with the automarker as tool and the DSA coursework rules governing activities
key_sources: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Activity-centered design model: design shapes learning indirectly through epistemic, physical and social structures
description: The article's Figure 1 (adapted from Goodyear & Ellis, 2008) portrays an activity-centric view in which teaching-as-design affects student learning activity only indirectly. Design works "through the specification of worthwhile tasks (epistemic structures), the recommendation of appropriate tools, artefacts and other physical resources (structures of place), and recommendation of divisions of labour etc. (social structures)". The model prioritises what students do, think, feel and say, treating everything else as stimulus or scaffold for their activity.
requirements: Teachers must design good learning tasks and communicate task specifications clearly to students
constraints: Design works indirectly; students adapt, interpret and customise what is designed
target_learning_goals: effective engagement in designed learning activities
examples: The article uses the model to argue teachers are obliged to help students locate, access and configure physical resources and find good ways of working with peers

article_title: Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach
citation: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z
title: ACAD framework's three design dimensions as relational conditions for learning
description: The Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD) framework (Goodyear & Carvalho, 2014) provides a holistic and relational understanding of design for learning. The article states that ACAD defines three main aspects to analyse when intentionally designing situations for learning: "(1) the set design, (2) the epistemic design, and (3) the social design", while recognising that "learning activity is always emergent and cannot be predefined". The article uses ACAD as the anchoring framework that its topologies operationalise, with particular emphasis on the under-studied set design.
requirements: Analysis must treat the three design aspects relationally rather than in isolation
constraints: Less attention has been given to the 'set design' in prior ACAD literature
target_learning_goals: Design and analysis of situations for learning
examples: The RICT case study analyses the course structure through the ACAD lens, with special emphasis on the set design component
key_sources: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Activity systems view of teaching capabilities as distributed activity
description: The article takes an activity systems view to foreground teaching as a distributed activity enacted collectively by people and technologies, including students, learning designers, IT staff, librarians, policymakers and accreditors. It focuses on 'teaching capabilities' rather than 'teacher capabilities' to acknowledge distributed agency, influenced by curricula, policies, leadership, disciplines, resources and socio-political contexts. Capabilities span global (macro), local (meso) and individual (micro) levels of the educational ecosystem.
requirements: Widening thinking beyond the individual teacher to the broader distributed activity system
constraints: The article states most existing literature takes a person-centred view that this framework deliberately departs from
target_learners: educational stakeholders in distributed teaching systems
target_learning_goals: collective enactment of teaching towards a sustainable university mission
examples: The article lists elements influencing distributed teaching capabilities, including educational policies, leadership, joint goals and visions, and physical and digital resources

Students follow an identify-model-specify-decide sequence: identifying map features, modelling potential impacts, specifying affected areas and communities, and determining adaptation strategies such as relocating people or raising sea defences.

A schema provided by the teacher to structure adaptation suggestions

understanding sea level rise impacts on social systems

article_title: Being proactive about anthropogenic environmental changes: augmenting students’ decision making with artificial intelligence (AI) technology
citation: Xi Xiang & Michael E. Meadows. (2025). Being proactive about anthropogenic environmental changes: augmenting students' decision making with artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10523-9
title: Activity 2: combating future forest fires using K-means clustering and Apache Zeppelin
description: A problem-based learning activity adapted from a forest fire prevention case study, in which students derive a resource allocation solution for wildfire response in Oregon using a frame-model-program-decide mode. "The K-means clustering algorithm is selected to partition the locations of historical forest fires into clusters", and cluster centroids assist in allocating firefighting infrastructure to regions most prone to burning. Students work with US forest fire data from 2000 to 2016 in the Apache Zeppelin web-based data science notebook.

Teacher explanation of the rules and steps of algorithmic design

making data-informed fire management and infrastructure investment decisions

description: The article analyses teachers' interview answers using categories based on a model from cultural-historical activity theory, citing Engeström's work. The framework structures the extraction of teachers' conceptions of the CLE implementations, treating the classroom implementation as an activity system whose components (teachers, tools, school culture) can be examined. It is used here as the coding and interpretive lens for the cross-country interview data.

constraints: Applied in this article to teachers' conceptions in four European national school-culture contexts

article_title: Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children’s learning and emotive engagement
citation: Chen, Huili; Park, Hae Won; Breazeal, Cynthia. (2020). Teaching and learning with children: Impact of reciprocal peer learning with a social robot on children's learning and emotive engagement. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.COMPEDU.2020.103836
title: Active role-switching (ARS) policy for educational agents
description: The article presents "a novel active role-switching (ARS) policy trained using reinforcement learning, in which the agent is rewarded for adapting its tutor or tutee behavior to the child's knowledge mastery level." Rather than fixing an agent in a single role, the ARS policy adaptively switches between tutor and tutee behavior during interaction, making the agent peer-like. The authors frame this as contributing "a new dimension of designing educational agents — actively adapting roles based on the student's engagement and learning needs."
requirements: The agent must be able to estimate the child's knowledge mastery level to adapt its role behavior
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
affective engagement
examples: In the experiment, children completed a collaborative word-learning activity with the peer agent, which adaptively switched between tutor and tutee roles.

title: Across-subject online experiment comparing AI-generated and human-made teaching videos
description: An online experiment with an "across-subject experimental design" in which 447 participants completed two treatment conditions presenting different mixes of AI-generated and human-made videos, with 1788 video treatments in total. content knowledge in a management course

article_title: Medical students' evaluation of digital problem-based learning: a mixed-methods systematic review.
citation: Rathleff Camilla Rams, Vergel John, Ryberg Thomas, Kristensen Jette Kolding, Telléus Patrik Kjaersdam. (2025). Medical students’ evaluation of digital problem-based learning: a mixed-methods systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07823-2
title: The ACAD framework categorizes DPBL design into social, epistemic, and set design
description: The Activity-Centered Analysis and Design (ACAD) model provides a metatheoretical framework for understanding complex learning situations by focusing on activities at the heart of student perceptions. In the context of DPBL, it categorizes instructional design options into three distinct categories: "social design" (how students engage with tasks individually, in groups, or as teams, including social roles), "epistemic design" (the tasks that students are asked to perform), and "set design" (the digital tools with which students interact). The review used this framework to categorize 453 student quotes and identify key design considerations for educators designing future DPBL interventions.
requirements: The framework requires categorization of student perceptions into social, epistemic, and set design modalities to identify design considerations.
target_learning_goals: Understanding how design choices in digital learning environments shape student experience

article_title: The Influence of Academic Emotions on Learning Effects: A Systematic Review.
citation: Tan Jing, Mao Jie, Jiang Yizhang, Gao Ming. (2021). The Influence of Academic Emotions on Learning Effects: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18189678
title: Two-dimensional (valence × arousal) classification of academic emotions into four groups
description: The review organizes academic emotions along two dimensions: valence (whether the stimulus is pleasant or unpleasant) and arousal (the emotional intensity a stimulus causes). Based on this classification it divides emotions into four groups: "positive arousal emotions (e.g., enjoyment, pride)", positive low-arousal emotions (e.g., relaxation), passive arousal emotions (e.g., anger, anxiety), and negative emotions (e.g., extreme depression, despair). This taxonomy underpins the review's comparisons of positive versus negative academic emotions on learning effects.
requirements: Academic emotions must be assessed with tools distinguishing valence and arousal, such as emotion scales or self-report instruments
constraints: The review notes arousal and potency produce different results in cognitive processes and on relevant neural matrices, so effects differ by emotion type
target_learning_goals: academic performance
learning strategies
motivation
cognitive load
examples: The review's included studies measured emotions with instruments such as PANAS, the Positive Emotion Self-Report Scale, and the Achievement Emotion Questionnaire

article_title: Active Commute in Relation to Cognition and Academic Achievement in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Future Recommendations.
citation: Phansikar, M.; Ashrafi, S.A.; Khan, N.A.; Massey, W.V.; Mullen, S.P. (2019). Active Commute in Relation to Cognition and Academic Achievement in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Future Recommendations. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16245103
title: Active commuting as a physically active context with distinctive cognitive-motor demands that may differ from leisure-time physical activity
description: The review frames active commuting to school as a form of leisure-time physical activity complementary to sport and chores, but argues it "may be unique in terms of some of its inherent cognitive-motor challenges": attentive navigation through outdoor life-space with distractions and dangers. In the discussion it contrasts ACS with leisure-time physical activity, suggesting the latter "calls for more neuromuscular complexity as compared to walking or bicycling", which may explain why leisure-time physical activity shows clearer academic benefits than ACS in the pooled mathematics analysis.
requirements: Understanding the ACS–cognition relationship requires accounting for dose (duration, frequency, intensity), mode, and whether commuting is done alone or in a group, as the review states these shape the activity received.
constraints: The review states ACS is not always discretionary for children, since they do not always choose their mode of transportation, and exposure to traffic and air pollution during commuting may counteract benefits.
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 4 to 18.5 years in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: executive functioning
academic achievement including mathematics, language, and reading outcomes
examples: The review contrasts studies where ACS showed positive associations (visuospatial accuracy, d2 Test of Attention, working memory) with studies using the flanker task and verbal fluency that found none.

citation: Chojnacki, G., Eno, J., Liu, F., Meyers, C., Konstantopoulos, S., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2013). Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Acuity Predictive interim assessment tool
description: Acuity Predictive is a technology-supported interim assessment tool aligned to Indiana's statewide ISTEP+ exam, implemented statewide by the Indiana Department of Education beginning in 2008. As described by Konstantopoulos and colleagues (2011), it is "a series of 30 – 35 item multiple choice tests in mathematics and ELA, administered three times during the school year." The intervention provided teachers with rapid access (within 24 hours) to class- and student-level performance reports, including predicted proficiency on the year-end test.
requirements: Volunteering schools administer the tests multiple times each school year and teachers are expected to use assessment information to improve ongoing instruction
constraints: Acuity is not a unique intervention; a significant number of control teachers reported using other interim assessment tools
target_learners: K-8 students in Indiana public schools
target_learning_goals: Improved mathematics and English Language Arts achievement via data-driven instruction
examples: In the 2009-10 RCT, schools volunteering for diagnostic assessments were randomly assigned to receive Acuity or to a one-year delay condition

article_title: The Effect of Practical Presentations' Strategy on the Achievement of the Ninth Graders Students of the Pre-Vocational Education Subject in Shobak District Schools
citation: Haroon M. Al Tawarah, Omar M. Mahasneh & Nourah A. Al-Hawartheh. (2017). The Effect of Practical Presentations' Strategy on the Achievement of the Ninth Graders Students of the Pre-Vocational Education Subject in Shobak District Schools. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p109
title: Pre/post achievement test for sanitation and environment waste recycling units
description: The study instrument was an achievement test (pre/final) measuring eight purposes across the sanitation and environment waste recycling units, five questions per purpose, spanning knowledge of plumbing spare parts, fixing and maintaining them, and environmental recycling content including classifying recycled substances and compost preparation. Validity was checked by specialized judges and reliability by test-retest on a pilot sample of 14 students with a two-week interval, yielding an alpha coefficient of 85.7%.
requirements: validated by a panel of specialized judges in curricula, testing and evaluating, plus teachers and supervisors
constraints: reliability estimated on a pilot sample outside the study sample of only 14 students
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skills in sanitation and environment waste recycling
examples: Test purposes included acknowledging health plumbing spare parts, fixing them, maintaining them, and determining steps to prepare compost
