article_title: Academic Controversy in Macroeconomics: An Active and Collaborative Method to Increase Student Learning
citation: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Academic controversy: a five-step cooperative group controversy procedure
description: Academic controversy is a cooperative learning technique in which "cooperative student groups of four members" investigate an issue, split into pro/con diads, and work toward a "best reasoned judgment" under instructor monitoring. The lesson proceeds through five steps: prepare a position, present and advocate it, engage in open discussion and critique, reverse perspectives, and synthesize a joint position. The article operationalized this procedure in eight macroeconomics lessons.
requirements: Groups of four students split into pro/con pairs, with an instructor overseeing and monitoring the controversy
Rules for criticizing ideas without criticizing people during open discussion
constraints: Examined here only in post-secondary macroeconomics at one community college
target_learning_goals: economic reasoning and understanding of macroeconomics content
critical thinking through considering multiple perspectives
examples: In the study, lesson packs were distributed on Tuesdays and group controversy sessions held in class on Thursdays, approximately every two weeks, across eight lessons in spring 2010
key_sources: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Academic Controversy in Macroeconomics: An Active and Collaborative Method to Increase Student Learning
citation: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Academic controversy lesson pack for macroeconomics
description: The lesson pack is the instructional artifact used in the experimental treatment, based on the Johnson and Johnson procedure. "It contained an issue page consisting of the question to be investigated and the steps to conduct the controversy," a rules page, background with key terms and potential resources, pages for research, position, and consensus notes, and rubrics for scoring. Students prepared positions outside class and turned in the completed pack with a group synthesis report.
requirements: Students find credible resources and prepare their assigned position outside of classroom time
Scoring via rubrics developed from Harvard University guidelines (Goodrich, 1997)
target_learning_goals: preparing and advocating evidence-based positions
synthesizing opposing arguments into a joint position
examples: Each student quad also wrote a report explaining the synthesis and supporting evidence, and students were assessed individually on controversy topics via class examinations
key_sources: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Using Videos and 3D Animations for Conceptual Learning in Basic Computer Units
citation: Unal Cakiroglu, Huseyin Yilmaz. (2017). Using Videos and 3D Animations for Conceptual Learning in Basic Computer Units. Contemporary Educational Technology, 8(4), 390-405. https://cedtech.net
title: Teachers should take an active role in and out of class when using videos and 3D animations to remedy misconceptions
description: The article concludes that the teacher's active contribution supported the success of remedying misconceptions with videos and 3D animations. In class, "The prominent roles were acting as guidance to the students, monitoring students , and focusing on the frequently observed misconceptions"; outside class, the teacher administered projects, followed activities, and evaluated homework step by step. The article states teachers' active role in and out of class activities affected conceptual understandings.
requirements: Teacher guidance such as suggesting slowing down, replaying, rewind or forwarding during video and animation tasks
constraints: In the homework condition students could not ask questions about the concepts, though this did not affect the difference in conceptual change between groups
target_learners: 10th-grade vocational high school students in the computer department
target_learning_goals: Remedying misconceptions about basic computer system concepts
examples: The classroom teacher introduced videos and animations with short notices, provided presentations and question-and-answer sessions, and sometimes let students work individually or together
key_sources: Unal Cakiroglu, Huseyin Yilmaz. (2017). Using Videos and 3D Animations for Conceptual Learning in Basic Computer Units. Contemporary Educational Technology, 8(4), 390-405. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1158165

article_title: The Effect of Metacognitive Teaching and Mathematical Prior Knowledge on Mathematical Logical Thinking Ability and Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Aminah, M., Kusumah, Y. S., Suryadi, D., & Sumarmo, U. (2018). The Effect of Metacognitive Teaching and Mathematical Prior Knowledge on Mathematical Logical Thinking Ability and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 45-62. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1134a
title: Under any teaching approach, teachers should accustom students to pose metacognitive questions to themselves and answer them with relevant reasons
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that, since no single teaching approach guarantees higher MLTA, teachers should accustom students to pose metacognitive questions to themselves and then attempt to answer the questions or solve the problems together with relevant reasons. The authors argue that by these continuous activities students' MLTA is expected to increase gradually. This principle generalizes the metacognitive questioning at the core of MTLA beyond the specific approach tested.
requirements: Teachers must habitually prompt students to pose metacognitive questions to themselves and answer them with relevant reasons
constraints: The article states there is no single or certain mathematics teaching approach which is able to guarantee students' higher grade MLTA
target_learning_goals: mathematical logical thinking ability
examples: In the study, MTL students were awakened to control and assess their thinking process through posed questions, answered with relevant reasons, connecting new knowledge with previous knowledge
key_sources: Aminah, M., Kusumah, Y. S., Suryadi, D., & Sumarmo, U. (2018). The Effect of Metacognitive Teaching and Mathematical Prior Knowledge on Mathematical Logical Thinking Ability and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 45-62. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1134a

article_title: Multimedia Approach and Its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers
citation: D.R. Robert Joan and S.P. Denisia. (2012). Multimedia Approach and its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers. li-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://www.eric.ed.gov
title: Achievement Test in Mathematics (50 marks, 45 minutes) with blueprint and weightage tables
description: The outcome measure for both groups, developed by the authors in 2012. The test was built from weightage tables covering objectives, content, form of questions and difficulty level, with the question paper prepared according to a blueprint. As printed, "Maximum Marks : 50" and "Maximum Time : 45 minutes"; weightage tables allocate marks across knowledge, understanding, application and skill, and across easy, average and difficult levels.
requirements: Prepared according to the blueprint and weightage tables on objectives, content, form of questions and difficulty level
constraints: Designed for the Mathematics content taught to prospective teachers in this study
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement across knowledge, understanding, application and skill objectives
examples: Administered as pre-test and post-test to both groups; marks were scored and tabulated for t-test analysis
key_sources: D.R. Robert Joan and S.P. Denisia. (2012). Multimedia Approach and its Effect in Teaching Mathematics for the Prospective Teachers. li-manager's Journal on School Educational Technology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101646

article_title: Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development
citation: Berker Bulut, Nuri Karasakaloğlu. (2017). Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i12.2688
title: Eight-week active listening training program organized around listening types
description: The experimental intervention was a weekly two-hour course for eight weeks (16 hours total) in which students studied informative texts, narrative texts, a poem and a video, each tied to a listening type (discriminant, listening for information, empathetic, critical, aesthetic) and "performing activities in accordance with the process steps of active listening method". Sessions progressed from defining active listening and listening types to applying each type to a curriculum-appropriate text.
requirements: Texts appropriate to students' levels, selected from books suitable for fourth and fifth grade levels and approved materials; audiovisual tools including a TRT School short film
constraints: Delivered within Turkish lesson hours (40-minute lessons, two per week); control group studied the same materials via traditional listening exercises such as note taking and teacher questions
target_learning_goals: vocabulary development and listening skill improvement
examples: Session 3 used the narrative text "Atatürk's High Sense of Humanity" for discriminant listening; Session 8 used the short film "The First Flying Man" for aesthetic listening
key_sources: Berker Bulut, Nuri Karasakaloğlu. (2017). Benefiting from Listening in Vocabulary Development. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 12. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i12.2688

article_title: Pre-Test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students' Academic Achievement and Permanence of Their Knowledge
citation: Kenan BAŞ, Esen DURMUŞ. (2019). Pre-test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students’ Academic Achievement and Permanence of their Knowledge. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.7n.2p.107
title: Researcher-developed Academic Achievement Test for the 'Resources of our Country' unit
description: A 50-question achievement test the researcher prepared for the 6th-grade 'Resources of our Country' unit, using Bloom's cognitive-domain levels and mixed formats: "Multiple Choice, Gap-Filling, True/False, and Matching". Expert opinion was consulted for validity, item difficulty (Pj = 56.9) and discrimination (rjx between 0.21 and 0.76) indices were examined, and reliability was established with KR-20 = 0.87. It served as pretest, posttest, and permanence test in both groups.
requirements: Expert opinion was consulted for scope and appearance validity and student-level appropriateness
constraints: The test covers only the 'Resources of our Country' unit objectives and acquirements
target_learning_goals: Social studies content knowledge of the Resources of our Country unit across knowledge, comprehension, practice, analysis and evaluation levels
examples: Applied as pretest before the eight-week intervention, as posttest after the unit, and as a permanence test four weeks after the last test
key_sources: Kenan BAŞ, Esen DURMUŞ. (2019). Pre-test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students’ Academic Achievement and Permanence of their Knowledge. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.7n.2p.107

article_title: An RCT of a CBT Intervention for Emerging Adults with ADHD Attending College: Functional Outcomes
citation: Laura D. Eddy, Arthur D. Anastopoulos, Melissa R. Dvorsky, Paul J. Silvia, Jeffrey D. Labban & Joshua M. Langberg (2021). An RCT of a CBT Intervention for Emerging Adults with ADHD Attending College: Functional Outcomes. Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2020.1867989
title: ACCESS: a two-semester CBT and mentoring program for college students with ADHD
description: ACCESS (Accessing Campus Connections and Empowering Student Success) is a cognitive-behavioral treatment program delivered over two academic semesters for emerging adults with ADHD attending college. The first-semester active phase includes "eight weekly group sessions (90 minutes each)" covering ADHD psychoeducation, behavioral strategies, and adaptive thinking, plus up to 10 weekly 30-minute individual mentoring sessions supporting implementation. The second-semester maintenance phase fades support to one group session and up to six mentoring sessions. Groups of four to six students used a discussion-based format with handouts and guest speakers from campus support services.
requirements: Delivery requires trained group leaders and mentors with weekly supervision by licensed doctoral-level clinical psychologists and a detailed treatment manual
constraints: Evaluated at two large public four-year universities; authors note findings may not generalize to other postsecondary settings or students with markedly lower intellectual abilities
target_learners: college students with ADHD (emerging adults, ages 18–30)
target_learning_goals: ADHD knowledge, behavioral strategies addressing executive functioning deficits, adaptive thinking skills, study skills, time management, daily life functioning
examples: In the RCT, 83.2% of the immediate treatment group attended at least 6 group sessions and 85.7% attended a majority of mentoring sessions; fidelity ratings were 96.4% and 95.6% for reviewed group and mentoring sessions.
key_sources: Laura D. Eddy, Arthur D. Anastopoulos, Melissa R. Dvorsky, Paul J. Silvia, Jeffrey D. Labban & Joshua M. Langberg (2021). An RCT of a CBT Intervention for Emerging Adults with ADHD Attending College: Functional Outcomes. Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2020.1867989

article_title: Accelerated Reader: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See. (2015). Accelerated Reader Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.gl-assessment.co.uk/products/new-group-reading-test/test-detail
title: Accelerated Reader: web-based reading management and monitoring programme
description: Accelerated Reader (AR) is a commercial web-based reading programme by Renaissance Learning that screens pupils with the STAR test, matches books to reading level and interest using the ATOS readability formula, and motivates independent reading through computerised quizzes, AR points and TOPS reports. The report describes it as "a whole-group reading management and monitoring programme that aims to foster the habit of independent reading". In the trial it was delivered for about 20 weeks as a catch-up intervention for weak readers in Year 7.
requirements: A well-stocked library banded by ATOS readability level
Regular subscription to the Renaissance Learning website for STAR tests and quizzes
Computers or tablets with internet connection
constraints: ATOS measures only readability level and does not take into account literary merit, thematic construction, quality and complexity of ideas or maturity of the content
The intervention involves no teaching at all
target_learners: Year 7 pupils below secure Level 4 in KS2 English
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Independent reading habit
Reading motivation
examples: Schools ran 40 minutes of daily independent reading, used library space for reading and quizzes, and purchased tablets and books with trial funding
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See. (2015). Accelerated Reader Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.gl-assessment.co.uk/products/new-group-reading-test/test-detail

article_title: Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course
citation: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166
title: Select modeling tasks by accessibility, independence and activity principles
description: For forming representations of modeling methodology in secondary schools, the article holds that "accessibility, independence and activity the methodical principles are considered to be the main principles of selection of tasks". Task selection should satisfy accessibility and clearness, since modeling is an intersubject method spanning mathematics, computer science and the researched area. Tasks should also be rich enough to show modeling's key property: approximate description of reality and checking model adequacy.
requirements: Tasks must satisfy the accessibility and clearness principle
Tasks should reflect the recurrence and variability of the modeling methodology, not only text tasks from algebra
constraints: Satisfying accessibility and clearness is described as the main difficulty of task selection
target_learning_goals: formation of representations of modeling methodology
examples: The article gives example tasks: proposing essential assumptions for a tent-production planning task, calculating train speed from wheel knocks, and drawing a bicycle in a graphics editor
key_sources: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166

article_title: The Impact of Task-Based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses
citation: Abdullah Sarani & Leila Farzaneh Sahebi. (2012). The Impact of Task-based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p118
title: Shift ESP classroom practice from passive lecture to active group learning to increase target-language exposure
description: For EFL contexts where learners have little contact with native speakers, the article recommends moving away from teacher-centred translation: "the focus of language teaching should be placed on changi ng the classroom practice fr om the traditional passive lecture to more active group learning so that learners can be more easily exposed to target language use." The principle rests on the study's finding that the interactive, feedback-rich task-based condition outperformed individual translation work, and it extends to implications for materials development and teacher training.
requirements: Learner-learner interaction during tasks so students can discuss vocabulary and monitor their language
constraints: Recommended for EFL contexts with limited native-speaker contact, such as Iran
target_learners: University ESP students in EFL contexts
target_learning_goals: Technical vocabulary acquisition
Communicative competence
examples: The experimental classes replaced text translation with pair and group tasks, giving students peer feedback the traditional group never received
key_sources: Abdullah Sarani & Leila Farzaneh Sahebi. (2012). The Impact of Task-based Approach on Vocabulary Learning in ESP Courses. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p118

article_title: Investigating the Efficiency of Scenario Based Learning and Reflective Learning Approaches in Teacher Education
citation: Hursen, C., & Gezer Fasli, F. (2017). Investigating the Efficiency of Scenario Based Learning and Reflective Learning Approaches in Teacher Education. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.2.264
title: 22-item multiple choice academic achievement test for the Teaching Practice course
description: A multiple choice academic achievement test developed by the researchers, used both to check group equivalence at pre-test and to measure post-test achievement. It began with 35 items, was reviewed by 10 experts for content validity, and "the test is finalized with 22 items after it was gone through certain analyses". "KR -20 internal consistency reliability of the multiple choice academic achievement test is found as 0.89", item difficulty indices ranged 0.40–0.80 with mean 0.52, and items below a discrimination index of 0.30 were removed.
requirements: Expert opinion (N=10) for content validity
Item discrimination index of at least 0.30
constraints: Designed to measure knowledge and skills gained during the 12-week Teaching Practice course only
target_learning_goals: teaching practice course achievement
examples: Scored 1-0 per item and assessed over 100 points before and after the application, with the mean of both scores forming actual performance
key_sources: Hursen, C., & Gezer Fasli, F. (2017). Investigating the Efficiency of Scenario Based Learning and Reflective Learning Approaches in Teacher Education. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.2.264

article_title: The Effect of Dynamic Web Technologies on Student Academic Achievement in Problem-Based Collaborative Learning Environment
citation: Agâh Tuğrul KORUCU, Hasan ÇAKIR. (2018). The Effect of Dynamic Web Technologies on Student Academic Achievement in Problem-Based Collaborative Learning Environment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://www.mojet.net
title: Researcher-developed 65-item Academic Achievement Test
description: The researcher developed an academic achievement test of 65 multiple-choice questions, each with 4 alternatives, prepared according to Bloom's Taxonomy steps as knowledge, comprehension and conceptual (analysis-synthesis) questions and mapped to an indicator chart of lesson objectives. It was reviewed by 5 experts, and internal consistency was calculated with the Kuder-Richardson-20 technique, yielding "Kr-20 test-value = .735"; test difficulty was 0.464, described as a normal difficulty level.
requirements: Content validity was provided by expert opinion; questions with high significance levels were retained because no other questions measured those objectives
constraints: Used as both pre-test and post-test in this study with pre-service ICT teachers
target_learning_goals: course content achievement in the Computer and Teaching Technologies application course
examples: Scoring assigned 1 for correct and 0 for wrong answers, and item discrimination power and reliability were determined after application
key_sources: Agâh Tuğrul KORUCU, Hasan ÇAKIR. (2018). The Effect of Dynamic Web Technologies on Student Academic Achievement in Problem-Based Collaborative Learning Environment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165485

article_title: Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level
citation: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://ber.journals.pu.edu.pk
title: Activity-based resiliency module combining self-directed reflection with group sharing
description: The researchers designed an instructional module of classroom activities targeting selected protective factors: creativity, self-esteem, self-efficacy, internal locus of control, autonomy, problem-solving skill, optimism and hope, sense of humor, stress coping skills and teacher-student relationship. "The modules is an amalgamation of self-directed reflection activities with group sharing in order to hear, more in- depth, other peoples’ stories and to identify which skills they feel need additional practice." It was delivered in one-hour daily sessions over three months by a researcher acting as resilience teacher, and was validated through expert opinion.
requirements: A resilience teacher spending one hour daily with a separate section of non-resilient at-risk students
Validation through expert opinion before use
constraints: Offered by a researcher who was not the students' regular teacher; limited to the selected protective factors due to a tight time schedule
target_learners: Non-resilient at-risk of failure students at secondary school level
target_learning_goals: Protective factors contributing to academic resilience
examples: Daily one-hour resilience activity sessions in a separate experimental section over three months
key_sources: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1210192

article_title: Activity-Based Teaching, Student Motivation and Academic Achievement
citation: Anwar, F. (2019). The effect of activity-based teaching techniques on student motivation and academic achievement. Journal of Education and Educational Development, 6(1), 154-170. https://journals.iobmresearch.com/index.php/JEED
title: Activity-Based Learning as a constructivist, engagement-centered teaching approach
description: Activity Based Learning (ABL) is defined in the article as "a learning process in which students are constantly engaged", a setup where students actively participate rather than sit as passive listeners. Its two key elements are the active role and involvement of students and collaboration amongst students. The article situates ABL in constructive learning, comprising prior knowledge and personal experiences, and cites Churchill (2003) that it helps students construct mental models for applied problem solving and transfer.
requirements: Students must be motivated enough to achieve their potential; the article states the method will not function properly without sufficient student motivation
constraints: The article frames ABL against traditional teaching, which it says does not utilize previous knowledge or let creativity bloom
target_learners: students at all levels of education, studied here at higher secondary level
target_learning_goals: critical and creative thinking skills
self-direction
applied problem solving and transfer of information and skills
examples: The experimental group in this study was taught five grade-11 education chapters through hands-on activities as an instantiation of ABL
key_sources: Anwar, F. (2019). The effect of activity-based teaching techniques on student motivation and academic achievement. Journal of Education and Educational Development, 6(1), 154-170. https://journals.iobmresearch.com/index.php/JEED

article_title: Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana
citation: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175
title: Action research as a framework for practitioner-led pedagogical intervention in language education
description: The study adopts action research, defined as a kind of study carried out by a practitioner, usually in collaboration with others, concerned with identification and solution of problems in a specific educational setting. The article identifies three defining characteristics: it is carried out by a practitioner, it is collaborative, and it is aimed at changing things. Nunan's five-stage procedure is described, from initiation by a practitioner through collaboration, objective data collection, dissemination, to an ongoing cycle in which the instructor "reflects on, returns to, and extends the initial enquiry".
requirements: A practitioner-researcher working within an educational institution
Collaboration among researcher, teacher and administrator roles
Objective data in the form of learner language and classroom interaction
constraints: The article notes action research is an emerging framework in educational research with several similar competing models
target_learners: Basic school (K-9) students in public junior high schools
target_learning_goals: Improving student attainment in English language
examples: The author negotiated roles with a headmistress (administrator) and a language teacher (teacher), observed lessons, and tracked the 2009 BECE results of the two cohorts as the ultimate data
key_sources: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175

article_title: Recommendations for the Investigation and Delivery of Music Programs Aimed at Achieving Psychosocial Wellbeing Benefits in Mainstream Schools
citation: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://www.asme.edu.au/
title: Matching musical activities to targeted wellbeing benefits: group, instrumental, product-creation, fun, challenging, and non-musical activities each serve distinct goals
description: The article presents an example list of how activities within a music group can be appropriated for particular goals: group activities facilitate social connection and communication; instrumental activities such as improvisation offer an accessible, non-confronting way to engage with difficult feelings; creating a musical product promotes ownership, pride and self-efficacy; fun activities increase engagement; challenging activities help at-risk groups face difficult issues; and non-musical activities let uncomfortable students participate and be recognised as contributing members.
requirements: A specific need or program goal must be identified before selecting activities; musical products should focus on expression rather than musical skill
constraints: The article states the list "is not intended as an exhaustive account of activities or benefits"
target_learning_goals: social connection
communication
self-efficacy
engagement with grief and loss
examples: Song sharing and instrumental improvisation are named as group activities providing an appropriate way for students to communicate feelings to one another
key_sources: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061963

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Activities Done by Using Activity Based Posters on the Students' Academic Achievements, Retention Levels in Their Learning
citation: İsmail Coşkun, Cevat Eker. (2018). The Effect of Teaching Activities Done by Using Activity Based Posters on the Students' Academic Achievements, Retention Levels in Their Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(4): 585-597. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.060402
title: Activity-based poster implementation procedure for the Celebrities English unit
description: An instructional element in which ninth-grade English students prepare and present posters on unit topics in addition to regular course materials. Students received 40 minutes of brief subject information, then prepared posters in groups over 120 minutes using "pictures  and notes they had obtained from various visual sources" plus their own drawings, then presented them for 80 minutes while peers asked questions. The cycle ran regularly for six weeks alongside the teacher's guidebook, course book and workbooks.
requirements: Materials such as paper, colored pencils, colored cartons, glue and visuals related to the subject must be available
Teacher guidance on what a poster is, how to prepare and interpret it, and how to use it with visuals
A suitable classroom environment for presenting the prepared posters
constraints: Studied only in a 9th-grade English course, the Celebrities unit, over six weeks in one Anatolian high school with 60 students
target_learners: 9th-grade English language students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary and grammar of the Celebrities unit (adjectives, comparatives and superlatives, jobs, appearances)
Communication and presentation skills
examples: In the study, the experimental group received poster preparation and presentation activities for six weeks while the control group used only guidebook, course book and workbook
key_sources: İsmail Coşkun, Cevat Eker. (2018). The Effect of Teaching Activities Done by Using Activity Based Posters on the Students' Academic Achievements, Retention Levels in Their Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(4): 585-597. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.060402

article_title: Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory
citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Three-level taxonomy of pupils' environmental education: Active, Fragmentary, and Passive
description: Based on the criteria, the article distinguishes three levels of environmental education. "Active" pupils seek environmental knowledge, defend plants and animals, and treat nature "as a goal rather than the means of environmental activities". Fragmentary pupils follow rules of behaviour in nature but rarely take initiative and act only when defence involves no conflict. Passive pupils comply only under adult control, do nothing to prevent ill-treatment of natural objects, and regard nature pragmatically as a means to their goals.
requirements: Assignment to levels rests on the three-criteria diagnosis of cognitive, relational and activity indicators
constraints: Levels were identified among senior pupils in the Kazan experimental schools
target_learning_goals: environmental education level assessment
examples: Table 1 and Table 2 report the distribution of the 215 pupils across the H/M/L levels before and after the experiment
key_sources: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85

article_title: The Effectiveness of WhatsApp Mobile Learning Activities Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Knowledge Management
citation: Chokri Barhoumi. (2015). The Effectiveness of WhatsApp Mobile Learning Activities Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Knowledge Management. Contemporary Educational Technology, 6(3), 221-238. https://cedtech.net
title: Activity theory as a three-level framework for analyzing factors influencing participation in mobile-mediated online learning communities
description: The article uses activity theory as the guiding framework to design and analyze interactions in a WhatsApp-mediated learning community. It states that "Activity theory is a framework that researchers use to design and analyze interactions between members of a group and discover factors influencing their participation in online discussion." The framework operates at three levels printed in Figure 1: the technological level (tools, habits, usability), the individual level (subjects and perceived affordances), and the community level (social presence, rules, division of labor), building on Engeström's extension adding community sharing of the same object.
requirements: An activity system with subjects, tools, community, rules, and division of labor, so that participation factors can be examined at each of the three levels
constraints: The article applies the framework to a single blended course context and to factors influencing online discussion participation
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and sharing through collaborative online discussion
examples: The researcher used the framework to interpret the achievement and attitude differences by examining usability and habits, perceived affordances, and social presence, roles, and rules
key_sources: Chokri Barhoumi. (2015). The Effectiveness of WhatsApp Mobile Learning Activities Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Knowledge Management. Contemporary Educational Technology, 6(3), 221-238. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105764

article_title: The Effects of Previewing Questions, Repetition of Input, and Topic Preparation on Listening Comprehension of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Rouhi, A., Nabavi, S.-M., & Mohebbi, H. (2014). The effects of previewing questions, repetition of input, and topic preparation on listening comprehension of Iranian EFL learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 73-85. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Activate learners' schematic background knowledge of the topic before a listening task
description: Before a listening task, teachers should provide or activate background knowledge relevant to the topic, for example through short topic-related texts read in the learner's first language. In this study such topic preparation produced the highest listening scores (M = 20.56), and the article concludes that "when prepared in terms of the topic of the listening task, learners can perform better."
requirements: A short topic-related passage in the learners' first language, plus brief teacher explanation and question preview, before hearing the text once
constraints: Topic preparation in this study was delivered in Persian (learners' mother tongue); the article notes future work should examine materials presented in English
The advantage over repetition of input was not statistically significant
target_learners: Iranian high school EFL learners aged 14-17 with 4-6 years of formal English instruction
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension of monologue and dialogue texts
examples: The topic preparation group read a very short Persian text about the locations of the listening texts, heard the researcher's explanation for five minutes, previewed questions for five minutes, then listened once
key_sources: Rouhi, A., Nabavi, S.-M., & Mohebbi, H. (2014). The effects of previewing questions, repetition of input, and topic preparation on listening comprehension of Iranian EFL learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 73-85. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: Investigating the Effects of Authentic Childhood Games in Teaching English
citation: Hursen, C., & Salaz, D. (2016). Investigating the effects of authentic childhood games in teaching English. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 11(2), 58-62. http://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/cjes/
title: Use varied active activities, including authentic childhood games, to promote active participation in kindergarten classrooms
description: The article concludes that kindergarten teachers should draw on activities that engage students actively, with authentic childhood games as an effective option for teaching English vocabulary. It states "teachers can use different activities to get students participate actively in kindergarten classrooms", grounded in the experimental advantage and teachers' observations of willing participation.
requirements: Teachers need good classroom management when using authentic childhood games, as the observing teachers stated
constraints: Evidence base is a single small experimental study with 43 kindergarten students learning English vocabulary
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
examples: Over six weeks the experimental group learned each week's five English vocabulary words through authentic childhood games while the control group was taught the same topics through traditional methods
key_sources: Hursen, C., & Salaz, D. (2016). Investigating the effects of authentic childhood games in teaching English. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 11(2), 58-62. http://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/cjes/

article_title: Conducting Museum Education Activities within the Context of Developing a Nature Culture in Primary School Students: MTA Natural History Museum Example
citation: Dilli, R. (2016). Conducting museum education activities within the context of developing a nature culture in primary school students: MTA natural history museum example. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(2), 75-84. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijese.2016.292a
title: Museum education should promote active participation rather than memorization or limiting students to set statements
description: The article argues that museum education requires that students not be pushed toward memorization or confined to certain statements, and that learners actively participate in the learning processes. In the study this was enacted by encouraging students to express their feelings and thoughts through two-dimensioned works and written works such as short stories and poems during the MTA museum program.
requirements: Students must be given opportunities to express their feelings and thoughts, e.g., through artistic and written works
target_learning_goals: developing nature culture and environmental consciousness
interpreting the natural environment
examples: In the study, students were encouraged to express their feelings and thoughts by two-dimensioned works as well as by written works such as short stories and poems, and one student wrote a poem about elephants living in Turkey.
key_sources: Dilli, R. (2016). Conducting museum education activities within the context of developing a nature culture in primary school students: MTA natural history museum example. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(2), 75-84. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijese.2016.292a

article_title: Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental, Study on Limits in College Calculus
citation: Cappetta, R.W., and Zollman, A. (2013). Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Limits in College Calculus. REDIMAT – Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(3), 343-357. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.35
title: ACE teaching cycle-based experimental calculus curriculum on limits
description: An experimental curriculum modeled on the ACE (Activity, Classroom Discussion, Exercise) teaching cycle, designed to initiate reflective abstraction on the concept of limit. Each day's lesson included reflective activities done in cooperative groups, an instructor debriefing discussion, and individual exercise sets. It covered the same topics, time, and textbook sections as the traditional curriculum, with identical limit examples and the same homework assignments; the stated differences were the collaborative activities and the teacher scripted interactions.
requirements: Scripted lesson plans, class activities, class work sets, and homework sets validated by an expert panel via a Delphi method of iterations
constraints: Evaluated only against a matched traditional section at one midwestern community college
target_learning_goals: understanding of the concept of limit
examples: Both curricula were field tested for content validity and approved by an expert panel of teaching-award recipient professors
key_sources: Cappetta, R.W., and Zollman, A. (2013). Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Limits in College Calculus. REDIMAT – Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(3), 343-357. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.35

article_title: The Effect of Twitter Activities in a Blended Learning Classroom Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Achievement and Attitudes
citation: Aicha Amry. (2018). The Effect of Twitter Activities in a Blended Learning Classroom Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Achievement and Attitudes. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Activity theory (Engeström's model) as a framework for analyzing factors influencing online participation
description: The article uses activity theory, rooted in Vygotsky's historico-cultural thesis and Leontiev's three levels (operations, actions, activities), to guide data analysis and interpretation of factors influencing students' participation in online Twitter discussions. It applies Engeström's extension, in which "the subject the relations of which to the community are mediatized by rules and the division of labor," organized into six principles (subject, object orientedness, tools, community, division of labor, rules) and three levels: technological, individual, and community.
requirements: The framework requires analyzing activity in context, including the artifact mediating the activity, rather than treating individuals in isolation
constraints: The article applies the framework to a single course (Computers in instruction) with female graduate students
target_learners: female master's students in educational technology
target_learning_goals: participation in online discussions
construction and sharing of knowledge
achievement in a course on computers in instruction
examples: The researcher designed the blended course's Twitter learning activities with activity theory and interpreted achievement and attitude differences at the technological, individual, and community levels
key_sources: Aicha Amry. (2018). The Effect of Twitter Activities in a Blended Learning Classroom Guided by Activity Theory on Students' Achievement and Attitudes. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176184

article_title: The Formation of Learners' Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine
citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Active means of training for the formation of learners' interest in physics
description: The article proposes five active means of physics training: physics in nature, physics in everyday life, physics in technics, physics in science, and history of physics. Each means connects the content of educational material to phenomena or achievements outside the lesson, for example "the explanation of various natural phenomena from the point of physics view" or "examples of various scientific achievements, where knowledge of physics have been used". These means, together with active learning methods, are the components of the developed technique for forming learners' interest in physics.
requirements: Connection between the content of educational material and its meaning in life finds a permanent place in physics lessons
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: formation of learners' interest in physics and motivation to study physics
key_sources: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008

article_title: The Formation of Learners' Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine
citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Active learning methods for the formation of learners' interest in physics
description: The article selects six active methods for teaching physics according to their influence on the development of learners' thinking: heuristic conversation, creation of problematic situations, home experiments, excursions, solving crosswords, and conducting physics dictations. For example, creation of problematic situations introduces learners to activity during which they are faced with facts that contradict their experience, and home experiments let learners reproduce fundamental physics experiments so that they will feel themselves "discoverers". These methods form the second component of the developed technique.
requirements: Home experiments require safety rules, simple equipment, curiosity, accessibility, and integration in the curriculum
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: development of learners' logical and creative thinking and formation of interest in physics
key_sources: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008

article_title: Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction
citation: Sahail M. Asassfeh. (2013). Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p85
title: Acuairning: language acquisition and learning as points on a single continuum
description: The article introduces 'acuairning', a blend of acquisition and learning, as a conceptual term placing natural acquisition and formal learning on one continuum rather than treating them as dichotomous. It proposes conceptualizing the learner's experience as depending on "the type, richness, intensity, naturalness, and meaningfulness of input" rather than on the geographical EFL/ESL setting. On this view, teachers can move learners from hyper-heightened consciousness associated with formal learning toward less-heightened consciousness, aligning with communicative language teaching principles, and the difference between implicit and explicit CF becomes less significant.
requirements: The learner must receive sufficient, adequate, comprehensible input for the EFL/ESL distinction to lose value
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal inviting reconceptualization, not as an empirically tested model
target_learners: EFL learners, especially those whose exposure to English is limited to the classroom context
target_learning_goals: Grammatical accuracy in EFL writing
Balancing fluency and accuracy in language learning
examples: The author argues the native/non-native distinction is tied to competence versus performance and that intuitive knowledge is constructed through interaction rather than inherent
key_sources: Sahail M. Asassfeh. (2013). Corrective Feedback (CF) and English-Major EFL Learners' Ability in Grammatical Error Detection and Correction. English Language Teaching, 6(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p85

article_title: Students' Perception of Peer Review in an EFL Classroom
citation: Liliya Harutyunyan & María Fernanda Poveda. (2018). Students’ Perception of Peer Review in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p138
title: Academic Writing Guide and staged writing worksheets for peer review training
description: The professor-investigators created a "100+ page guide for academic writing and peer review" given to students to introduce the peer review tool and train them in academic argumentative essay writing. It is entirely in English, describes academic writing at university level and peer review as a tool for developing critical thinking, collaborative work, and essay quality, and includes structure and vocabulary exercises. It outlines four essay types, though only the argumentative essay was actively worked through. Staged worksheets ran from prewriting listing through thesis statement, outline, introduction and conclusion, first and second draft, to final version.
requirements: Time to work through the guide; time limitations meant only the argumentative essay was actively covered
constraints: Only the argumentative essay type was actively worked through on this occasion
target_learners: university EFL students at levels 7-8 (B2 CEFR)
target_learning_goals: academic argumentative essay writing
peer review skills
examples: Students produced a 500-700 word argumentative essay with a fixed four-paragraph structure of 5-8 sentences each
key_sources: Liliya Harutyunyan & María Fernanda Poveda. (2018). Students’ Perception of Peer Review in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p138

article_title: High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical but Not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea
citation: Mirko Marušić & Josip Sliško. (2014). High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical But not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. http://www.edpsycinteractive.org/topics/affect/humed.html
title: Intervene early with active learning to improve students' attitudes about physics and thinking skills
description: Because traditional physics teaching gives students the impression that logic matters for physics while hardly showing that creativity is a necessary part of doing physics, the authors argue attitudes are hard to change later. They report that both active-learning packages improved attitudes toward physics developing logical and creative thinking in a single semester, and conclude it is necessary to act as early as possible to improve students' attitudes about physics and learning physics.
requirements: Active-learning formats such as RPQ or ED replacing traditional teaching lacking laboratory exercises and experiments
constraints: Students extensively exposed to traditional methods find their attitudes difficult to change in one or two semesters of university education
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes about the impact of physics learning on logical and creative thinking
examples: Both methods provided a significant improvement in students' attitudes towards creative thinking in both genders over one semester
key_sources: Mirko Marušić & Josip Sliško. (2014). High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical But not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. http://www.edpsycinteractive.org/topics/affect/humed.html

article_title: A Comparative Study of English Language Teaching Practices at the Access Program and Public Schools
citation: Iqbal, M., & Rafi, M. S. (2018). A Comparative Study of English Language Teaching Practices at the Access Program and Public Schools. Bulletin of Education and Research, 40(3), 231-249. https://pu.edu.pk/journals/index.php/ber/
title: Access classroom practices: activity-based, technology-supported English teaching without examination pressure
description: The Access classroom combines multimedia-rich facilities (multimedia, computer, CDs, white board, UPS) with activity-based teaching and continuous rather than high-stakes assessment. Teachers "teach English language through; showing movies, role plays, group work, peer work, songs, video and board games etc. which are not common in Pakistani public schools." Teachers and students may rearrange the classroom to their needs, and both are free of pass-fail examination pressure, which the article contrasts with the chalk-and-talk, Grammar Translation Method of public schools.
requirements: Modern teaching gadgets (multimedia, computer, CDs, white board, UPS), teachers trained by local and American trainers, and absence of pass-fail examinations with continuous assessment instead
constraints: The article describes this pattern as operating in the after-school Access setting; these practices are reported as not common in Pakistani public schools
target_learners: Secondary-age English learners from low socio-economic backgrounds in after-school classes
target_learning_goals: Development of English linguistic competence and performance across listening, speaking, reading and writing
examples: Access teachers were trained by local trainers and by American trainers in Pakistan and in the United States, and used movies, role plays, group and peer work, songs and games
key_sources: Iqbal, M., & Rafi, M. S. (2018). A Comparative Study of English Language Teaching Practices at the Access Program and Public Schools. Bulletin of Education and Research, 40(3), 231-249. https://pu.edu.pk/journals/index.php/ber/

article_title: Graduation Coaching in a Rural District School
citation: Zeller, P. J., Carpenter, S., Lacefield, W. E., & Applegate, E. B. (2013). Graduation coaching in a rural district school. GEAR UP Learning Centers, Western Michigan University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555555
title: Activity Reporting System for coaching process documentation and fidelity monitoring
description: An Excel-based Activity Reporting System with three components — a Daily Log, an Activity Log, and a Case Notes Log — allowed the coach to "maintain electronic case notes and logs and to track the number, type, and duration of coaching contacts and activities." The system documented that 79% of the coach's available time went to intervention and provided "data validation controls to maintain the accuracy and integrity of the information collected." It served both intervention management and embedded formative and summative evaluation.
requirements: Coach diligence in recording service data after each contact
Data validation controls within each component
constraints: Additional time contributed by referral support services personnel is not captured by the system
target_learners: at-risk 9th-grade students on a coaching caseload
target_learning_goals: monitoring intervention fidelity
formative and summative program evaluation
examples: Daily Log data recorded planning time and contact time in minutes for student, parent, and teacher contacts, plus caseload status and intervention service type
key_sources: Zeller, P. J., Carpenter, S., Lacefield, W. E., & Applegate, E. B. (2013). Graduation coaching in a rural district school. GEAR UP Learning Centers, Western Michigan University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1033208

article_title: Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and Its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Ibrahim, H. G. (2017). Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(8), 185-194. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1142431.pdf
title: Author-developed 31-question achievement test covering four cognitive levels with reliability of 0.84
description: The study prepared an achievement test in the form of multiple choice and true or false questions to measure students' abilities in remembering, understanding, analyzing and applying the course content. The final test included 31 questions distributed as 9 for remembering, 8 for understanding, 7 for application, and 7 for analysis, with one point per correct answer (maximum 31, minimum 0). The reliability coefficient reached 0.84 and intrinsic validity 0.89, which the article describes as acceptable.
requirements: Application to an exploratory sample to identify appropriate time and ensure validity and reliability
constraints: Designed for the specified educational content of the Computer Course
target_learning_goals: cognitive achievement at the levels of remembering, understanding, application and analysis
examples: The test time was calculated as 36 minutes using the equation taking the mean of the first and last student's times (32 and 53 minutes respectively)

Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers. article_title: Effect of Jigsaw II, Reading-Writing-Presentation, and Computer Animations on the Teaching of "Light" Unit
citation: Koç, Y., Yildiz, E., Çaliklar, Ş., & Şimşek, Ü. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw II, reading-writing-presentation, and computer animations on the teaching of “Light” Unit. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2861
title: Active learning methods influence epistemological beliefs about sources and testability of knowledge
description: The article proposes that the methods and techniques used in learning-teaching environments are extensively influential on epistemological beliefs, which are considered an area of individual differences. It argues that through Jigsaw II and animations, students realized that the only source of knowledge is not the teacher or the book, that knowledge can be accessed through various sources, and that the correctness of knowledge is testable. These recognitions made a positive influence on their epistemological beliefs.
requirements: Instructional methods that expose students to multiple sources of knowledge beyond teacher and textbook
constraints: Reading-writing-presentation method did not influence epistemological beliefs, possibly because students had difficulty working in groups and tended to work individually
target_learning_goals: epistemological beliefs about sources of knowledge and testability of knowledge
key_sources: Koç, Y., Yildiz, E., Çaliklar, Ş., & Şimşek, Ü. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw II, reading-writing-presentation, and computer animations on the teaching of “Light” Unit. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2861

article_title: Looking for a Needle in a Haystack: CALL and Advanced Language Proficiency
citation: Burston, J., & Arispe, K. (2018). Looking for a Needle in a Haystack: CALL and Advanced Language Proficiency. CALICO Journal, 35(1). https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.31594
title: ACTFL Performance Descriptors and Can-Do Statements as external criteria for establishing competence level, task difficulty, and appropriateness
description: The authors adopt the ACTFL Performance Descriptors (PD) and NCSSFL-ACTFL Can-Do Statements (CDS) as external criteria for establishing student competence level, task difficulty, and appropriateness. The PD document was used to "determine the mode of communication in which students engaged: interpretive, interpersonal or presentational" and to analyze domain descriptions at the advanced level. The CDSs were used to corroborate that the objective of the task was at the proficiency level or just one sub-level beyond the participant's competence level.
requirements: Researchers must independently code studies using PD and CDS documents, determining mode of communication and analyzing domain descriptions at the advanced level.
constraints: The choice of ACTFL guidelines admittedly and intentionally biases assessment of learning outcomes in the direction of explicit qualitative descriptors and quantitative testing.
target_learning_goals: Advanced-level foreign language proficiency
key_sources: Burston, J., & Arispe, K. (2018). Looking for a Needle in a Haystack: CALL and Advanced Language Proficiency. CALICO Journal, 35(1). https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.31594

article_title: Action Research in Urban Schools: Empowerment, Transformation, and Challenges
citation: Razfar, A. (2011). Action Research in Urban Schools: Empowerment, Transformation, and Challenges. Teacher Education Quarterly, 38(4), 25-44. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ949874
title: Action research as a critical, collaborative, ground-up paradigm for teacher empowerment and transformation
description: The article defines action research as systematic inquiry conducted by teachers to understand and improve their own school contexts, drawing on Freire's critical pedagogy. It frames action research as a 'critical' tool for empowering educators and underserved communities to define and analyze their own social problems, develop new understandings, and act. Change is assumed to come from the ground up rather than top-down, and inquiry must be a collaborative partnership with colleagues at the school. The article further draws on Cooper and Gause's concept of 'collaborative activism' as the essence of transformative leadership.
requirements: Teachers must be active in a K-12 educational setting where they develop and implement an action plan appropriate for that context
Inquiry must be a collaborative partnership with other colleagues at the school
constraints: The paradigm was developed and applied in the context of a master's program at a Hispanic-serving liberal arts college serving urban educators
target_learning_goals: Developing critical inquiry skills
Fostering teacher empowerment and transformative practice
Building collaborative partnerships
key_sources: Razfar, A. (2011). Action Research in Urban Schools: Empowerment, Transformation, and Challenges. Teacher Education Quarterly, 38(4), 25-44. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ960617

article_title: Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Zand Vahid, Bazi Ramin, Keshmiri Fatemeh. (2026). Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09628-3
title: Assessing Competency in Evidence-Based Medicine (ACE) tool, Persian version
description: The ACE tool, developed by Ilic et al., was used to assess EBM competency. It "consists of a clinical scenario followed by 15 dichotomous questions assessing four domains of EBM competency: clinical question formulation, evidence searching, critical appraisal, and application of evidence to patient care". Each item was scored as correct (1) or incorrect (0), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 15. The Persian version has previously demonstrated acceptable validity and reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79). Assessments were independently scored by two trained researchers blinded to group allocation, with excellent inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa > 0.90).
requirements: Two trained researchers blinded to group allocation for independent scoring
constraints: Assesses competency through simulated clinical scenarios rather than direct observation in authentic clinical practice
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clerkship rotations
target_learning_goals: EBM competency across question formulation, evidence searching, critical appraisal, and application of evidence
examples: Administered one week before and one week after the intervention period in this study
key_sources: Zand Vahid, Bazi Ramin, Keshmiri Fatemeh. (2026). Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09628-3

article_title: The effects of flipped classroom versus lecture-based learning on academic performance and perceptions of classroom environment among nursing students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yousefi Mahboubeh Sadat, Fooladzadeh Dehghan Mohsen, Ilkhani Mahnaz, Khajoei Rahimeh, Heidari Saeide, Jokar Mozhgan. (2026). The effects of flipped classroom versus lecture-based learning on academic performance and perceptions of classroom environment among nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09746-y
title: Integrate active, student-centered pedagogies such as the flipped classroom into nursing curricula
description: The article's conclusion recommends that nursing programs integrate active, student-centered approaches: "These results highlight the potential value of integrating active, student-centered pedagogies into nursing curricula." In the trial this meant pre-class videos and slides with in-class case-based group problem solving, question-and-answer sessions, and discussion, with the instructor acting as facilitator. The recommendation is qualified by the authors' call for larger, more diverse samples.
requirements: Students need access to devices and the Internet to retrieve pre-class materials
Instructors need pre-class materials and structured in-class scenarios aligned with session objectives
constraints: Evidence base is a single-institution trial with small sample, four sessions only, and no long-term follow-up
target_learning_goals: fluids and electrolytes knowledge
application of theoretical knowledge to clinical scenarios

This includes shifting from lecturer to facilitator, structuring group dynamics, and creating psychologically supportive environments. description: The article distinguishes two broad learning approaches in medical education. "Passive learning is the traditional lecture-based, one-way information transfer with minimal feedback and interaction, often resulting in memorization through rehearsal"; "active learning, in contrast, engages students through case-based discussions, simulations, and flipped classrooms, fostering an active role for the students and promoting critical thinking and long-term retention". title: Conceptual framework linking pedagogical design quality and implementation feasibility to learning outcomes and adoptability at scale
description: The review proposes a conceptual framework (Figure 2) in which pedagogical design quality and implementation feasibility mediate between intervention features and outcomes. Design-quality inputs include "Threshold competence requirement", "Debriefing dividend", and "Preparation paradox"; feasibility inputs include scalability constraints, resource intensity, and faculty time and coordination. Pedagogical design quality points to observed learning outcomes, and implementation feasibility points to adoptability at scale, which also depends on learning outcomes.
requirements: Pedagogical design quality factors (debriefing, sequencing, task-complexity match) must be present for favourable learning outcomes
constraints: Framework synthesises evidence from 20 studies in pre-licensure diabetes education; the review notes few studies reported equity-related data

Clinical skills and reasoning
Learner engagement and self-efficacy

citation: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033
title: Active dissemination, not passive diffusion, is required for adoption of GenAI item-writing innovations, scaffolded within educators' zone of proximal development
description: Drawing on diffusion-of-innovations literature and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, the article argues that passive diffusion alone is often insufficient for spreading GenAI item-writing practices. If existing item-writing skills represent the zone of achieved development, prompt crafting lies within educators' zone of proximal development, "achievable through structured guidance, institutional support, and exemplar modelling." Scaffolded prompts serve as an educational bridge from dependence to autonomy while maintaining assessment standards.
requirements: Institutional, structured engagement with contextualised evidence; deliberate alignment of innovation with educator beliefs and professional values
constraints: Even well-designed innovations frequently fail to spread effectively in educational contexts; availability of structured prompts does not guarantee their use
target_learning_goals: Developing autonomous prompt-engineering competence
examples: In the authors' faculty development workshops, when participants were invited to share prompts previously used for item-writing, none reported applying pre-published examples

title: Active Learning–GenAI Synergy Framework
description: The article's theoretical contribution positions generative AI tools within Kolb's experiential learning cycle and active learning principles, so that AI functions "as cognitive partners, metacognitive mirrors, and equity tools" rather than as a standalone intervention. The framework structures AI use around weekly experiential cycles (drafting with AI, ethical reflection, peer discussion, revision) and an Ethical Integration Protocol. The authors conclude "the pedagogical framework mediating AI interaction—rather than the technology itself—determines educational outcomes".
requirements: Sustained engagement over repeated experiential learning cycles; the article reports cognitive partnerships required approximately 6-8 weeks to develop effectively
constraints: The cultural and institutional specificity of Pakistani higher education may limit generalizability, requiring cross-cultural validation

target_learning_goals: EFL/ESL writing proficiency
metacognitive awareness and ethical AI use
digital literacy

title: Use objective actigraphy with night-to-night resolution rather than retrospective subjective questionnaires when relating sleep to academic outcomes
description: The article argues that objective, high-resolution sleep measurement reveals associations with academic performance that subjective questionnaires miss. It notes that "actigraphy can provide high-sensitivity sleep patterns by night-to-night or weekday-weekend resolution," whereas PSQI relies on one-month retrospective self-report vulnerable to bias and misperception. The authors suggest "a relatively high-resolution and precise sleep measure tool (actigraphy device here) can be used and provide more valuable information in the sleep study."

Sleep diaries or objective temperature/illumination cues to label bedtime and wake time
constraints: PSG remains the gold standard but is difficult to implement in home settings and costly for long-term recording, per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding sleep-related predictors of academic performance
examples: 33 students wore an actigraphy device for 14 consecutive days while completing the PSQI, BDI, and PSS and daily sleep diaries, with the final exam held two weeks after the recordings ended

Students in groups of five to six rotate through scenarios with pre-allocated roles, followed by a 15-minute debrief; scenarios end in cardiac arrest prompting ALS initiation. title: 12-week active-break intervention protocol for university management students
description: The intervention comprises four 15-minute active breaks per day for 12 weeks, "performed collectively at predetermined times coordinated with the course schedule, approximately every 60–90 min of class activity", combining light-to-moderate aerobic exercise, resistance work, stretching, breathing and mindfulness. Table 1 structures the program in three phases: mobilization (weeks 1–4), intensification with breathing (weeks 5–8), and optimization of resilience with interval training and mindfulness (weeks 9–12). Instructors monitored duration and heart rate with a Polar Vantage V2 watch to keep intensity light-to-moderate.

constraints: Activities limited to light-to-moderate intensity to minimize risk; the pilot sample was small, homogeneous management students, limiting generalizability
target_learners: university students in management training courses
target_learning_goals: stress management and resilience
executive functioning
decision-making competence
examples: Weeks 1–4 used stretching and neck mobilization; weeks 9–12 used 30-second circuits (jumping jacks, mountain climbers) plus square breathing and mindful walking

citation: Bradley LJ, Meyer KE, Kerr MS, Maddux SD, Heck AJ, Reeves RE, Handler EK. (2025). Do active learning techniques promote higher academic performance in an online graduate anatomy course? Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70066

description: The study concludes that active learning's academic performance benefits are driven mainly by the processes of preparing and teaching one's assigned content, not by listening to peers teach. As the authors put it, "the benefits of active learning techniques on academic performance are primarily attributable to active techniques that require students to teach the content specifically covered by the examination questions." All four techniques studied shared this teaching/learning phase structure, yet only taught content showed higher scores.

constraints: Passively receiving peer instruction showed no performance improvement; results come from a single university, single cohort, one anatomy course, and asynchronous online delivery

target_learners: graduate health-professions students in online courses
target_learning_goals: retention and examination performance on specifically taught course content
examples: Across 5 units and 15 objectives, students who taught an objective's content performed significantly higher on that objective's examination question than students who taught other objectives, regardless of which of the four techniques was used

target_learning_goals: surgical competence and complication outcomes following focused procedure-specific training
examples: The study compared 6-year revision rates for 274 knees operated on by PFA-trained trial surgeons vs 208 knees operated on by nontrial surgeons, finding an adjusted RR of 0.35, and used this to argue registry comparisons may be confounded by training
