article_title: Exploring the Challenges of Implementing Managers' Competency Assessment Center in the Health System: A Phenomenological Study.
citation: Naghshi Maryam, Janati Ali, Raoofi Samira, Khodayari-Zarnaq Rahim. (2024). Exploring the Challenges of Implementing Managers' Competency Assessment Center in the Health System: A Phenomenological Study. Ethiopian Journal of Health Sciences. https://doi.org/10.4314/ejhs.v34i6.2
title: Two-theme taxonomy of Assessment Center implementation challenges: internal and external
description: The article organizes the challenges of implementing Managers' Competency Assessment Centers in Iran's health system into a two-theme taxonomy derived from conventional content analysis of 33 semi-structured interviews. Internal challenges "directly affecting the performance of the assessment center" comprise five sub-themes (assessed managers, assessors, assessment tools, assessment process, and development training courses); external challenges are "often rooted in organizational beliefs and culture or political approaches" and comprise extra-organizational, organizational, cultural, and political sub-themes.
requirements: Derived from conventional content analysis of semi-structured interviews with executive officers, assessors, assessed managers, and senior managers of the Assessment Center
constraints: Findings come from one Assessment Center context in Iran's health system; the authors note the sample was restricted to a specific Assessment Center, which may impact generalizability
target_learners: Health system managers assessed at operational and middle levels
Assessors and executive officers of competency assessment centers
target_learning_goals: Selection, promotion, and development of managerial competencies
examples: The study categorized interview data into 2 main themes and 9 sub-themes using MAXQDA-18 software

article_title: Training supported by simulated persons to promote the development of specific communication skills in advance care planning.
citation: Götze K, Otten-Marré S, Loupatatzis B, in der Schmitten J. (2025). Training supported by simulated persons to promote the development of specific communication skills in advance care planning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 42(1):Doc11. https://doi.org/10.3205/zma001735
title: Ten extensive role scripts for simulated persons in the ACP facilitator qualification
description: Ten role scripts of about 10,000 words were developed by ACP coaches in collaboration with an SP coach, based on real people in ACP conversations. Scripts formulate the role's biography, emotional and mental situation, attitudes and ACP-relevant facts, and include acting aids such as 'inner monologues and non-verbal and verbal cues such as posture or voice modulation'.
requirements: Medical facts must be combined with their subjective significance for the particular role to achieve as homogeneous an interpretation as possible by different SPs
constraints: In roles intended to train more complex communication skills, medical details take a back seat to life story, thoughts and emotions
target_learners: Simulated persons, both professional actors and trained laypersons, rehearsing ACP roles
target_learning_goals: Standardised portrayal of ACP conversation roles, including emotions, inner attitude and body language
examples: Figure 2 shows exemplary sections from the role scripts, including inner monologues and non-verbal and verbal cues
key_sources: Götze K, Otten-Marré S, Loupatatzis B, in der Schmitten J. (2025). Training supported by simulated persons to promote the development of specific communication skills in advance care planning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 42(1):Doc11. https://doi.org/10.3205/zma001735

article_title: Training supported by simulated persons to promote the development of specific communication skills in advance care planning.
citation: Götze K, Otten-Marré S, Loupatatzis B, in der Schmitten J. (2025). Training supported by simulated persons to promote the development of specific communication skills in advance care planning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 42(1):Doc11. https://doi.org/10.3205/zma001735
title: Run SP-supported ACP training in small groups of at most four participants with one SP and one qualified ACP coach per group
description: Role-plays take place in small groups of a maximum of four participants, each guided by a qualified ACP coach with one SP per group. Advance rotation plans keep each participant with the same SP in the same roles, SPs receive a separate retreat room to prepare and get in and out of role, and a debriefing is offered after performances.
requirements: One SP must be available per small group at the appropriate times in addition to the ACP coach, and an SP coach must be available during and after assignments for questions and debriefing
constraints: Simulation can reactivate SPs' own experiences of serious illness or loss, and emotionally charged, possibly hostile, behaviour towards SPs occurs, requiring special attention from ACP and SP coaches
target_learners: ACP facilitator course participants and the simulated persons supporting them
target_learning_goals: Awareness of the importance of the conversational setting and observation of verbal and non-verbal communication
examples: Continuous on-site quality assurance by SP coaches was found necessary after two to three performances, at new course centres, and when introducing new SPs or new roles

article_title: Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing.
citation: Huang Yue, Jia Jin, Zhan Jun, Li Bo, Gu Qiong, Li Zhengyu. (2024). Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05936-8
title: Use accessible, low-cost animal-tissue models to give trainees realistic surgical practice before operating on patients
description: The article argues that because commercial simulators are costly and "their application limited due to high cost and low-grade simulation", while "Animal models can highly mimic human tissues, and their cost is much lower", choosing an appropriate animal model creates a real-life experience that helps trainees practice surgical skills before performing them on patients. The porcine stomach model (total cost ￥41) embodies this principle for obstetric skills.
requirements: An animal tissue locally available at low cost
Pre-processing to make the tissue safe and usable
Supervision by trainers during incision, repair and suturing steps
constraints: Limited where porcine or other animal stomachs are not readily available
No hemorrhage simulation
Short shelf life of fresh tissue
target_learning_goals: Fundamental obstetric surgical skills prior to supervised practice on patients
examples: The porcine stomach model is described as suitable both for hospital simulation centers and as a homemade simulation model, and the same stomach can be sutured several times by a group of students
key_sources: Huang Yue, Jia Jin, Zhan Jun, Li Bo, Gu Qiong, Li Zhengyu. (2024). Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05936-8

article_title: Creating a safe space: medical students' perspectives on using actor simulations for learning communication skills.
citation: Antila Asta Kristiina, Lindblom Sari, Louhiala Pekka, Pyörälä Eeva. (2024). Creating a safe space: medical students’ perspectives on using actor simulations for learning communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06184-6
title: Small-group actor simulation with structured reflective debriefing for communication skills
description: The course pattern places simulations in small groups with a professional actor and a clinical teacher: "The simulation involves a small group of six to ten students, an actor, and a clinical teacher." Students take turns playing the doctor while others observe; the actor improvises from short vignettes. After each simulation, a reflective debriefing facilitated by the clinical teacher proceeds from the student doctor's perspective, then the actor's, then the whole group, enabling participation, observation, feedback, and reflection.
requirements: A trained improvising actor portraying the patient
A clinical teacher facilitating the debriefing
A small group of six to ten students
constraints: Some students found long feedback discussions uncomfortable and views on time allocation between simulations and feedback varied
target_learning_goals: doctor-patient communication
handling challenging encounters
breaking bad news
examples: Scenarios included shared decision-making, unmotivated patients, patient fears, medical errors, and breaking bad news
key_sources: Antila Asta Kristiina, Lindblom Sari, Louhiala Pekka, Pyörälä Eeva. (2024). Creating a safe space: medical students’ perspectives on using actor simulations for learning communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06184-6

article_title: The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition.
citation: Lebert, A., & Vilarroya, Ó. (2024). The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition. Ann NY Acad Sci, 1541, 37–52. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.15238
title: Use active learning rather than traditional lecturing, favoring smaller classes and upper-level courses where effects are largest
description: The article recommends active learning — instructional methods involving students as active participants rather than passive recipients — as the practical implementation of EL strategies and as aligned with enactivist principles. It reviews meta-analytic evidence that "Student performance on assessment scores was found to be higher under active instruction in a proportion similar to the Freeman et al. study", supporting active formats across STEM and humanities settings.
requirements: Instruction must involve students as active participants through real-world roles, projects, simulations, problem- or case-based work, or small-team collaboration
constraints: The article notes the relative beneficial effect is smaller in larger classes and introductory courses, so class size and course level moderate expected gains
target_learners: undergraduate and college students in STEM and in humanities and social science programs
target_learning_goals: improving examination and assessment performance through active engagement with material
examples: The article cites Freeman et al.'s 225-study meta-analysis and Kozanitis and Nenciovici's 104-study meta-analysis as the evidence base for the recommendation.
key_sources: Lebert, A., & Vilarroya, Ó. (2024). The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition. Ann NY Acad Sci, 1541, 37–52. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.15238

article_title: Design, implementation and evaluation of e-learning program for common diseases to smartphone-based medical students: at a developing university.
citation: niromand Elham, Mansoory Meysam Siyah, Ramezani Ghobad, Khazaei Mohammad Rasool. (2024). Design, implementation and evaluation of e-learning program for common diseases to smartphone-based medical students: at a developing university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-05023-4
title: Four-phase action research cycle for developing mobile medical education: needs assessment, application design, training, and evaluation
description: The study used "an action research approach, divided into four phases: needs assessment, application design, training, and evaluation". Needs assessment gathered faculty and student nominations of diseases; design included content development, expert validation and three-step application design (server, application, management panel); training involved video production, a Telegram learning group and app installation; evaluation combined exam scores and a student questionnaire. The authors frame this as integrating research with the educational situation to improve the education process.
requirements: participation of teaching faculty, instructional specialists, a filming team, and a software development team
expert validation of recorded content before final production
constraints: the reported cycle produced content for only 15 diseases given "financial and time constraints"
target_learning_goals: common disease education suitable for virtual and mobile teaching
examples: Ten faculty members listed candidate diseases; 30 interns prioritized the top 20; 15 were selected for content production

article_title: Relationships between psychological characteristics, academic fit and engagement with academic performance in veterinary medical students.
citation: Muca Edlira, Molino Monica, Ghislieri Chiara, Baratta Mario, Odore Rosangela, Bergero Domenico, Valle Emanuela. (2023). Relationships between psychological characteristics, academic fit and engagement with academic performance in veterinary medical students. BMC Veterinary Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12917-023-03695-0
title: Academic fit as the educational form of person–environment fit theory
description: The article applies person–environment fit theory to education, where "Academic fit was firstly described by Schmitt et al. (2008) and refers to the person–environment fit in the context of an educational environment". It is defined as how a chosen course fits a student's interests and needs, and the article embeds it in a model in which psychological characteristics shape fit, which in turn shapes well-being (engagement, exhaustion) and performance. The framework treats person and environment as mutually influencing.
requirements: Measurement of perceived fit with validated scales (here 6 items, Cronbach's alpha 0.79) alongside measures of psychological characteristics and well-being
constraints: Studied here in a cross-sectional design with veterinary students, so causal direction between fit and outcomes is not established
target_learners: veterinary medical students (years 1–4, University of Turin)
target_learning_goals: academic performance (GPA)
student well-being (engagement and exhaustion)
examples: The study tested a full SEM in which academic fit mediated between internal locus of control/self-efficacy and engagement, exhaustion and GPA
key_sources: Muca Edlira, Molino Monica, Ghislieri Chiara, Baratta Mario, Odore Rosangela, Bergero Domenico, Valle Emanuela. (2023). Relationships between psychological characteristics, academic fit and engagement with academic performance in veterinary medical students. BMC Veterinary Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12917-023-03695-0

article_title: Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children.
citation: Gallen Courtney L., Schaerlaeken Simon, Younger Jessica W., Project iLEAD Consortium Younger Jessica Wise, O’Laughlin Kristine D., Anguera Joaquin A., Bunge Silvia A., Ferrer Emilio E., Hoeft Fumiko, McCandliss Bruce D., Mishra Jyoti, Rosenberg-Lee Miriam, Gazzaley Adam, Uncapher Melina R., Anguera Joaquin A., Gazzaley Adam. (2023). Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-29427-w
title: ACE-C continuous performance task (CPT) for group-administered sustained attention assessment in classrooms
description: The Adaptive Cognitive Evaluation Classroom (ACE-C) battery includes a CPT adapted from the Test of Variables of Attention for iPad administration in group school settings. Participants "press a button with the index finger on their dominant hand when the symbol appeared at the top of the screen (target) and to withhold responses when it appeared at the bottom". It has a 'sustained' condition with targets on 33.3% of trials and an 'impulsive' condition with targets on 66.6% of trials, and yields RT, RTV and d-prime per condition. Adaptive algorithms with a psychometric staircase allow repeated assessment without floor or ceiling effects.
requirements: Administered on iPads with trained researchers facilitating group sessions; data cleaned by excluding no-response and anticipatory (RT < 200 ms) trials and RT-based outliers (outside three MADs of the grade median)
constraints: The article states the sustained attention measure "was limited to a digital version of a continuous performance task (CPT) completed on an iPad"
target_learning_goals: assessment of sustained attention as a component of executive function in school contexts
examples: Administered to 725 students in group sessions of 7 to 83 students lasting approximately 50 minutes, in classrooms, libraries, cafeterias, and gymnasiums
key_sources: Gallen Courtney L., Schaerlaeken Simon, Younger Jessica W., Project iLEAD Consortium Younger Jessica Wise, O’Laughlin Kristine D., Anguera Joaquin A., Bunge Silvia A., Ferrer Emilio E., Hoeft Fumiko, McCandliss Bruce D., Mishra Jyoti, Rosenberg-Lee Miriam, Gazzaley Adam, Uncapher Melina R., Anguera Joaquin A., Gazzaley Adam. article_title: Bronchoscopy simulation training in the post-pandemic world.
citation: Vieira Lais Meirelles Nicoliello, Camargos Paulo Augusto Moreira, Ibiapina Cássio da Cunha. (2022). Bronchoscopy simulation training in the post-pandemic world. Jornal Brasileiro de Pneumologia. https://doi.org/10.36416/1806-3756/e20210361
title: AccuTouch Endoscopy Simulator: high-fidelity virtual bronchoscopy simulator with automated performance metrics
description: The AccuTouch Endoscopy Simulator (Immersion Medical) is a high-fidelity virtual bronchoscopy simulator consisting of a flexible scope, a computer with monitor and software, a face-replica interface with nasal access, and hardware detecting operator movements to simulate mechanical resistance, coughing, and respiratory movements. "At the end of the examination, the equipment provides metrics related to the performance of the trainee, including procedure time, “red out” time, number of contacts with the bronchial walls, bronchial segments inspected, and use of the suction button, thus ensuring feedback." It was used in most of the studies the review examined, with positive results.
requirements: Computer with monitor and simulation software
Hardware for detecting the movements performed by the machine operator
constraints: Virtual simulators can cost as much as USD 100,000.00, which the review suggests solving by sharing equipment among institutions
target_learning_goals: flexible bronchoscopy technique
airway navigation and inspection
procedural efficiency and dexterity
examples: The review states this simulator was used in most of the studies reviewed, with positive results, and that it can reproduce multiple clinical scenarios, inject lidocaine aliquots, and perform biopsies
key_sources: Vieira Lais Meirelles Nicoliello, Camargos Paulo Augusto Moreira, Ibiapina Cássio da Cunha. (2022). Bronchoscopy simulation training in the post-pandemic world. Jornal Brasileiro de Pneumologia. https://doi.org/10.36416/1806-3756/e20210361

article_title: Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education.
citation: Driessen, E. P., Knight, J. K., Smith, M. K., & Ballen, C. J. (2020). Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(4), ar52. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-04-0068
title: A working definition of active learning for undergraduate biology: an interactive, engaging process implemented through nine strategy types
description: The article constructs a working definition from the summarized input of 148 literature articles and 105 community survey responses: "Active learning is an interactive and engaging process for students that may be implemented through the employment of strategies that involve metacognition, discussion, group work, formative assessment, practicing core competencies, live-action visuals, conceptual class design, worksheets, and/or games." The definition is intended to be used confidently by the BER community because it is based on an average of literature and instructor responses.
requirements: The definition is grounded in BER literature and community input from undergraduate biology education; the article states it cannot be generalized across disciplines
constraints: Definitions and strategies were solicited from the BER community only, so results may not generalize to other DBER subjects or to instructors without a BER background
target_learning_goals: Transparency and reproducibility of teaching practices and research findings in biology education
examples: The definition appears in Box 1 of the article and synthesizes the 10 definition categories developed by open coding of literature and survey definitions
key_sources: Driessen, E. P., Knight, J. K., Smith, M. K., & Ballen, C. J. (2020). Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(4), ar52. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-04-0068

article_title: Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education.
citation: Driessen, E. P., Knight, J. K., Smith, M. K., & Ballen, C. J. (2020). Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(4), ar52. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-04-0068
title: Active-Learning Strategy Guide: a reference defining 300+ active-learning strategies
description: The article introduces the Active-Learning Strategy Guide, a list of unique strategies collected from the literature and surveys with definitions from published literature or dictionary definitions. The article states: "The utility of this list, which we call the Active-Learning Strategy Guide can also be used by the education research community and disciplinary practitioners interested in learning about active-learning strategies." A living-document version is maintained online with community contributions welcome.
requirements: Definitions for each unique strategy were needed to categorize strategies reliably, so the guide provides definitions drawn from published literature or dictionary definitions
constraints: The article notes that strategies used and efficacy measured in studies may vary based on fidelity of implementation
target_learning_goals: Defining, elaborating, and providing specificity when using the term active learning to characterize teaching practices
examples: The guide defines each unique strategy (Supplemental Appendix B) using published literature or dictionary definitions (Supplemental Appendix C), with a living-document version accepting community submissions

article_title: Improving Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Biology Students through a Scalable Peer Mentorship Program.
citation: Wilton Mike, Katz Daniel, Clairmont Anthony, Gonzalez-Nino Eduardo, Foltz Kathy R., Christoffersen Rolf E. (2021). Improving Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Biology Students through a Scalable Peer Mentorship Program. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-02-0039
title: 22-item academic habit complexity survey instrument
description: The authors developed a novel, program-specific 22-item instrument measuring "academic habit complexity", the construct of implementing multiple academic habits for success in CHEM 1A. Items were authored and fit to a Rasch model, with validity evidence drawn from ethnographic observation, cognitive interviews, relationships to other variables, and other data. Constructs originated from BIOME classroom ethnography and focus group discussions with first-year biology students, and the latent regression uses the instrument's logit scale to estimate program effects while accounting for measurement error.
requirements: Rasch model fit of item responses as a precondition for the latent regression modeling strategy
constraints: The article states the instrument may be uniquely tailored to the academic context of students in this major and may not apply to other programs, and it was only tested with three cohorts of biology majors at one institution
target_learning_goals: measuring students' adoption and diversity of effective academic habits
examples: An average non-BIOME student was estimated to have a 51% chance of endorsing reworking CHEM 1A problems from tests and quizzes versus 59% for an equivalent BIOME student

article_title: Effects of Active Learning Education on Arterial Stiffness of Older Adults with Low Health Literacy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Uemura Kazuki, Yamada Minoru, Kuzuya Masafumi, Okamoto Hiroshi. (2021). Effects of Active Learning Education on Arterial Stiffness of Older Adults with Low Health Literacy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis. https://doi.org/10.5551/jat.58354
title: Use active learning health education, rather than passive didactic instruction, to promote health behavior change in older adults with low health literacy
description: The article recommends structuring health education so learners search topics, discuss ideas in small groups, plan behavioral changes, implement healthy behaviors, and self-monitor, rather than passively listening. The program involved "participation in activities (e.g., discussion, presentation, planning) rather than passive listening". The authors argue this promotes sustainable behavioral change and self-management.
requirements: Weekly sessions with small groups of 4 to 5 participants, homework searching assigned topics, group discussion, behavioral-change planning, and self-monitoring of physical activity
constraints: Effects demonstrated over 24 weeks in community-dwelling older adults with low health literacy; maintenance beyond intervention cessation was not assessed
target_learners: community-dwelling older adults with low health literacy
target_learning_goals: health promotion behaviors including physical activity, diet/nutrition, and cognitive activity; self-management of healthy lifestyle
examples: Participants were given homework to search assigned topics, raised and discussed ideas in the subsequent class, planned a behavioral change, and self-monitored physical activity with an accelerometer
key_sources: Uemura Kazuki, Yamada Minoru, Kuzuya Masafumi, Okamoto Hiroshi. (2021). Effects of Active Learning Education on Arterial Stiffness of Older Adults with Low Health Literacy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis. https://doi.org/10.5551/jat.58354

article_title: Effects of Active Learning Education on Arterial Stiffness of Older Adults with Low Health Literacy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Uemura Kazuki, Yamada Minoru, Kuzuya Masafumi, Okamoto Hiroshi. (2021). Effects of Active Learning Education on Arterial Stiffness of Older Adults with Low Health Literacy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis. https://doi.org/10.5551/jat.58354
title: 24-week weekly 90-minute active learning health promotion program with group work and self-monitoring
description: A weekly 90-minute class for 24 weeks addressing "the role of exercise, diet/nutrition, and cognitive activity in health promotion among older adults". Participants searched assigned topics as homework, discussed ideas in small groups of 4 to 5, planned behavioral changes, and self-monitored physical activity using an accelerometer recorded in a notebook. The median attendance rate was 91.7%.
requirements: Small groups of 4 to 5 participants; homework topic search between sessions; accelerometer self-monitoring with notebook records
constraints: Compared against a didactic health education class covering similar themes; effects assessed only at baseline and week 24
target_learners: older adults aged 65 and older with low health literacy
target_learning_goals: healthy lifestyle planning, self-management, and behavior change in daily life
examples: Group work results were summarized for the entire class, and the extent to which participants led a healthy lifestyle was regularly reviewed as part of group work

article_title: The development and pilot testing of an ACP simulation-based communication-training program: Feasibility and acceptability.
citation: Chen Jui-O; Chang Shu-Chen; Lin Chiu-Chu. (2021). The development and pilot testing of an ACP simulation-based communication-training program: Feasibility and acceptability. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254982
title: ACP-SCT program: a three-axis simulation-based communication training program for nurses
description: The ACP-SCT program is a three-week, twelve-hour training program for hemodialysis nurses built on three axes: professional knowledge of ACP legislation and advance directives, communication skills practiced through scenario simulation and role play guided by the PREPARED model, and debriefing with weekly reflective journals. The article states "The ACP-SCT program had three main axes", with expert validation yielding an average CVI of 0.89. Sessions ran once weekly for four hours, with role-play turns of approximately 25 to 30 minutes per participant.
requirements: Delivered by a facilitator specializing in palliative care with an ACP counselor role, with standardized patients for role-play scenarios
constraints: Piloted only with nurses due to time, personnel, and resource constraints; the article recommends extending future versions to a variety of healthcare professionals
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of advance care planning and advance directives
Communication skills for ACP and end-of-life discussions
examples: Week 1 used TBL with iRAT and tRAT; Weeks 2 and 3 used breakout-group role play with standardized patients on scenarios such as refusing life-sustaining treatments and signing advance directive documents
key_sources: Chen Jui-O; Chang Shu-Chen; Lin Chiu-Chu. (2021). The development and pilot testing of an ACP simulation-based communication-training program: Feasibility and acceptability. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254982

article_title: Breakfast and Exercise Improve Academic and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents.
citation: Kawabata Masato, Lee Kerry, Choo Hui-Cheng, Burns Stephen F. (2021). Breakfast and Exercise Improve Academic and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents. Nutrients 13(4). https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13041278
title: Acute physiological mechanisms account for short-term cognitive benefits of breakfast and exercise
description: The article frames the observed improvements as arising from acute rather than long-term effects: satiation and hunger alleviation, improved fuel and nutrient provision for the central nervous system, and increased synthesis or levels of brain neurotransmitters for breakfast; and exercise-induced catecholamine increases that speed processing, plus possible BDNF-mediated neuroplasticity. The authors state the single-morning intervention "affirms previous literature that some of the improvement elicited from breakfast and exercise is from the acute effects rather than long-term changes in nutritional status or physical fitness".
requirements: Acute intake timing within the morning, since the cognitive reaction-time benefit appeared only at the test-series immediately after the intervention
constraints: The reaction-time improvement did not last until the final test-series, and any BDNF effect may have been limited because the exercise was of moderate rather than higher intensity
target_learning_goals: attention, processing speed, and academic task performance
examples: The authors postulate cocoa flavonols in the Milo drink and hazelnut spread may have contributed to acute cognitive improvements, though this is speculative without a non-cocoa control breakfast
key_sources: Kawabata Masato, Lee Kerry, Choo Hui-Cheng, Burns Stephen F. (2021). Breakfast and Exercise Improve Academic and Cognitive Performance in Adolescents. Nutrients 13(4). https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13041278

article_title: Onwards and upwards: The development, piloting and validation of a new measure of academic tenacity- The Bolton Uni-Stride Scale (BUSS).
citation: Kannangara Chathurika Sewwandi, Allen Rosie Elizabeth, Carson Jerome Francis, Khan Samia Zahraa Noor, Waugh Gill, Kandadi Kondal Reddy. (2020). Onwards and upwards: The development, piloting and validation of a new measure of academic tenacity- The Bolton Uni-Stride Scale (BUSS). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235157
title: Academic tenacity as a multifaceted construct combining grit, resilience, strengths-use, self-control, well-being and growth mind-set
description: Academic tenacity is defined in the article as "the combination of grit, resilience, strengths-use, self-control, psychological well-being and a growth mind-set that provides students with the capacity to thrive at university." The article argues these constructs are strongly interrelated and that measuring one or two alone is overly simplistic. The BUSS operationalises this construct in a single 12-item scale so institutions can take a targeted approach to improving achievement.
requirements: Measurement should cover all six constituent characteristics rather than one or two factors alone
constraints: The authors' contention that academic tenacity outperforms competing measures such as grit alone is untested; they state "Further research is needed to test this assertion"
Developed at a single institution; the authors state it needs to be tested in other universities and in different countries
target_learning_goals: identifying at-risk students for peer mentoring and support services
cultivating academic tenacity through targeted interventions
examples: The BUSS items were drawn from the Grit Scale, Self-Control Scale, CD-RISC 10, Mindset Quiz and WEMWBS, with two strengths-use items generated deductively from a literature review
key_sources: Kannangara Chathurika Sewwandi, Allen Rosie Elizabeth, Carson Jerome Francis, Khan Samia Zahraa Noor, Waugh Gill, Kandadi Kondal Reddy. (2020). Onwards and upwards: The development, piloting and validation of a new measure of academic tenacity- The Bolton Uni-Stride Scale (BUSS). PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235157

article_title: Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence.
citation: Sander Paul, de la Fuente Jesús. (2020). Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(15). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155567
title: Academic Behavioural Confidence (ABC) Scale, Spanish-validated version
description: The Academic Behavioural Confidence scale is a 24-item self-report instrument for university students. The article describes it as "a psychometric measure of the confidence of undergraduate students in their anticipated study-related behaviours in a largely lecture-based course". Prior work established "a four-factor model (confidence in attaining grades, studying, attending classes and discussing course material) with adequate reliability and validity". In this study the Spanish-validated version was completed online by Spanish undergraduates, and its four-subscale structure was re-validated by confirmatory factor analysis with item 24 deleted.
requirements: Students respond to the stem "How confident are you that you will be able to..." on a five-point scale from "not at all confident" to "very confident", with higher scores indicating greater confidence in self-efficacious study skills or behaviours.
constraints: Item 24, attend tutorials, "was largely not applicable to those Spanish students" and was deleted for the confirmatory analysis.
The reduced two-item attendance scale's alpha of 0.625 "seems poor", which the authors attribute to the small number of items.
target_learners: undergraduate students in largely lecture-based university courses
target_learning_goals: confidence in anticipated study-related behaviours: attaining grades, studying, attending classes and discussing course material
examples: In this study the scale was completed in Spanish via an online platform by Psychology, Primary Education and Educational Psychology undergraduates at two Spanish universities.
key_sources: Sander Paul, de la Fuente Jesús. (2020). Undergraduate Student Gender, Personality and Academic Confidence. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(15). https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155567

article_title: Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning.
citation: Wijnia, L. & Servant-Miklos, V. F. C. (2019). Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 915–929. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09923-3
title: Achievement goal theory's 2×2 framework: mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals
description: Achievement goal theory (AGT), developed from work on mastery goals (developing competence) and performance goals (outperforming others), was refined by Elliot (1999) and Pintrich (2000) into a performance-approach/performance-avoidance distinction that was empirically validated. Elliot and McGregor (2001) extended the approach/avoidance distinction to mastery goals, yielding four goals: "mastery-approach (striving to learn or improve skills), mastery-avoidance (striving to avoid learning failures or skill decline), performance-approach (striving to outperform others or appear talented), and performance-avoidance (striving to avoid doing worse than others or appearing less talented)". The article notes AGT remains marred by unresolved controversies over labels, measures and definitions.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish the goal dimensions; the article notes Hulleman et al. (2010) showed the 'outperforming others' and 'demonstrating ability' dimensions are differently associated with performance outcomes
constraints: AGT lacks clear founding fathers and carries unresolved controversy among its proponents, including the mastery versus multiple goals debate
target_learners: higher-education and medical students in PBL contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals relate to learning outcomes and motivation in PBL
examples: Of the four studies in the meta-analysis that included AGT measures, only two distinguished performance-approach from performance-avoidance goals and only one differentiated mastery-approach from mastery-avoidance goals
key_sources: Wijnia, L. & Servant-Miklos, V. F. C. (2019). Behind the times: a brief history of motivation discourse in problem-based learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 915–929. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09923-3

article_title: Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students.
citation: Donkin Rebecca, Askew Elizabeth, Stevenson Hollie. (2019). Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1745-1
title: Achievement goal theory explains how performance-oriented goals and moderate anxiety drive engagement with video feedback and online learning resources
description: The article uses achievement goal theory as its explanatory framework for why the video group engaged more than the control group. Performance-oriented goals, "whereby students want positive affirmation of their proficiency when performing a learning activity which thereby focusses their motivation to achieve", were notable in the video group because the task was assessed by an Instructor. The article also draws on the idea that moderate anxiety is motivating and that the social system of learning, including being scrutinised, engages students in online environments.
requirements: A learning activity where performance is assessed by an expert or Instructor rather than only by peers
Feedback structures that students perceive as consequential for demonstrating proficiency
constraints: The framework is applied interpretively in the discussion rather than tested directly in the study design
The article notes motivation is multi-faceted and likely influenced by many explicit and implicit variables
target_learners: Undergraduate students in performance-assessed practical courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding motivation to engage with formative feedback and online learning resources
examples: The article interprets the video group's higher tutorial attendance and time on task as evidence that the anxiety of being recorded and assessed by an expert promoted participation in voluntary learning activities, while the control group's lower anxiety reduced interest and engagement
key_sources: Donkin Rebecca, Askew Elizabeth, Stevenson Hollie. (2019). Video feedback and e-Learning enhances laboratory skills and engagement in medical laboratory science students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1745-1

article_title: How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures.
citation: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z
title: Three validated EBM knowledge tests: ACE, Berlin, and Fresno
description: The article evaluates three commonly used EBM knowledge instruments: "the ACE (Assessing Competency in EBM) Tool with binary answering format", the Berlin Questionnaire with multiple-choice format, and the Fresno test with open-ended answers. The ACE is a 15-item Yes/No test scored 0–15 across four domains; the Berlin is a 15-item five-option multiple-choice test scored 0–15 built around clinical scenarios; the Fresno is an 18-item open-ended test scored 0–124 with scenario-based questions rated in four grade categories.
requirements: The Fresno test requires substantially more time for completion than the other two tests.
constraints: The Fresno test examines each of four EBM areas with a single question, which the authors note may be insufficient for a comprehensive knowledge assessment.
target_learning_goals: assessing EBM knowledge: question formulation, literature search, evidence appraisal and application
examples: All three instruments were translated into Croatian and back-translated, with two statements corrected for clarity.
key_sources: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z

article_title: The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls.
citation: Fuhrmann Delia, Schweizer Susanne, Leung Jovita, Griffin Cait, Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2019). The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls. Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1080/17588928.2018.1504762
title: Academic Diligence Task (ADT): a behavioral measure of diligence as time allocated to tedious math versus games
description: The Academic Diligence Task (Galla et al., 2014) models real-world schoolwork choices: in a split-screen interface, participants freely allocate time between "complete simple single-digit arithmetic problems" and playing entertaining games such as Tetris. Math is deliberately simple and boring so diligence is not confounded with math ability. In this study it was used unaltered with adolescent girls, with diligence operationally defined as the percentage of time spent doing math over a 20-minute session.
requirements: Simple, boring arithmetic so that time-on-math reflects diligence rather than math ability
Instructions highlighting the alleged benefits of practicing math, with participants left alone to reduce demand characteristics
constraints: The article notes the ADT could be improved by including temptation and boredom questionnaire items for both math and games, and by assessing math aptitude and attitudes
target_learning_goals: academic diligence: regulating behavior in the service of academic goals despite tempting distractions
examples: In this study, 40 girls completed three blocks choosing between math and games; diligence averaged 84.14% of time on math, and the task showed convergent validity with grit and self-control questionnaires in its original validation
key_sources: Fuhrmann Delia, Schweizer Susanne, Leung Jovita, Griffin Cait, Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2019). The neurocognitive correlates of academic diligence in adolescent girls. Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1080/17588928.2018.1504762

article_title: Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Puolakanaho, A., Lappalainen, R., Lappalainen, P., Muotka, J. S., Hirvonen, R., Eklund, K. M., Ahonen, T. P. S., & Kiuru, N. (2018). Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-018-0973-8
title: Acceptance and commitment therapy's six core psychological processes as a trans-diagnostic framework for preventive school-based intervention
description: The article frames acceptance and commitment therapy as a third-wave cognitive therapy in which "acceptance and commitment intervention models combine mindfulness and acceptance with behavioral principles and an understanding of personal values." Recent models aim to reinforce six core psychological processes: flexible present-moment attention and mindfulness, perspective-taking on thinking and feeling, clarifying values and goals, acting in line with those values, willingly accepting unwanted feelings while acting consistently with them, and increasing defusion skills — seeing interfering thoughts as thoughts rather than literal truths. Each process is a trainable psychological skill applicable in any life domain, making ACT a trans-diagnostic treatment that the authors argue can serve preventively to alleviate stress and promote well-being such as academic buoyancy.
requirements: Exercises that target each of the six core processes across program modules
Trained coaches for guidance and motivational feedback in supported delivery
constraints: Studies in school settings were rare at the time; most prior evidence came from clinical samples with face-to-face group delivery
target_learners: Adolescents (11–16-year-olds and ninth-graders) in school settings
target_learning_goals: Psychological flexibility
Defusion and acceptance skills
Values clarification and valued action
Mindfulness
examples: Youth COMPASS operationalizes the processes across five modules: Direction For Life (values/goals), Me And My Mind (defusion), Stalking Myself (present-moment acceptance), Me and Myself (self-as-context/self-compassion), and Me and Other People (valued action in social life)
key_sources: Puolakanaho, A., Lappalainen, R., Lappalainen, P., Muotka, J. S., Hirvonen, R., Eklund, K. M., Ahonen, T. P. S., & Kiuru, N. (2018). Reducing Stress and Enhancing Academic Buoyancy among Adolescents Using a Brief Web-based Program Based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-018-0973-8

article_title: A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi.
citation: Bvumbwe, T.M. & Mtshali, N.G., 2018, 'A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi', Curationis 41(1), a1766. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v41i1.1766
title: Implement nursing education transformation through formal academic–practice partnerships
description: The model advocates formal, structured strategic relationships between educational and clinical practice settings spanning practice, education and research. The article states that "Academic practice partnership is an important mechanism to strengthen nursing education, practice and research and help nurses become well positioned to lead change and advance health." Figure 1 shows all strategies should be implemented through a collaborative approach, with mutual and shared goals and resource sharing.
requirements: Well-defined strategic relationships between educational and clinical practice settings
constraints: The article ties success of transformation strategies to implementation within this formal collaboration
target_learners: nursing students transitioning between theory blocks and clinical practice
target_learning_goals: narrowing the theory–practice gap and preparing practice-ready graduates
examples: Participants reported that mutual collaboration among academic and practice staff lets them share expertise and build each other's capacity
key_sources: Bvumbwe, T.M. & Mtshali, N.G., 2018, 'A middle-range model for improving quality of nursing education in Malawi', Curationis 41(1), a1766. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v41i1.1766

article_title: Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school.
citation: Hornstra, Lisette; Majoor, Marieke; Peetsma, Thea. (2017). Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 606-629. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12167
title: Multiple goal perspective: three latent achievement goal profiles and their transitions in upper elementary school
description: The study applies the multiple goal perspective, which "posits that certain combinations of achievement goals are more favourable than others in terms of educational outcomes". Using latent profile analysis in two domains, three profiles were identified: an "approach‐oriented" profile with relatively high mastery and performance-approach goals and low performance-avoidance goals; a "moderate/indifferent" profile with average scores on each goal; and a "multiple goals" profile with relatively high avoidance goals alongside high mastery and performance-approach goals. Profile membership was mostly stable (78.12% in language, 85.22% in mathematics).
requirements: Measurement of mastery, performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals per domain (Goal Orientation Questionnaire) so profiles can be derived with latent profile analysis
constraints: The study used a trichotomous goal framework and did not include mastery-avoidance goals, arguing younger students rarely adopt them
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and effort in language and mathematics
examples: Latent profile analyses in Mplus 6.1 across three waves yielded a 3-profile solution for both mathematics and language
key_sources: Hornstra, Lisette; Majoor, Marieke; Peetsma, Thea. (2017). Achievement goal profiles and developments in effort and achievement in upper elementary school. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 606-629. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12167

article_title: Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model.
citation: Williams, S. N., Thakore, B. K., & McGee, R. (2017). Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-01-0021
title: Academy for Future Science Faculty coaching program
description: The Academy for Future Science Faculty is "a novel coaching program aiming to positively influence biomedical science PhD students' persistence into academic careers, with a particular focus on encouraging and supporting URM students." Cohort 1 recruited 99 students entering PhD programs in Fall 2011, of whom 51 self-identified as URMs, subdivided into 10 coaching groups of 10 students each with faculty coaches from different institutions. The intervention combined annual 2- or 3-day in-person meetings in Chicago with between-meeting videoconferences and email, covering career planning, professional development, and diversity topics. Coaches received diversity training informed by social science theory.
requirements: Faculty coaches selected for track record of mentoring URM scientists
Diversity training for coaches including social science theories and building a community of support
Students and coaches from different institutions to provide an outside voice
constraints: The program was not designed to substitute for social communities of graduate school research groups and departments
Recruiters were unable to recruit more URM coaches (including Black/African-American, Hispanic male, or Native American coaches) for this cohort
target_learners: Early-stage URM biomedical PhD students in the United States interested in academic careers
target_learning_goals: Career planning and professional development
Persistence into academic careers
Coping with isolation, discrimination, and microaggressions
examples: Students completed individual development plans and self-assessment documents discussed in coaching groups
Sample meeting topics included "Stereotypes, Assumptions, Bias, Difference, Diversity, Discrimination: Realities of Biomedical Research Communities"
key_sources: Williams, S. N., Thakore, B. K., & McGee, R. (2017). Providing Social Support for Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic Minority PhD Students in the Biomedical Sciences: A Career Coaching Model. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-01-0021

article_title: Distributed practice. The more the merrier? A randomised bronchoscopy simulation study.
citation: Bjerrum Anne Sofie, Eika Berit, Charles Peder, Hilberg Ole. (2016). Distributed practice. The more the merrier? A randomised bronchoscopy simulation study. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.30517
title: Accutouch high-fidelity virtual reality bronchoscopy simulator (CAE Healthcare)
description: The training and assessment platform used in the study: "an Accutouch high-fidelity virtual reality simulator from CAE Healthcare®, Quebec, Canada." It consists of a proxy flexible bronchoscope, a robotic interface device, a computer with simulation software, and a monitor. The virtual patient responds to trainee instrumentation with coughing, and the simulator provides force-feedback which enhances realism. It supplies metrics including procedure time, wall collisions, time in red-out, and percent-segments-entered.
requirements: An instructor introduction, an airways atlas, and a 15-min instruction video available on the simulator preceded training
constraints: Testing was done without simulator utilities or the atlas, and simulator-measured metrics only; OSATS assessments were deselected due to lack of assessor blinding opportunity and feasibility
target_learning_goals: Flexible bronchoscopy navigation and systematic inspection of the bronchial system to the sub-segmental level
examples: Participants practised unsupervised on the same simulator case three times per session with a 20-minute time limit per case
key_sources: Bjerrum Anne Sofie, Eika Berit, Charles Peder, Hilberg Ole. (2016). Distributed practice. The more the merrier? A randomised bronchoscopy simulation study. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.30517

article_title: Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training.
citation: Sattler David N., McKnight Patrick E., Naney Linda, Mathis Randy. (2015). Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130450
title: Anchoring bias from academic grading habits distorts grant rating scale use
description: The article proposes that reviewers, accustomed to academic grading where scores below the 60th percentile all receive the same fail grade, may inappropriately apply that model to grant scales. On the NIH 9-point scale, a score in the 55% range represents a "good" proposal whereas 0% to 11% represents a "poor" proposal; a reviewer intending a poor score near the 50th percentile would inflate it to mid-scale, producing restriction of range and inaccurate scoring. The training video teaches this bias explicitly.
requirements: Reviewers must be taught that grant scale percentages do not have equivalent meaning to academic grading percentages
constraints: The article states it did not examine all cognitive biases that may affect the selection of scale values, as doing so was beyond the scope of the study
target_learners: Grant peer reviewers transitioning from academic grading contexts
target_learning_goals: Accurate use of the full range of grant rating scales
examples: The video gave the example that a 50-percent-range score typically means failing in academia but mid-range on the NIH scale means a good proposal.
key_sources: Sattler David N., McKnight Patrick E., Naney Linda, Mathis Randy. (2015). Grant Peer Review: Improving Inter-Rater Reliability with Training. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130450

article_title: Understanding the challenges to facilitating active learning in the resident conferences: a qualitative study of internal medicine faculty and resident perspectives.
citation: Sawatsky Adam P., Zickmund Susan L., Berlacher Kathryn, Lesky Dan, Granieri Rosanne. (2015). Understanding the challenges to facilitating active learning in the resident conferences: a qualitative study of internal medicine faculty and resident perspectives. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v20.27289
title: ACTIVE teaching format for resident noon conferences
description: A structured conference format the authors built from this study's results to give faculty a way to facilitate active learning with minimal faculty development time and effort. "This ACTIVE format was centered on 3–5 focused learning points, clinical questions, small group break-out discussions, and frequent summarization." It is presented as one example of an easily implemented alternative to comprehensive lecturing.
requirements: Faculty development or guidelines and training for faculty unfamiliar with facilitating active learning.
constraints: The article notes structured formats like problem-based and team-based learning require large programmatic change and may not fully suit the residency environment; the ACTIVE format is offered as one example needing further work.
target_learning_goals: resident interaction and engagement
medical knowledge achievement
examples: The authors report using this study's results to build the format, described in a cited prospective controlled study of the ACTIVE format versus standard lecture.
key_sources: Sawatsky Adam P., Zickmund Susan L., Berlacher Kathryn, Lesky Dan, Granieri Rosanne. (2015). Understanding the challenges to facilitating active learning in the resident conferences: a qualitative study of internal medicine faculty and resident perspectives. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v20.27289

article_title: Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine.
citation: Ilic Dragan, Nordin Rusli Bin, Glasziou Paul, Tilson Julie K, Villanueva Elmer. (2014). Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-114
title: ACE tool: a 15-item dichotomous assessment of EBM competency across steps 1-4
description: The ACE tool presents users with a patient scenario, a search strategy and a hypothetical article extract, then asks 15 yes/no questions covering question formulation, literature searching, critical appraisal and application of evidence. Items 1-11 assess knowledge and skills, while items 12-15 assess attitudes toward implementing EBM in clinical practice. The authors state it "provides a novel assessment that measures user performance across the four main steps of EBM" and is the first such instrument with a dichotomous outcome measure.
requirements: Requires a patient scenario, search strategy and article extract; scoring is one point per correct answer to a maximum of 15
constraints: In its current form, with only one patient scenario, search strategy and article, it does not necessarily permit repeated use on the same cohort; it assesses only steps 1-4, not the evaluation step
target_learners: medical trainees at novice, intermediate and advanced EBM levels
target_learning_goals: evidence based medicine competency: asking answerable questions, searching, critical appraisal, applying evidence
examples: 342 Monash medical trainees completed the tool online with a 60-minute limit; mean completion time was 12.8 minutes
key_sources: Ilic Dragan, Nordin Rusli Bin, Glasziou Paul, Tilson Julie K, Villanueva Elmer. (2014). Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-114

article_title: Can training in advanced clinical skills in obstetrics, neonatal care and leadership, of non-physician clinicians in Malawi impact on clinical services improvements (the ETATMBA project): a process evaluation.
citation: Ellard David R, Chimwaza Wanangwa, Davies David, O'Hare Joseph Paul, Kamwendo Francis, Quenby Siobhan, Griffiths Frances, on behalf of The ETATMBA Study Group. (2014). Can training in advanced clinical skills in obstetrics, neonatal care and leadership, of non-physician clinicians in Malawi impact on clinical services improvements (the ETATMBA project): a process evaluation. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2014-005751
title: Accredit professional training for non-physician clinicians to raise its status and quality
description: During development and delivery of the ETATMBA training, the authors found that accreditation mattered for how the programme was received: "it became clear that raising the status and quality of the educational experience through accreditation was a vital strategy." NPCs in Malawi are described as often undervalued with no clear career pathways, so formal accreditation is presented as a way of legitimising and strengthening their educational experience. The principle applies to designing up-skilling programmes for cadres of health workers who lack established professional recognition.
requirements: A credentialing body or partner (in this case Malawian institutions) able to accredit the training programme
constraints: The article states this as a strategy learned during programme establishment in Malawi, not a tested manipulation
target_learners: Non-physician clinicians and other undervalued mid-level health worker cadres
target_learning_goals: Professional development and advanced clinical skills recognition
examples: After ETATMBA, the accredited approach was extended to a further 60 NPCs in obstetrics and five other specialties with Malawi Ministry of Health support
key_sources: Ellard David R, Chimwaza Wanangwa, Davies David, O'Hare Joseph Paul, Kamwendo Francis, Quenby Siobhan, Griffiths Frances, on behalf of The ETATMBA Study Group. (2014). Can training in advanced clinical skills in obstetrics, neonatal care and leadership, of non-physician clinicians in Malawi impact on clinical services improvements (the ETATMBA project): a process evaluation. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2014-005751

article_title: Identifying context factors explaining physician's low performance in communication assessment: an explorative study in general practice.
citation: Essers G, van Dulmen S, van Weel C, van der Vleuten C, Kramer A. (2011). Identifying context factors explaining physician's low performance in communication assessment: an explorative study in general practice. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2296-12-138
title: Communication assessment of GPs and registrars should explicitly account for context factors
description: The article argues that low scores on generic communication instruments like the MAAS-Global may reflect context factors rather than inadequate performance, so assessment should explicitly include context. The authors conclude "there is a need to explicitly account for context factors in the assessment of GP (and GP registrar) communication performance" and that doing so may "do justice to the complexity, diversity and specifics of daily general practice" while retaining mastery of separate communication skills.
requirements: Assessment frameworks must be complemented by knowledge of which context factors were present in the consultation being judged
constraints: The identified factor list is not exhaustive: the authors do not claim to have found all relevant context factors, and the findings await validation
target_learning_goals: Fair assessment of doctor-patient communication performance in daily practice
examples: The study inferred context factors from low MAAS-Global item scores in 17 real-life consultations and judged the communication adequate despite low scores.
key_sources: Essers G, van Dulmen S, van Weel C, van der Vleuten C, Kramer A. (2011). Identifying context factors explaining physician's low performance in communication assessment: an explorative study in general practice. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2296-12-138

article_title: Analysis of student performance in large-enrollment life science courses.
citation: Creech, L. R., & Sweeder, R. D. (2012). Analysis of Student Performance in Large-Enrollment Life Science Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 11(4), 386–391. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.12-02-0019
title: Add active- and collaborative-learning experiences and free-response assessment in large-enrollment science courses to address the gender performance gap
description: The authors recommend curricular changes to address the gender gap their HLM analyses revealed across the curriculum. They state that active- and collaborative-learning experiences could be added, which may benefit female and racial minority students, and note that courses using predominantly free-response exams showed no gender bias. They also flag class size as a factor, since the PHY 431 gap grew as enrollment grew.
requirements: Courses currently show a significant gender gap after controlling for entering GPA and prior grades
constraints: The article states class size is only a correlation in this example, and the exam-format link is an author interpretation rather than a tested manipulation
target_learners: female students in large-enrollment science courses
target_learning_goals: fair assessment of science performance
persistence in science majors
examples: The study analyzed 12 MSU life sciences courses and found PHY 431's gender gap grew as enrollment rose from around 300 to more than 525 students
key_sources: Creech, L. R., & Sweeder, R. D. (2012). Analysis of Student Performance in Large-Enrollment Life Science Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 11(4), 386–391. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.12-02-0019

article_title: Physical activity and academic achievement across the curriculum (A + PAAC): rationale and design of a 3-year, cluster-randomized trial.
citation: Donnelly Joseph E, Greene Jerry L, Gibson Cheryl A, Sullivan Debra K, Hansen David M, Hillman Charles H, Poggio John, Mayo Matthew S, Smith Bryan K, Lambourne Kate, Herrmann Stephen D, Scudder Mark, Betts Jessica L, Honas Jeffery J, Washburn Richard A. (2013). Physical activity and academic achievement across the curriculum (A + PAAC): rationale and design of a 3-year, cluster-randomized trial. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2458-13-307
title: Increase school physical activity through classroom active lessons rather than PE, since PE offers limited moderate-to-vigorous activity
description: The article recommends that if physical activity is to be increased in elementary schools, venues other than PE should be developed, because PE is "generally restricted to 30-minute sessions, 2 or 3 days/week, and provides limited amounts of moderate-to-vigorous activity (MVPA) due to large class sizes, lack of space and equipment." Classroom active lessons embed MVPA in instruction without reducing academic time and without requiring children to make a volitional choice to be active.
requirements: Classroom teachers willing and trained to deliver active lessons; administrator tolerance for in-class activity
constraints: The article notes focus group feedback suggested administrators and teachers would not tolerate 60 minutes/day of MVPA in the classroom
target_learning_goals: Increased moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and academic achievement simultaneously
examples: The authors state that if successful, the A + PAAC approach could be easily and inexpensively scaled and disseminated across elementary schools using existing personnel and infrastructure

(2013). Physical activity and academic achievement across the curriculum (A + PAAC): rationale and design of a 3-year, cluster-randomized trial. article_title: A small tabletop experiment for a direct measurement of the speed of light
citation: Kenichiro Aoki and Takahisa Mitsui. (2007). A small tabletop experiment for a direct measurement of the speed of light. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.3996
title: Design introductory measurement experiments that are conceptually clear, visible, tabletop-sized, safe, and inexpensive
description: The article enumerates its design requirements for a student experiment: the concept must be comprehensible to non-science and non-engineering majors, the optical path in air must be visible, the experiment must fit on a tabletop, students must conduct it safely without difficulty, accuracy must not sacrifice clarity for precision, and the setup must be inexpensive. It reports satisfying all these requirements, which the authors say no previously published speed-of-light experiment met together.
requirements: Low-cost, explicitly documented electronics for the pulsed laser and detector

Laser output chosen to balance safety against beam visibility; the article says safety glasses are ill-advised to skip, though the beam "does not seem to necessitate such safety precautions at this time"
constraints: The authors could not find prior experiments satisfying all requirements, especially because most simpler ones require large space
target_learning_goals: direct measurement of a fundamental physical constant
independent experimental work with basic instrumentation
examples: The realized setup occupies about 1.5 m by 0.5 m and uses a 30 µW pulsed laser with feedback circuitry keeping average output constant
key_sources: Kenichiro Aoki and Takahisa Mitsui. (2007). A small tabletop experiment for a direct measurement of the speed of light. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.3996

article_title: Comparing the Matter and Interactions Curriculum with a Traditional Physics Curriculum: A Think Aloud Study
citation: Keith R Bujak, Richard Catrambone, Marcos D. Caballero, M Jack Marr, Michael F Schatz, Matthew A Kohlmyer. (2008). Comparing the Matter and Interactions Curriculum with a Traditional Physics Curriculum: A Think Aloud Study. http://modeling.asu.edu/R&E/research.html
title: A reorganized curriculum must first acknowledge students' previous traditional physics education before fundamentally reorganizing existing and building new knowledge
description: The authors recommend that curricula built on a fundamentally reorganized knowledge structure, such as M&I, must "first acknowledge students' previous “traditional” physics education experiences before it can fundamentally reorganize existing and build new knowledge". The recommendation rests on the finding that M&I students avoided the momentum principle and made poor attempts at utilizing more traditional physics approaches despite the curriculum's sound-principled organization.
requirements: Curriculum designers must account for learners' prior instruction organized around formulas and simple physics facts
constraints: Grounded in a single small think-aloud study at one institution; the authors state the factors controlling incorrect solutions remain somewhat uncertain
target_learners: undergraduates entering reformed introductory physics courses after prior traditional physics exposure
target_learning_goals: reorganizing physics knowledge around fundamental principles
transferable conceptual problem solving
examples: M&I students' near complete avoidance of the momentum principle and poor attempts at utilizing more traditional physics approaches in the think-aloud transcripts

article_title: Celebrating 30 Years of K-12 Educational Programing at Fermilab
citation: M. Bardeen, M. P. Cooke. (2011). Celebrating 30 Years of K-12 Educational Programming at Fermilab. Proceedings of the DPF-2011 Conference, Providence, RI. http://ed.fnal.gov
title: Design programs so students actively participate and teachers facilitate rather than lecture
description: The authors cite educational research showing that effective learning takes place when students actively participate in their learning and teachers facilitate rather than lecture. They apply this in designing engagement with particle physics for young students, noting that preparing materials of publishable quality usually requires assistance from instructional design professionals.
requirements: Preparing materials of publishable quality usually requires assistance from professionals in instructional design
constraints: Helping teachers move from sage on the stage to guide on the side may take sustained contact over several years
target_learning_goals: engaging students with particle physics
active learning in science
examples: Exploration-based activities are described as most effective: creating interest and awareness in the short term and understanding in the longer term.

article_title: ACER: A Framework on the Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics
citation: Caballero, M. D., Wilcox, B. R., Pollock, S. J., & Pepper, R. E. (2012). ACER: A Framework on the Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.0987
title: ACER framework: four components for analyzing students' use of mathematics in upper-division physics
description: ACER is a theoretical framework organizing how students employ mathematical tools in complex upper-division physics problems, comprising "Activation of the tool , Construction of the model , Execution of the mathematics , and Reflection on the results (ACER)." It is "grounded in task analysis... and resource theory," and was motivated by observing difficulties in student Taylor approximation solutions. It serves as "a scaffold onto which elements of a student's solution can be organized by researchers or instructors," helping describe where students are challenged and why.
requirements: The framework targets complex, canonical "back of the book" style problems typical of upper-division courses; it was developed via task analysis of such problems and requires articulating the elements needed to complete each problem.
constraints: The article states: "The ACER framework is not general enough to be applied to experimental or open-ended problems." Where activities like coordinating representations, interpretation and prediction, and metacognition fit is "an open research agenda."
target_learners: upper-division physics majors in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics
target_learning_goals: fluent use of mathematical tools (e.g., Taylor approximations) to make inferences about physical systems
examples: The authors applied ACER to organize observations from eight think-aloud interviews on Taylor approximations and use it to critique old and design new problems.
key_sources: Caballero, M. D., Wilcox, B. R., Pollock, S. J., & Pepper, R. E. (2012). ACER: A Framework on the Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.0987

article_title: Upper-division Student Understanding of Coulomb's Law: Difficulties with Continuous Charge Distributions
citation: Bethany R. Wilcox, Marcos D. Caballero, Rachel E. Pepper and Steven J. Pollock. (2012). Upper-division Student Understanding of Coulomb's Law: Difficulties with Continuous Charge Distributions. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Upper-division+Student+Understanding+of+Coulomb%27s+Law
title: The ACER framework for students' use of mathematics in upper-division physics
description: The ACER framework, constructed by Caballero et al. leveraging task analysis and resource theory, organizes investigation of how students "Activate, Construct, Execute, and Reflect upon" mathematical resources in upper-division physics. It is not a model or rubric for student reasoning but "a scaffold for organizing the elements of a student's solutions," letting instructors pinpoint difficulties at key solution nodes. This paper demonstrates its application to the Coulomb's Law integral for continuous charge distributions.
requirements: A researcher-guided outline of key elements in a correct solution is created to structure the analysis
constraints: The article scopes application to problems determining potential or field from a static, arbitrary charge distribution that cannot be solved using Gauss' Law
target_learners: junior and senior physics, engineering physics, and astrophysics majors in upper-division E&M
target_learning_goals: connecting mathematical expressions to physics concepts
translating a physical description into a mathematical equation
examples: The framework's Construction component enumerates four key elements: selecting coordinates, expressing dq, selecting limits, and expressing the difference vector
