article_title: Trends of development of the methodical system of teaching physics in high schools of Kazakhstan
citation: Kerimbayev Nurassyl Nurymuly. (2012). Trends of development of the methodical system of teaching physics in high schools of Kazakhstan. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Trends+of+development+of+the+methodical+system+of+teaching+physics+in+high+schools+of+Kazakhstan
title: Replace the traditional class-task system with active-activity, problem-based, individualized methods supported by ICT
description: The article argues that modern education requires active-activity methods and problem approaches that account for individual student features, asserting that "the traditional class-task system with its methods is now ineffective and insufficient". It recommends information and communication technologies as the solution for organizing creative, educational and research activity, noting that password-based login enables individual learning paths for each student. The principle is a design recommendation grounded in the author's conceptual argument, not in reported data.
requirements: Requires introduction of information and communication tools and changed organizational forms of learning
constraints: The article offers no empirical support; the claim of ineffectiveness of the traditional system is asserted, not tested
target_learning_goals: motivation and proactive learning
independent knowledge acquisition
creative and research activity
examples: The article lists multimedia presentation, virtual laboratories, individualized learning paths, and network communication as the concrete mechanisms

article_title: Feedback from students' tests as a tool in teaching
citation: Radoslav M. Dimitrić. (2013). Feedback from students' tests as a tool in teaching: A case study. https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.5173
title: Action vs. process conception of function (Dubinsky & Harel), used as an interpretive lens with the author's formal-definition caveat
description: The paper adopts the psychology-of-function distinction between an action conception (plugging numbers into an algebraic expression and calculating, one step at a time) and a process conception ("a dynamic transformation of quantities according to some repeatable means"), citing Dubinsky & Harel (1992). The author uses it to interpret errors such as students inventing formulas for an abstractly given function f. He argues, however, that perceptions and metaphors are not enough: precise formal definitions of the concepts and of two and higher dimensions must be taught prior to or simultaneously with conception work.
requirements: Students must encounter precise formal definitions of the concepts, not only metaphors, for the metaphors to become operational and stable
constraints: The author presents this as an interpretive lens from prior literature, not as a tested result of this study
target_learners: undergraduate science majors in Calculus III
target_learning_goals: concept of function
multivariable calculus concepts
examples: The author reads students' attempts to invent a concrete formula for f in the chain-rule problem as reflecting the action conception of function

article_title: Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics
citation: Wilcox, B. R., Caballero, M. D., Rehn, D. A., & Pollock, S. J. (2013). ACER: An Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.0791
title: The ACER framework structures analysis of students' mathematical problem solving into four components: Activation, Construction, Execution, and Reflection
description: ACER is an analytical framework designed to guide and structure investigations of students' difficulties with sophisticated mathematical tools in upper-division physics. It organizes expert-identified solution elements into four components: "Activation of the tool, Construction of the model, Execution of the mathematics, and Reflection on the result". The framework focuses on key nodes in solutions to reduce noise, is grounded in a resource view of knowledge, and is deliberately usable by instructors without deep backgrounds in learning theories. It targets back-of-the-book or exam-type problems rather than open-ended ones.
requirements: Must be operationalized for a specific mathematical tool by mapping a problem or problem set onto the framework components via modified task analysis
constraints: Not designed to be applied to open-ended problems
Its structure is not meant to approximate students' actual solutions
Developed for upper-division canonical problems; the authors note upper-division students work quickly and externalize fewer steps than introductory students
target_learners: upper-division physics majors (physics, engineering physics, astrophysics)
target_learning_goals: coordinating mathematical tools with physics concepts when solving canonical upper-division problems
examples: The authors operationalized ACER for direct integration via Coulomb's Law (elements CA1-CA4, CC1-CC4, CE1-CE3, CR1-CR2) and for Taylor series approximation (TA1-TA3, TC1-TC4, TE1-TE4, TR1-TR2)
key_sources: Wilcox, B. R., Caballero, M. D., Rehn, D. A., & Pollock, S. J. (2013). ACER: An Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.0791

article_title: Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics
citation: Wilcox, B. R., Caballero, M. D., Rehn, D. A., & Pollock, S. J. (2013). ACER: An Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.0791
title: Modified task analysis procedure for operationalizing ACER without a knowledge extraction expert
description: This is the article's method for turning the general ACER structure into tool-specific elements. A subject matter expert solves canonical problems while documenting reasoning and mapping solution elements onto ACER components; other SMEs then reach consensus on element classification. Unlike formal task analysis, "Our modified task analysis does not include a KEE", a removal made for practical reasons. The resulting operationalized framework is refined against patterns in student work that the experts' own solutions did not exhibit.
requirements: Multiple content experts must document solutions and reach consensus on classifying each element into Activation, Construction, Execution, or Reflection
The operationalized framework must remain flexible to modification based on emergent analysis of student work
constraints: Removing the knowledge extraction expert makes it more difficult to ensure identified elements are complete from a novice's point of view as well as an SME's
target_learning_goals: characterizing student difficulties with specific mathematical tools
examples: The modified task analysis produced element lists for Coulomb's Law integration and Taylor series, which were then applied to 172 and 116 exam solutions respectively
key_sources: Wilcox, B. R., Caballero, M. D., Rehn, D. A., & Pollock, S. J. (2013). ACER: An Analytic Framework for Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-Division Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.0791

article_title: Decoding Pure Rotational Molecular Spectra for Asymmetric Molecules
citation: S. A. Cooke and P. Ohring. (2012). Decoding Pure Rotational Molecular Spectra for Asymmetric Molecules. arXiv:1204.3226 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.3226
title: Involve students actively in spectral assignment early, before formal theory, using the provided web and smartphone resources
description: The conclusions state the information provided "allows for students to adopt an alternativ e approach to consid- ering the quantum mechanical, asymmetric rigid rotor", in which "students are actively involved early, that is in the task of spectral assignment". The web and smartphone resources support this endeavor, and the tools "facilitate, and prompt, in depth discussion about the under lying theory and application of micr owave spectroscopy". This rests on the argument that broadband spectra can now be collected in a few hours in an undergraduate lab.
requirements: The template patterns (Table 1, Figures 3–8) and the free web/mobile plotting tools
constraints: Modern broadband spectra remain complex and may not be as easily interpreted as classroom NMR or low-resolution IR spectra
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate physics and chemistry students
target_learning_goals: interpreting asymmetric-top rotational spectra
connecting spectral patterns to underlying theory
examples: Students performing broadband rotational spectra experiments in an undergraduate physical chemistry lab, which can now be collected in a few hours or less

article_title: Multiple-choice Assessment for Upper-division Electricity and Magnetism
citation: Bethany R. Wilcox and Steven J. Pollock. (2013). Multiple-choice Assessment for Upper-division Electricity and Magnetism. https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4619
title: Accuracy-and-consistency scoring as a mechanism for capturing partial understanding in multiple choice
description: The article's explanatory account of why its novel format can preserve the diagnostic value of free-response items: a student's selections are scored not only for correctness but for internal coherence, so partial credit reflects partially complete justifications and inconsistent selections are penalized. Rubric R2 "awards points for reasoning elements that are consistent with the choice of method" and "subtracts points from students with reasoning elements that are inconsistent with their choice of method". The authors argue this lets scores "reﬂect subtle differences between students’ understanding" and supports analyzing the nature and consistency of student ideas.
requirements: Reasoning elements whose consistency or inconsistency with each method choice can be judged in advance
A rubric (R2) that weights elements by importance and awards method partial credit for possible-but-not-easiest choices
constraints: The CUE violates the single-construct assumption behind Cronbach's Alpha, so consistency statistics are conservative; whether the format retains the FR version's sensitivity to pedagogical differences is not yet established
target_learning_goals: multi-step conceptual justification in upper-division electrostatics
examples: Under R2, students selecting Direct Integration on Q3 receive partial credit plus additional credit for the consistent reasoning element about the integral form of Coulomb's Law
key_sources: Bethany R. Wilcox and Steven J. Pollock. (2013). Multiple-choice Assessment for Upper-division Electricity and Magnetism. https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4619

article_title: Using river locks to teach hydrodynamic concepts

title: Where museums and science centers are distant or absent, teachers should propose accessible learning activities in the students' living region
description: Because "the presence of museums and science centers a re not a reality in the most of Northeast of Brazil", the article recommends that "the teacher can propos e accessible activities in his living region and to arouse the enthusiasm of the student for scientiﬁc knowledge". The Sobradinho river lock visit is the article's worked example, chosen "once it is the nearest structure of this kind to Senhor do Bonﬁm - BA, Brazil".

constraints: The article notes that non-formal education, though outside the scholar environment, is not free of a degree of intentionality and systematization

target_learning_goals: connecting classroom physics to everyday and regional contexts
arousing enthusiasm for scientific knowledge
examples: Choosing the Sobradinho river lock, the nearest structure of its kind to Senhor do Bonfim - BA, as the visit destination

article_title: Active learning in pre-service science teacher education
citation: Montalbano V., Benedetti R. (2013). Active learning in pre-service science teacher education. ICPE-EPEC 2013 Proceedings. https://www.progettolaureescientifiche.eu
title: Active laboratory experiences followed by metacognitive reflection on the teacher's role support pre-service teacher education
description: The article concludes that experiences of active learning in the physics laboratory, followed by reflection on how the teacher favours active learning, are useful in pre-service education: "Some experiences of active learning in physics laboratory followed by meta cognitive reflection on t he role of teacher in favouring this process seem to be useful in pre -service teacher's education." The reflection makes teachers aware of which activities were effective.

An explicit metacognitive reflection phase on the teacher's role

article_title: Student Difficulties with the Dirac Delta Function
citation: Bethany R. Wilcox and Steven J. Pollock. (2014). Student Difficulties with the Dirac Delta Function. https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.6311
title: The ACER framework as operationalized for delta function problems in junior-level electrostatics
description: ACER (Activation, Construction, Execution, Reflection) is "an analytical framework that characterizes student difficulties with mathematics in upper-division physics by organizing the problem-solving process into four general components." The authors operationalize it for delta function use in expressing volume charge densities by having a content expert document solution steps and refining the outline against student work. The resulting element codes include A1, A2, C1, C2, C3, E1, R1, and R2, which were used to code exam solutions and classify interview moves.
requirements: Operationalization for a specific mathematical tool in a specific physics context: a content expert works through problems exploiting the targeted tool while documenting their steps, and the outline is refined based on analysis of student work.
constraints: The element codes are for labeling purposes only and are not meant to suggest a particular order, nor are all elements always necessary for every problem.
target_learning_goals: using mathematical tools (the Dirac delta function) to express and interpret volume charge densities in electrostatics
examples: Exams were coded by scoring each operationalized ACER element appearing in a student's solution, and interview moves were classified into the four framework components.
key_sources: Bethany R. Wilcox and Steven J. Pollock. (2014). Student Difficulties with the Dirac Delta Function. https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.6311

article_title: Unpacking Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics
citation: Caballero, M. D., Wilcox, B. R., Pollock, S. J., & Doughty, L. (2015). Unpacking Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics: Where do we go from here? arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.7660
title: The ACER framework organizes upper-division students' use of mathematics in problem solving into four components
description: ACER is an analytical framework developed through a modified task analysis with disciplinary experts to organize upper-division students' use of mathematics on canonical back-of-the-book problems. Expert negotiation "produced the four components of the ACER framework: Activation of the tool - selecting which mathematical tool will be used to facilitate a solution to the problem", followed by Construction of the model, Execution of the mathematics, and Reflection on the results. The authors stress the process is fluid and non-linear and that ACER organizes rather than models student work.
requirements: Operationalization for a specific mathematical tool requires a detailed task analysis documenting the conceptual and procedural resources needed
constraints: ACER was designed to investigate how students use mathematics in back-of-the-book style problems and does not capture difficulties that appear exclusively conceptual
target_learning_goals: using mathematics appropriately when solving upper-division physics problems
examples: The framework was operationalized for Taylor series, Coulomb's Law, and Dirac delta functions in studies of 2nd and 3rd year physics courses
key_sources: Caballero, M. D., Wilcox, B. R., Pollock, S. J., & Doughty, L. (2015). Unpacking Students' Use of Mathematics in Upper-division Physics: Where do we go from here? arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.7660

article_title: Upper-division student difficulties with the Dirac delta function

title: ACER framework: Activation, Construction, Execution, Reflection for analyzing mathematical tool use in physics problem solving
description: The ACER framework organizes physics problem solving with mathematical tools into four components: "activation of mathematical tools, construction of mathematical models, execution of the mathematics, and reflection on the results." article_title: Upper-division student difficulties with Separation of Variables
citation: Bethany R. Wilcox and Steven J. Pollock. (2015). Upper-division student difficulties with Separation of Variables. https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.03938v1
title: The ACER framework for analyzing mathematical tool use in physics problem solving
description: ACER (Activation, Construction, Execution, Reflection) organizes the problem-solving process into four general components: "activation of mathematical tools, construction of mathematical models, execution of the mathematics, and reﬂection on the results". In this article the authors operationalize ACER for SoV problems in Cartesian and spherical electrostatics and use it to organize and categorize student difficulties.

examples: The authors operationalized ACER with elements A1-A3, C1-C3, E1-E4, and R1-R4 for canonical Cartesian and spherical SoV exam problems and coded exam solutions, CUE responses, and interviews against it.

title: ACER framework operationalized for boundary conditions in electrodynamics

Exam questions mostly targeted Construction and Execution and did not provide a complete picture of Activation or Reflection

upper-division physics problem solving

article_title: Action Physics
citation: Lachlan P. McGinness and C. M. Savage. (2016). Action Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.06075
title: Action physics: unified introductory instruction from many-paths quantum physics through stationary action mechanics to relativity
description: Action physics is a unified first-year university curriculum organised around the principle of stationary action, running from many-paths quantum physics through ray optics, classical mechanics and relativity. Its rationale is "uniting different areas of physics under the stationary action principle, and explaining classical physics in terms of quantum physics".
requirements: Students are required to take mathematics courses covering: complex numbers, differential equations, and partial differentiation
constraints: Action physics "does not naturally incorporate friction, a central part of everyday experience"
The "electromagnetism part of the curriculum is outside the domain of action physics"
target_learners: first-year university physics majors, described as high-achievers at the national level
target_learning_goals: understanding the stationary action principle
explaining classical physics in terms of quantum physics
a unified view of quantum, classical and relativistic physics
examples: The 2014 module was "assessed by two homeworks, a lab logbook and a final exam question"
Topic progression ran from many-paths quantum physics, Fermat's principle and the stationary action principle for mechanics to Euler-Lagrange equations, general coordinates, symmetry and relativity
key_sources: Lachlan P. McGinness and C. M. Savage. (2016). Action Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.06075

article_title: Developing an Action Concept Inventory
citation: Lachlan P. McGinness and C. M. Savage. (2016). Developing an Action Concept Inventory. arXiv:1605.01786. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.01786
title: Action Concept Inventory (ACI): a multiple-choice test of action physics and many-paths quantum mechanics concepts
description: The Action Concept Inventory (ACI) is "a test that measures student understanding of action principles in introductory mechanics and optics", also covering key many-paths quantum mechanics concepts. Its current version, available in supplemental material, comprises 19 questions classified against ten expert-supported concepts, developed through a multi-stage iterative cycle of literature review, expert consultation, and student think-aloud interviews.
requirements: Administered to students who complete both pre- and post-instruction tests, using the supplemental question set and correct answers
constraints: The current version does not meet the internal validity criterion for evaluating understanding of a single construct, so it should not be regarded as a fully developed concept inventory
target_learning_goals: action principles in introductory mechanics and optics
many-paths quantum mechanics concepts
examples: Administered pre and post instruction to the 2014 and 2015 ANU Physics 2 classes, and to 61 ANU physicists
key_sources: Lachlan P. McGinness and C. M. Savage. (2016). Developing an Action Concept Inventory. arXiv:1605.01786. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.01786

article_title: iPad Screencasts as Evidence of Accountable Disciplinary Knowledge
citation: Eleanor C. Sayre, Claudia Fracchiolla, Ben Van Dusen. (2016). iPad Screencasts as Evidence of Accountable Disciplinary Knowledge. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08105
title: Accountable Disciplinary Knowledge (ADK) framework
description: The article defines Accountable Disciplinary Knowledge as "what counts" as important to a community or discipline: the kinds of activities that participants engage in, the problems they value and solve, and methods for solving those problems. Because ADK is determined on a community basis, its details vary with the norms and expectations of the community, and it is continually rendered and refined by its members, so it varies across communities and time. Demonstrating one's ADK is central to being accepted as a member of a community of practice. The authors use ADK to investigate what counts as solving problems well in a high school physics classroom.
requirements: ADK is determined on a community basis, so analysis requires identifying the norms and expectations of the specific community studied
constraints: The details of what counts will vary across communities and across time
target_learning_goals: understanding disciplinary practices and values in physics problem solving
key_sources: Eleanor C. Sayre, Claudia Fracchiolla, Ben Van Dusen. (2016). iPad Screencasts as Evidence of Accountable Disciplinary Knowledge. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08105

article_title: A Problem-Solving Framework to Assist Students and Teachers in STEM Courses
citation: Jeffrey A. Phillips, Jeremy E. McCallum, Katharine W. Clemmer, Thomas M. Zachariah. (2015). A Problem-Solving Framework to Assist Students and Teachers in STEM Courses.
title: ACE-M framework: Analyze the Task, Create a Plan, Execute the Plan, and Monitor Understanding and Actions
description: ACE-M is a four-component problem-solving framework for STEM courses that gives monitoring equal standing with the cognitive components of analyzing, planning, and executing. The authors stress that "Monitoring is not a fourth, separate component; rather, it is integrated into the other components", and that the framework implies a non-linear, recursive process in which monitoring may send the solver back to an earlier component. Each component carries monitoring prompts, such as asking whether given information is contradictory or whether alternative plans exist.
requirements: Instructors stress to students that the framework is a recursive process, using components rather than steps, and scaffold students with prompts used across all problems
constraints: The authors note other models that include monitoring along with confidence and creativity are likely too complex for classroom use, so ACE-M keeps monitoring simple and integrated
target_learning_goals: problem-solving
metacognitive monitoring
self-regulation during problem solving
examples: Used as the foundation for problem-solving instruction in lower-division chemistry, mathematics, and physics courses, with monitoring prompts embedded in the A, C, and E component descriptions
key_sources: Jeffrey A. Phillips, Jeremy E. McCallum, Katharine W. Clemmer, Thomas M. Zachariah. (2015). A Problem-Solving Framework to Assist Students and Teachers in STEM Courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.07853

article_title: Varied reasoning schema in students' written solutions
citation: Nandana Weliweriya, Justyna P. Zwolak, Eleanor C. Sayre, Dean Zollman. (2017). Varied reasoning schema in students’ written solutions. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02262
title: ACER framework for analyzing mathematics use in upper-division physics problem solving
description: The ACER (Activation-Construction-Execution-Reflection) framework models physics problem solving as four components: "Activation (determining the proper mathematical tool); Construction (making a mathematical model); Execution (performing mathematical steps); and Reflection (checking the final solution)." Students may move freely among components in any order, visiting each several times with different sub-codes. The authors modified it for mechanics homework, extending sub-codes to cover errors.
requirements: Sub-codes must be adapted to the specific physics topic and problems at hand
constraints: It was developed from think-aloud interview data on conceptually-rich research-based problems, which differ from traditional homework problems; written solutions provide sparse reasoning evidence
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate physics majors and minors
target_learning_goals: using mathematical tools (integrals, differential equations, coordinate systems) in physics problem solving
examples: Coded 12 students' written solutions to classical mechanics homework problems from Taylor's textbook
key_sources: Nandana Weliweriya, Justyna P. Zwolak, Eleanor C. Sayre, Dean Zollman. (2017). Varied reasoning schema in students’ written solutions. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02262

article_title: Teaching the Doppler Effect in Astrophysics
citation: Stephen W. Hughes, Michael Cowley. (2016). Teaching the Doppler Effect in Astrophysics. European Journal of Physics (author-created version). http://dx.doi.org/10.1088/1361-6404/aa5446
title: Teach the astrophysical Doppler effect with acoustic waves, since the underlying principle is the same at velocities far below the speed of light
description: The article recommends demonstrating Doppler principles acoustically because "the principle demonstrated using acoustic waves is the same" as for the electromagnetic waves that predominate in astrophysics, provided velocities are much less than the speed of light so relativistic effects do not arise. A reflected-fan experiment makes the shift large enough to see in a spectrum: with 40 kHz sound and blade-tip speeds near 17.3 m/s the calculated shift is a few kHz, easily visible in the spectrum.
requirements: Interpretation must stay within the non-relativistic regime, and the reflected-wave measurement uses the ultrasound equation with its factor of 2
constraints: Relativistic effects, which often apply in astrophysics, are not reproduced by the acoustic analogue
target_learning_goals: understanding the Doppler shift as the basis of astronomical velocity measurements
examples: The article introduces astrophysical applications including redshift measurements of recessional galaxies, Doppler spectroscopy of exoplanets, and Zeeman Doppler Imaging before presenting the acoustic demonstration
key_sources: Stephen W. Hughes, Michael Cowley. (2016). Teaching the Doppler Effect in Astrophysics. European Journal of Physics (author-created version). http://dx.doi.org/10.1088/1361-6404/aa5446

article_title: Student Difficulties with Boundary Conditions in Electrodynamics
citation: Ryan, Q. X., Wilcox, B. R., & Pollock, S. J. (2017). Student Difficulties with Boundary Conditions in Electrodynamics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06203
title: ACER framework operationalized for boundary conditions in electrodynamics
description: ACER (Activation, Construction, Execution, Reflection) is an analytical framework that 'characterize[s] student difficulties with upper-division problem solving by organizing the problem-solving process into four general components'. The authors extend it from mathematical tools to a physics concept, operationalizing it for BCs with elements such as C1 (writing complex field expressions), C3 (setting up equations at the boundary), E1 (simplifying exponentials), and R2 (checking limiting behaviors). It provided 'an organizing structure for our analysis that helped us identify nodes in students' work where key difficulties appear' and informed interview protocol design.
requirements: Must be operationalized for the specific physics topic by a content expert mapping problem-solving steps onto the framework components, with consensus among content experts.
constraints: The authors note ACER 'does not explicitly address the nuance associated with representations', such as translation between verbal, mathematical, graphical, and pictorial representations.
Written solutions analyzed with ACER often do not reveal the reasoning mechanism behind student errors.
target_learning_goals: diagnosing student difficulties in upper-division physics problem solving
examples: The framework was applied to exam solutions (N=158), CURrENT responses (N=500), and think-aloud interviews (N=11) in junior-level electrodynamics at CU Boulder.
key_sources: Ryan, Q. X., Wilcox, B. R., & Pollock, S. J. (2017). Student Difficulties with Boundary Conditions in Electrodynamics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06203

article_title: Operationalizing the AAPT Learning Goals for the Lab
citation: N.G. Holmes and Emily M. Smith. (2014). Operationalizing the AAPT Learning Goals for the Lab. http://cperl.lassp.cornell.edu/content/learning-objectives-intro-physics-lab-courses-cornell-university
title: Model-comparison lab activities require linearly related variables, competing models, simple data collection, and messy data
description: When choosing a lab activity to meet iterative experimentation and quantitative fitting goals, the authors specify a reusable configuration of activity features. They needed "an activity that involved two continuous and linearly-related variables; two reasonable models that could be compared; relatively simple data collection so that students could focus on the analysis and iterate; and relatively messy data that would warrant iteration and reflection." This pattern makes the data genuinely ambiguous, forcing students to improve the experiment to distinguish the two models.
requirements: Two reasonable models that could be compared
Data messy enough to warrant iteration and reflection
constraints: The features are stated as the authors' design choices for their own mechanics activity, not as tested conditions
target_learning_goals: collect data and revise an experimental procedure iteratively and reflectively
evaluate the process and outcomes of an experiment quantitatively
key_sources: N.G. Holmes and Emily M. Smith. (2014). Operationalizing the AAPT Learning Goals for the Lab. http://cperl.lassp.cornell.edu/content/learning-objectives-intro-physics-lab-courses-cornell-university

article_title: Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach to Measuring the Effects of Class Size and Other Classroom Characteristics on Student Learning in an Active-Learning Based Introductory Physics Course
citation: Connor Gorman, David Webb, Kevin Gee. (2016). Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach to Measuring the Effects of Class Size and Other Classroom Characteristics on Student Learning in an Active-Learning Based Introductory Physics Course. University of California, Davis. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Hierarchical+Linear+Modeling+Approach+to+Measuring+the+Effects+of+Class+Size
title: Active-learning introductory physics course structure with discussion-lab sections
description: The courses studied are introductory physics courses for bioscience majors at a large public R1 university on the quarter system, built on active-learning techniques. During the regular academic year "students spend five hours per week in discussion-lab (DL) where they engage in activities in groups of about five students each and synthesize the material as a whole class, both with guidance from a teaching assistant (TA)." An additional 1.5 hours per week are spent in lecture; lecturers teach two lectures of about 165 students each, broken into DLs of approximately 30 students, usually mixing students from the two lectures.
requirements: Teachers must be physically present for active-learning techniques to work, per the article's reasoning
constraints: Overflow classrooms are sometimes used which hold approximately 20 students each
The DL curriculum is rather rigid and how DL is actually taught can vary between DLs based on TA style and potential modifications
target_learners: undergraduate bioscience majors in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: understanding of physics principles and problem-solving skills applicable to biological fields
examples: DLs usually consist of a mixture of students from two related, but distinct, back-to-back lectures taught by the same lecturer.
key_sources: Connor Gorman, David Webb, Kevin Gee. (2016). Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach to Measuring the Effects of Class Size and Other Classroom Characteristics on Student Learning in an Active-Learning Based Introductory Physics Course. University of California, Davis. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Hierarchical+Linear+Modeling+Approach+to+Measuring+the+Effects+of+Class+Size

article_title: An electronic data management and analysis application for ABET accreditation
citation: Adeel Sabir, Nisar A. Abbasi, Md Nurul Islam. (2018). An electronic data management and analysis application for ABET accreditation. https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.05845
title: ACT: a multi-user Microsoft Access application for managing and analyzing ABET accreditation assessment data
description: ACT (Accreditation Tool) is a database application built entirely in Microsoft Access, with a distributed frontend of interactive forms and a backend on a secure network server. It manages data for ABET criteria 3 and 4 through six tabs (Basic Data, Metrics, Assessment, Feedback, Reports-1, Reports-2), and "allows efficient data management for the documentation-intensive criterion 3 and 4, and enables the users to manage and view the assessment data in the form of customized reports". The program and its user guide are available to educators and evaluators.
requirements: Users log in with a username and password, and data entry is completed in four sequential steps through tabbed forms linked to backend tables with referential integrity constraints
constraints: The application was demonstrated on ABET criteria document 2017-2018, with SOs A through K; the authors note it can be adapted to the post-2019-2020 criteria by using different SO labels once COs are remapped
target_learners: engineering faculty and accreditation evaluators in higher education
target_learning_goals: outcomes-based assessment of student outcomes and continuous program improvement for accreditation
examples: Used by the Department of Electrical Engineering at the authors' institution; demonstrated through illustrative examples on data gathered over multiple academic terms
key_sources: Adeel Sabir, Nisar A. Abbasi, Md Nurul Islam. (2018). An electronic data management and analysis application for ABET accreditation. https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.05845

article_title: Activity Theory in Didactics of Mathematics -- What is Taken As Shared
citation: Maha Abboud-Blanchard, Aline Robert, Janine Rogalski et Fabrice Vandebrouck. (2017). Pour une théorie de l'activité en didactique des mathématiques : Un résumé des fondements partagés, des développements récents et des perspectives. Cahiers du laboratoire de didactique André Revuz n°18, IREM de Paris. http://www.irem.univ-paris-diderot.fr/
title: An Activity-Theory framework adapted to mathematics didactics studies student activities in relation to the teaching received
description: The article presents an adaptation of Activity Theory for studying school mathematics learning in relation to instruction. Researchers analyse student classroom activities — what students do, say and write — distinguishing tasks from activities, and study the arrows from teacher activities to student activities and from student activities to learning. The framework includes Leplat's double-regulation schema: 'Cela inclut, plus précisément, le schéma de double régulation de Leplat (1997).' It is used for diagnosis and elaboration of what happens in class, combining experimental observation and theoretical analysis.
requirements: Research must establish early a mathematical reference analysis of the notions to be taught
Access to student activities is obtained by analysing proposed tasks and comparing expected activities with actual classroom unfoldings
constraints: Student thought remains unobservable; only traces of activity can be collected
The arrow from activities to learning rests on global hypotheses more than precise results
target_learning_goals: operational mathematical knowledge, i.e. not only the text of knowledge but its implementation
examples: Analyses of teacher discourse during knowledge-exposition phases, where student activities are especially inaccessible, are used to infer possible student activities
key_sources: Maha Abboud-Blanchard, Aline Robert, Janine Rogalski et Fabrice Vandebrouck. (2017). Pour une théorie de l'activité en didactique des mathématiques : Un résumé des fondements partagés, des développements récents et des perspectives. Cahiers du laboratoire de didactique André Revuz n°18, IREM de Paris. http://www.irem.univ-paris-diderot.fr/

article_title: Activity Theory in Didactics of Mathematics -- What is Taken As Shared
citation: Maha Abboud-Blanchard, Aline Robert, Janine Rogalski et Fabrice Vandebrouck. (2017). Pour une théorie de l'activité en didactique des mathématiques : Un résumé des fondements partagés, des développements récents et des perspectives. Cahiers du laboratoire de didactique André Revuz n°18, IREM de Paris. http://www.irem.univ-paris-diderot.fr/
title: The article contrasts the Activity-Theory framework with TSD and TAD by what each treats: effective classroom unfolding versus situation potential and systemic norms
description: The article positions its framework against complementary frameworks. TSD first focused on designing situations potentially favourable to learning, concerning the potential attached to a situation rather than its effective unfolding, whereas the use of TA inverts this weighting; TSD concepts like the didactic contract treat actors as generic subjects filling a function, while TA treats them as singular acting subjects. TAD works partly on global visions of the educational system from constraints and norms, analysing praxeologies and levels of determination, also treating actors as subjects subjected to an institution.
requirements: Theories are to be used as guarantees of coherence in the cutting-up of reality, not as carcan
constraints: The article states it remains to explain what this framework contributes compared with other theories frequently used in mathematics didactics
target_learning_goals: choosing and articulating theoretical frameworks for analysing mathematics classrooms
examples: The notion of FUG was invented because no good introduction situation could be found in terms of the tool/object dialectic — an example of turning a 'bruit' into a productive source of novelty
key_sources: Maha Abboud-Blanchard, Aline Robert, Janine Rogalski et Fabrice Vandebrouck. (2017). Pour une théorie de l'activité en didactique des mathématiques : Un résumé des fondements partagés, des développements récents et des perspectives. Cahiers du laboratoire de didactique André Revuz n°18, IREM de Paris. http://www.irem.univ-paris-diderot.fr/

article_title: Mastery Learning-Like Teaching with Achievements
citation: Tobias Wrigstad and Elias Castegren. (2019). Mastery Learning-Like Teaching with Achievements. PACM Progr. Lang. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.03510
title: Achievement Unlocked: an achievement-based course system where students choose when and how to demonstrate mastery
description: Achievement Unlocked reifies formal course goals as a large set of roughly 70 achievements derived from course goals and checked against the ACM/IEEE CS 2013 curriculum. Achievements belong to grade levels 3, 4 or 5, and "to pass with a certain grade, a student must pass 100% of the achievements belonging to that grade, and those below". Achievements are not tied to specific assignments or dates; students map them to course activities and attempt demonstration when they choose. The authors describe it as similar to mastery learning, with constructive alignment as the main inspiration.
requirements: Achievements must be derived from the formal course goals and checked against a curriculum reference
constraints: The authors note that folding assignments into the achievement system "possibly comes at a cost of making the achievements idea less pure"
target_learners: second-year university computer science and IT engineering students
target_learning_goals: imperative and object-oriented programming
programming methodology and tools
basic software engineering
technical communication
examples: In the 2016 course, about 60 of the 70 achievements were demonstrated in lab sessions, with around 30 presentation slots per session cycle and a maximum of 4 achievements per demonstration
key_sources: Tobias Wrigstad and Elias Castegren. (2019). Mastery Learning-Like Teaching with Achievements. PACM Progr. Lang. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.03510

article_title: Resources for Supporting Students with and without Disabilities in Your Physics Courses
citation: Amanda Lannan, Erin Scanlon, & Jacquelyn J. Chini. (2019). Resources for Supporting Students with and without Disabilities in Your Physics Courses. The Physics Teacher. https://aapt.scitation.org/journal/pte
title: Accessible physics course resources pattern: alternative print access, tactile representations, virtual labs, accessible calculators and data analysis, and inclusive physical layout
description: The article describes several resource types physics instructors can use to create "flexible options for how students access content, demonstrate their understanding, and engage with the course," spanning off-the-shelf products, assistive technologies, and high-tech and low-tech options. Reading applications such as Vital Source, Dolphin EasyReader, and Voice Dream Reader support alternative access to text; special library services such as Book Share, Learning Ally, and the national library services provide audio and braille textbook files. Tactile representations of diagrams can be created via the 3D OPAL project, the Sensational Blackboard, or 3Doodler Start; virtual labs such as PhET simulations offer increased independence for students with dexterity or mobility impairments and can be repeated at home; talking calculators and data sonification tools such as SAS Graphics Accelerator provide accessible calculation and data analysis; and physical layout considerations include seating preferences, visual access via projectors or overhead mirrors, and microphones for auditory access.
requirements: Instructors consider the accessibility of the simulations and technologies they choose, such as PhET's alternative input, screen reader descriptions, and sonification features
constraints: Tactile graph conversion of data sets can give access to overall trends but can be tedious and/or complicated to access more specific information
target_learners: students with visual, hearing, dexterity, mobility, and attention impairments in postsecondary physics courses
target_learning_goals: access to physics content, laboratory work, and data analysis
examples: An introductory circuits lab experiment could be conducted with a PhET simulation in addition to physical equipment, allowing students with dexterity impairments to create and test circuits
key_sources: Amanda Lannan, Erin Scanlon, & Jacquelyn J. Chini. (2019). Resources for Supporting Students with and without Disabilities in Your Physics Courses. The Physics Teacher. https://aapt.scitation.org/journal/pte

article_title: Supporting students with ADHD in introductory physics courses: Four steps for instructors
citation: Caroline Bustamante, Erin Scanlon, & Jacquelyn J. Chini. (2019). Supporting Students with ADHD in Introductory Physics Courses: Four Steps for Instructors. University of Central Florida.
title: Demonstrate understanding that accommodations such as extended test time and reduced-distraction environments promote equity in the class
description: The article recommends instructors become familiar with the school's accommodation policy and federal regulations so the request process is smooth, and treat accommodations as promoting fairness rather than special treatment. It argues a fair exam tests knowledge of required material rather than the speed of recall within a preset time limit, and that accommodations may alleviate anxiety and pressure associated with ADHD and are essential in leveling the playing field for students pursuing STEM degrees. Instructors should also extend an open invitation for students to feel comfortable speaking about their needs.
requirements: Become familiar with the school's accommodation policy and federal regulations so the process is smooth when a student requests accommodations
Extend an open invitation for students to feel comfortable speaking about their needs as learners
constraints: Some individuals with ADHD are apprehensive about disclosing their diagnoses for fear of judgement or special treatment, and many want autonomy in their studies and do not want sympathy — empathy is welcome and necessary
target_learners: postsecondary students with ADHD and other diagnosed impairments
target_learning_goals: accurate demonstration of comprehension on exams and equitable access to STEM degrees
examples: The article notes the contributing student was registered with the university's Disability Services Office and received extended time on exams and a quiet, secluded environment for taking exams
key_sources: Caroline Bustamante, Erin Scanlon, & Jacquelyn J. Chini. (2019). Supporting Students with ADHD in Introductory Physics Courses: Four Steps for Instructors. University of Central Florida. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.12448

article_title: A cross-context look at upper-division student difficulties with integration
citation: Wilcox, B. R., & Corsiglia, G. (2019). A cross-context look at upper-division student difficulties with integration. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00474
title: The ACER framework: Activation, Construction, Execution, and Reflection on mathematical tools in physics problem solving
description: The ACER framework is an analytical framework for structuring investigations of student difficulties with sophisticated mathematical tools in physics problem solving. It comprises four components: "activation of the mathematical tool, construction of the mathematical model, execution of the mathematics, and reﬂection on the results." The framework was designed to be applicable across contexts and tools while being operationalizable for specific topics, and is grounded in resources and epistemic framing perspectives. In this article it facilitates cross-context comparison of integration difficulties across gravitation, electrostatics, and magnetostatics.
requirements: The framework must be operationalized for specific topics and tools through expert modified task analysis to capture tool- and context-specific aspects of student difficulties
constraints: The broad structure is designed to be applicable across contexts, but the operationalization process is important to ensure context-specific difficulties are captured
target_learning_goals: using multi-variable integration as a mathematical tool in physics problem solving
examples: The authors operationalized ACER for direct integration by identifying elements A1-A4 (activation), C1-C4 (construction), E1-E3 (execution), and R1-R2 (reflection) through expert task analysis
key_sources: Wilcox, B. R., & Corsiglia, G. (2019). A cross-context look at upper-division student difficulties with integration. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00474

article_title: Bringing personalized learning into computer-aided question generation
citation: Yi-Ting Huang, Meng Chang Chen, and Yeali S. Sun. (2012). Bringing personalized learning into computer-aided question generation. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Bringing+personalized+learning+into+computer-aided+question+generation
title: Ability estimation based on acquisition distribution
description: The article proposes a statistical method that estimates an examinee's ability as a grade level by connecting test performance to knowledge-acquisition age distributions: the method 'draws a connection b e- tween students' abilities and the acquisition age distrib u- tions'. An examinee has ability theta if s percent of items in a test have been correctly answered, each by r percent of the population. It aggregates item quantile functions via a normal approximation of order statistics and combines current with historical estimates using an Exponential Moving Average, avoiding pre-calibrated item parameters.
requirements: A distribution of knowledge acquisition for each item's underlying knowledge, or item parameters from an Item Response Theory item characteristic curve to infer the grade level at which r percent of the population answers correctly
Historical test records combined with current responses via the EMA smoothing constant
constraints: The distribution of item difficulties of the questions in a test was assumed as a normal distribution
The method does not take account of incorrect responses; the authors propose penalizing the estimated value when an examinee selects an incorrect answer as future work
target_learners: English language learners in senior high school (grades defined by the six semesters)
target_learning_goals: Measuring learner ability in vocabulary, grammar, and reading comprehension to match question difficulty to knowledge level
examples: Implemented on the AutoQuiz Web-based system of the IWiLL learning platform, generating personalized vocabulary, grammar, and reading comprehension multiple-choice questions
key_sources: Yi-Ting Huang, Meng Chang Chen, and Yeali S. Sun. (2012). Bringing personalized learning into computer-aided question generation. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Bringing+personalized+learning+into+computer-aided+question+generation

article_title: Toward Personalized XAI: A Case Study in Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Cristina Conati, Oswald Barral, Vanessa Putnam, Lea Rieger. (2024). Toward Personalized XAI: A Case Study in Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Preprint submitted to the JAI – Special Issue on Explainable Artificial Intelligence. https://www.ubc.ca
title: ACSP explanation functionality: six dynamically generated why/how explanation pages in a tab-based incremental interface
description: The explanation functionality is an addition to the ACSP applet that lets students access explanations of the AI-driven adaptive hints. It is structured around three tabs, each providing a self-contained incremental why explanation (WhyHint, WhyLow, WhyRules), with three how pages (HowScore, HowHint, HowRank) reachable from the second tab. Each explanation is "dynamically derived from the current state of the underlying ACSP AI models, as they evolve based on the user's real-time interaction". Users can give feedback via an "I would have liked to know more" button on every page.
requirements: Explanations are triggered by clicking the button "Why am I delivered this hint?" after a hint is delivered
The design relies on Kulesza et al.'s criteria of iterative, sound, complete, and not overwhelming explanations, prioritizing why over how explanations to avoid excessive complexity
constraints: The article states the design sacrifices completeness when needed to avoid excessive complexity; the Behavior Discovery algorithms (clustering, rule extraction) are deliberately not explained
target_learners: University students with computer science knowledge sufficient to learn constraint satisfaction problems
target_learning_goals: Learning the AC-3 algorithm for solving constraint satisfaction problems
More effective use of the ACSP applet's interactive tools
examples: In the formal study, 24 of 30 explanation-condition participants accessed the functionality, initiating explanations for 3/4 of hints received and spending an average of 38.5s per hint looking at explanation pages
key_sources: Cristina Conati, Oswald Barral, Vanessa Putnam, Lea Rieger. (2024). Toward Personalized XAI: A Case Study in Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Preprint submitted to the JAI – Special Issue on Explainable Artificial Intelligence. https://www.ubc.ca

article_title: Sources of E, D, B, H in electro- and magnetostatics: critical comments
citation: Yu.A. Koksharov. (1944). Sources of E, D, B, H in electro- and magnetostatics: critical comments. Faculty of Physics, M.V. Lomonosov Moscow State University. https://www.physics.msu.ru
title: Accompany every formula in a textbook with an explicit statement of its applicability domain
description: Drawing on the 1944 Coulomb's Law Committee report, the article endorses the committee's advice that textbook errors most often arise because authors do not delineate the applicability of their statements, treating a special case as general. The committee advised making it a mandatory rule "сопровождение каждой формулы в учебнике текстом ( выделенным курсивом ), описывающим область её применимости". The author's analysis of current Russian and foreign electromagnetism textbooks shows "этот совет по прежнему актуален".
requirements: textbook authors must state, in highlighted text next to each formula, the conditions under which it holds
constraints: the recommendation originates in the Coulomb's Law Committee report for physics teachers, as reported by the article
target_learning_goals: avoid misapplying formulas beyond their validity conditions
examples: The article applies this principle by explicitly deriving the conditions (e.g. absence of fictitious polarization currents, homogeneous simple dielectric with field lines perpendicular to boundaries) under which textbook statements about D and H hold.
key_sources: Yu.A. Koksharov. (1944). Sources of E, D, B, H in electro- and magnetostatics: critical comments. Faculty of Physics, M.V. Lomonosov Moscow State University. https://www.physics.msu.ru

article_title: The academic career in physics as a "deal": Choosing physics within a gendered power structure and excellence as an extra hurdle for women
citation: Meytal Eran-Jona and Yosef Nir. (2020). The academic career in physics as a 'deal': Choosing physics within a gendered power structure and excellence as an extra hurdle for women. arXiv:2010.13115v1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.13115v1
title: The academic career 'deal' with personal-marital, professional-occupational and financial components
description: The article's central framework portrays the academic physics career as a 'deal' that students weigh at the postdoc crossroads. It 'has three main components: personal-marital, professional-occupational, and financial', spanning relocation abroad, job insecurity, and scholarships below market wages. Young women examine what it offers and what prices they will pay before deciding whether to go abroad or quit the academic race.
requirements: Operates at the postdoc crossroads, which the article describes as often requiring a cumulative period of about four years abroad for a tenure-track position in physics
constraints: Framed in the Israeli context, where postdoctoral study abroad is an expected step toward an academic position
target_learners: female physics Ph.D. students in Israel
Israeli female postdoctoral fellows in physics
target_learning_goals: understanding gendered barriers to academic physics careers
career decision-making about postdoctoral study and academic employment
examples: Interviewees weighed relocation, integrating children into new schools and a new language, spouse employment abroad, and scholarships that usually do not suffice for a family when deciding whether to go for a postdoc

article_title: Developing a learning goal framework for computational thinking in computationally integrated physics classrooms
citation: Daniel P. Weller, Theodore E. Bott, Marcos D. Caballero, and Paul W. Irving (2021). Developing a learning goal framework for computational thinking in computationally integrated physics classrooms. https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07981
title: Frame computational thinking learning goals as actionable practices so teachers can classify classroom behavior for assessment
description: The article recommends organizing CT framework components as actionable, verb-based practices rather than abstract ideas, so the framework can serve as an evaluation tool for teachers and not only a research instrument. Because the framework is "made up of actionable items", the authors expect "it will be easier for teachers to classify behavior in the classroom with the framework".
requirements: Practice titles and definitions must be written in action-based form that maps onto observable student behavior in the classroom
target_learning_goals: assessment of students' development of computational thinking
examples: The framework was designed with teachers of all levels of computational experience in mind, so its components use actionable practice wording rather than idea-based concepts

article_title: Assessing Scientific Practices in Physics Paper-based Assessments
citation: Amali Priyanka Jambuge and James T. Laverty. (2021). Assessing Scientific Practices in Physics Paper-based Assessments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.13028
title: ACER framework for describing student use of mathematics in physics problem-solving
description: The ACER framework articulates what it means to use math in physics through four components: "Activation of the tool, Construction of the model, Execution of the mathematics, and Reflection of the results." Each component is an epistemic frame consisting of subcodes (resources) between which students shift while solving problems, such as making assumptions or developing representations under Construction. The authors adopted ACER to analyze written and verbal work products because its components aligned with their evidence statements, it remains accessible to instructors unfamiliar with the underlying theoretical constructs, and it organizes written work products, extending its utility to introductory-level mathematical reasoning.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be designed so each ACER component can potentially be elicited; subcodes depend on the nature of the assessment tasks
constraints: The article notes theoretically grounded approaches like ACER can pose challenges for instructors unfamiliar with the theoretical constructs, which ACER partially bridges
target_learning_goals: using mathematics to do physics (blending math with physics concepts)
examples: The authors coded Catherine's accident-reconstruction response with subcodes A3, A2, C2, C1, E2, R2, R3, A3, A2, C1, E2, R1, covering every ACER component

An accelerator experiment for junior and senior high school students to improve students' involvement in fundamental physics. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.00576
title: Accel Kitchen: a university accelerator-facility outreach workshop for junior and senior high school students
description: Accel Kitchen is a workshop series held in December 2018 and July 2019 at the Cyclotron and Radioisotope Center (CYRIC), Tohoku University, in which twelve junior and senior high school students per workshop participated in the ongoing francium production and laser-trapping experiment for two days. The article describes it as "the first opportunity for junior and senior high school students to know about the particle beam experiment in Japan." Participants worked in three groups supported by researchers and undergraduate mentors, and the workshops contributed to the CYRIC Fr experiment, including the first Fr trapping using Group C's optimum magnetic field.

radiation education
career exploration in physics and radiation-related fields

article_title: Lessons for instructor-student interactions in physics from the world of improvisational theater
citation: Colin G. West. (2022). Lessons for instructor-student interactions in physics from the world of improvisational theater. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01819
title: Practice active listening in student interactions: actively seek hidden meaning and invite clarification before responding
description: Borrowed from improv, active listening means not merely paying attention but "specifically ('actively') looking for possible points of confusion, and inviting clarification as needed." In physics interactions, the instructor should actively seek out hidden meaning in vague or nonstandard student language before deploying established strategies, since premature assumptions can close the instructor's ears to the student's actual ideas.
requirements: Instructor must resist the urge to jump in with prepared responses to anticipated misconceptions
Instructor must identify what the student is expressing even in vague or nonstandard terms
constraints: The article illustrates the principle with a single first-person anecdote rather than a systematic study
target_learning_goals: clarify student conceptual understanding
break vicious cycles of miscommunication about terminology
examples: In a circuit problem, the author assumed a student's ambiguous "it" referred to current and missed that the student's real confusion was between "potential" and "potential difference"; once identified, the conversation became productive

article_title: A Perspective on K-12 AI Education
citation: Nathan Wang, Paul Tonko, Nikil Ragav, Michael Chungyoun, and Jonathan Plucker. (2022). A Perspective on K-12 AI Education. Technology and Innovation, Vol. 22. http://dx.doi.org/10.21300/23.1.2023.2

description: The article argues AI can be accessible without expensive computational infrastructure: "A low-end laptop with internet access can take advantage of free cloud-based computing platforms, such as Google Colab, with access to numerous publicly available datasets". For high school students with no programming experience, visual AI development software such as AI Studio lets users drag and drop code blocks and piece together an AI model as a flowchart, skipping syntax and debugging; built-in layers of abstraction can be peeled away until students work directly with code.
requirements: A low-end laptop with internet access; standard school-district computational infrastructure
constraints: Visual tools reduce the barrier of entry initially; the article notes abstraction layers are removed as students become more comfortable

target_learning_goals: building AI models
understanding neural networks
examples: AI Studio users drag and drop code blocks to assemble a model as a flowchart before transitioning to code

article_title: Lost in Translation: Reimagining the Machine Learning Life Cycle in Education
citation: Lydia T. Liu, Serena Wang, Tolani Britton, Rediet Abebe. (2022). Lost in Translation: Reimagining the Machine Learning Life Cycle in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03929
title: Build education prediction models for actionability, not just interpretability
description: This principle holds that ML prediction tools in education should surface actionable insights — information a student or practitioner can act on — rather than stopping at interpretable feature weights or percentile risk levels. Participants "repeatedly pointed to the value of building models that provide actionable insights", noting that feature importance analysis of non-mutable traits such as demographics distracts from more actionable behavioral factors like absences.
requirements: Prediction outputs must connect to helpful actions, such as telling a student that absences may hurt class performance, rather than only reporting percentile rankings or deficit labels.
constraints: Feature importance analysis of non-mutable traits such as demographics was judged not always useful for developing interventions and may distract from analysis of actionable behavioral factors.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students at academic risk
teachers, academic advisors, and administrators using risk predictions
target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes through actionable feedback rather than deficit-minded risk labels
examples: A participant contrasted telling a student they are in the 10th percentile for something with telling them we are worried because you have been absent a lot, the latter leading to clearer interventions.
key_sources: Lydia T. Liu, Serena Wang, Tolani Britton, Rediet Abebe. (2022). Lost in Translation: Reimagining the Machine Learning Life Cycle in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03929

article_title: A framework for designing experimental tasks in contemporary physics lab courses
citation: Lahme S Z, Pirinen P, Rončević L, Lehtinen A, Sušac A, Müller A and Klein P. (2023). A framework for designing experimental tasks in contemporary physics lab courses. https://www.jyu.fi/digiphyslab
title: Action Research provides the iterative plan-act-observe-reflect cycle for implementing and improving experimental tasks
description: The article uses Action Research as the second structural basis, describing "an ongoing process of innovation consisting of several linked cycles of four steps: plan, act, observe, and reflect." In the framework, design principles 3 to 5 link to AR: after implementation, reflection can lead either to accepting the task or to modification, whereupon "a new cycle of planning, acting, overserving, and reflecting is performed."
requirements: Iterative cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting based on implementation experiences
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of experimental tasks through evaluation

article_title: Exploring EFL students' prompt engineering in human-AI story writing: an Activity Theory perspective
citation: David James Woo, Kai Guo, Hengky Susanto. (2024). Exploring EFL Students’ Prompt Engineering in Human-AI Story Writing: An Activity Theory Perspective.
title: Activity Theory as a framework for analyzing EFL students' human-AI story writing as a mediated activity system
description: The study applies Engeström's Activity Theory, in which a subject acts on an object using tools within a community with a division of labor and rules. Each EFL student writing a story with an NLG tool is modeled as an individual activity system where "Activity theory (AT; Engeström, 1987) provides a framework to analyze how EFL learners interact with NLG tools as a mediated activity system". Rules are operationalized as students' conditions or purposes for prompting, and contradictions (primary to quaternary) drive system change and improvement.
requirements: Data on activity-system elements (rules, tool, object, community) must be collectable and differentiable in qualities, as the authors state they selected elements accordingly
constraints: The framework was applied in the specific context of EFL secondary students' short story writing with self-built NLG tools; the authors note individual students have different activity systems
target_learning_goals: English language short story writing
prompt engineering of generative-AI tools
examples: Students' rules were elicited via the reflection question about deciding which words, sentences or paragraphs to put into an NLG tool, then analyzed as the rule element of each activity system

article_title: Developing and implementing an Einsteinian science curriculum from Years 3 to 10 : Part A Concepts, rationale and learning outcomes
citation: Kaur, T., Kersting, M., Blair, D., Adams, K., Treagust, D., Santoso, J., Popkova, A., Boublil, S., Zadnik, M., Ju, L., Wood, D., Horne, E., & McGoran, D. (2023). title: Teach abstract Einsteinian concepts through activity-based group learning with toys, models and analogies
description: The first of the article's six pedagogical principles holds that abstract Einsteinian concepts should be introduced through hands-on activities in small groups, followed by teacher-led whole-class discussion. The article states: "We draw on an activity-led instructional approach that uses hands-on activities in small groups to introduce abstract concepts", citing evidence that this promotes inclusivity, benefits female learners, and deepens conceptual understanding. Examples include constructing triangles on a curved surface (a wok) and mapping toy-car photon trajectories to show parallel lines crossing.

constraints: Activities must be selected or refined through trial to ensure they effectively reveal the relevant concepts

target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of abstract Einsteinian physics concepts such as curved space and photon momentum

article_title: How do we assess computation in physics?
citation: Sabo, H. C., Odden, T. O. B., & Caballero, M. D. (2023). How do we assess computation in physics? https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22How+do+we+assess+computation+in+physics%22
title: Two-axis framework for computational physics assessment: activities (task types) crossed with forms (foci and manner of assessment)
description: The article organizes computational physics assessment along two axes: assessment activities, broad task categories such as exams or assignments, and assessment forms, the focus and manner of assessment. The authors' insight is that "these two aspects of assessment are related but somewhat independent of one another; they can be combined in different ways," so instructors can mix and match them for better coverage.

constraints: As Generative AI, such as ChatGPT, becomes increasingly common, the authors expect it will likely change how we think of computational physics assessment.

examples: For example, a computational problem on a written exam (activity) could be assessed with a rubric or progress on steps (form).

article_title: Measuring Five Accountable Talk Moves to Improve Instruction at Scale
citation: Ashlee Kupor, Candice Morgan, Dorottya Demszky. (2023). Measuring Five Accountable Talk Moves to Improve Instruction at Scale. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10749
title: Accountable Talk framework operationalized as five instructor talk moves
description: The article operationalizes Accountable Talk theory (O'Connor et al., 2015) as five measurable instructor moves: Adding on, Connecting, Eliciting, Probing, and Revoicing. As the article states, "The talk moves we chose are part of the Accountable Talk Framework that encourages instructors to promote student participation in an equitable way". Each move is defined in the annotation guide (e.g., Revoicing restates students' ideas anticipating their intent) and labelled with printed distributions from Adding on at 25% to Connecting at 4%.
requirements: Annotated instructor utterances and trained classifiers to measure move frequency at scale
constraints: Talk moves are sparse in the data; the framework was applied to online small-group computer science instruction in English
target_learners: online course instructors, especially novices with limited pedagogical training
target_learning_goals: promoting student participation, equitable discussion, and rigorous thinking
examples: Code in Place 2023 created training for these talk moves based on input from education faculty and Stanford section leaders

article_title: Aligning Tutor Discourse Supporting Rigorous Thinking with Tutee Content Mastery for Predicting Math Achievement
citation: Mark Abdelshiheed, Jennifer K. Jacobs, and Sidney K. D'Mello. (2024). Aligning Tutor Discourse Supporting Rigorous Thinking with Tutee Content Mastery for Predicting Math Achievement.
title: Accountable talk and tutor talk moves as discursive techniques for rigorous classroom discussion
description: Accountable talk theory defines an explicit set of discursive techniques that promote rich, knowledge-building classroom discussion, organizing talk around three accountabilities. The article states that "Accountable talk outlinesthree general requirements of classroom discussions: accountability to the learning community, to content knowledge, and to rigorous thinking". Within this, talk moves are linguistic acts intended to facilitate dialogue; the study operationalizes six tutor talk moves (e.g., Keeping Students Together, Restating, Press for Accuracy, Press for Reasoning, Revoicing) and measures them automatically with a fine-tuned RoBERTa model (macro F1 0.765).
requirements: Tutors who organize discussions promoting equitable participation where student thinking is made explicit and publicly available
constraints: The study analyzed only tutor talk moves, not student talk moves, and could not identify which student a talk move was directed to
target_learning_goals: Mathematical reasoning and content knowledge in algebra and geometry
examples: Six tutor talk moves were micro-averaged per tutorial session between assessment rounds for each student

article_title: The end of multiple choice tests: using AI to enhance assessment
citation: Klymkowsky, M.W. & Cooper, M.M. (2024). The end of multiple choice tests: using AI to enhance assessment. Living preprint. https://www.authorea.com
title: Formative assessment feedback must be actionable and embraced by instructors and course designers to make a difference
description: The article argues that class-level AI analyses of multiple-choice/concept-inventory questions with student explanations provide a richer evidence base about student understanding than percent correct, because they include student explanations of their thinking. But the authors state plainly that "the idea of actionable formative assessment has to be embraced by instructors and course designers," and that this likely involves rethinking what is taught in a course. Feedback that goes unread and unused, as much summative feedback does, cannot improve learning.
requirements: Instructors and course designers must act on the analyses, adapting instruction, introducing or reviewing background materials, and engaging students with targeted in-class questions.
constraints: Previously, timely and economical analysis of open-ended formative assessment was impractical; the article frames AI bots as the enabling condition rather than claiming effects without instructor uptake.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment science courses
target_learning_goals: formative assessment
instructor responsiveness to student thinking
examples: The authors suggest follow-on in-class questions such as asking what the correct answer leaves out, and redesigning instructional activities when persistent ideas are shared by many students.

article_title: Framing the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Through Physics-Based Quantities
citation: White Brahmia, S., & Thompson, P. (2025). Framing the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Through Physics-Based Quantities. https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/?awardId=2417104
title: ACRA framework: Amount, Change, Rate, and Accumulation as the four essential quantities of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
description: The ACRA framework, developed by Samuels (2022) and adopted and extended by this article, formulates the evaluation theorem of the FTC as a relationship among four quantities: "the four essential quantities of calculus are: Amount, Change, Rate, Accumulation". F(x) is the value of the accumulating quantity, x the value of the independent quantity, and F′(x) a rate of change of accumulation with respect to x; the integral is an infinite sum of products of rate and infinitesimal change. The article extends ACRA into physics by mapping foundational quantities — change in velocity, displacement, work, and impulse — onto the same structure (Table 2).
requirements: Instruction and assessment must emphasize that F′(x) is a rate — the rate of change of accumulation with respect to variations in x
constraints: Gauss's law is far out of scope as a context for a calculus course, per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding the definite integral as accumulation of rate-times-change products
connecting calculus procedures to quantitative meaning
examples: Table 2 maps ∆v, displacement, work, and impulse each as an accumulation equal to an infinite sum of rate × input change

citation: Scott C. Scharlach. (2025). Academic Miscommunication in Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00142

description: The article coins Academic Miscommunication as "the phenomenon in which a student interprets the professor's words, assignments, or other aspects of the curriculum in a manner that deviates from what the professor had intended."
