citation: Gintaras Dūda (2025). Teaching STEM Courses using Ignatian Pedagogy. Creighton University.
title: A repertoire of active-engagement pedagogies for IPP-based STEM instruction
description: This pattern organizes the active-engagement pedagogies the article recommends for the Experience component of the IPP in STEM courses. The article states: "Some examples of active-engagement pedagogies that are particularly relevant for STEM instruction include:" and enumerates flipped-classroom/Just-in-Time Teaching, Peer Instruction/Think-Pair-Share, Interactive Lecture Demonstrations, Problem-based Learning, Inquiry-based Learning, Modeling Instruction, and POGIL. The author argues these stack with the IPP rather than competing with it.
requirements: Class time must be structured around active engagement rather than passive lecturing, since the article stresses that both IPP and cognitive science indicate students must engage actively with material to learn deeply
constraints: The article notes instructors do not have to choose between the IPP and other best-practice methods; both can coexist and make a course stronger together
target_learners: university STEM students across curriculum levels
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding in STEM subjects
active engagement with course material
examples: The flipped general physics course breaks lecture up with think-pair-share clicker questions, group problem solving, interactive demonstrations, and field trips such as riding elevators while standing on scales
key_sources: Gintaras Dūda (2025). Teaching STEM Courses using Ignatian Pedagogy. Creighton University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05806

article_title: Beyond named methods: A typology of active learning based on classroom observation networks
citation: Meagan Sundstrom, Justin Gambrell, Colin Green, Adrienne L. Traxler, and Eric Brewe. (2025). Beyond named methods: A typology of active learning based on classroom observation networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01124
title: A five-type typology of active learning instruction spanning clicker lectures to long groupwork activities
description: The article defines a typology of active learning instruction derived from clustering classroom observation networks rather than named methods. As printed: "We identify five types of active learning instruction: clicker lecture, dialogic clicker lecture, dialogic lecture with short groupwork activities, short groupwork activities, and long groupwork activities." The types are characterized by network measures such as transitions between lecturing, clicker questions, posing questions, moving and guiding groupwork, and following up. The typology is offered as a way to describe what actually happens during instruction, since method names may not reflect enacted activities.
requirements: Classroom video observations coded with a structured protocol such as the COPUS at two-minute intervals, converted to observation networks and grouped by cosine similarity clustering
constraints: Derived from 30 introductory physics and astronomy instructors at 27 US institutions implementing four named methods; the article states the names of methods may not reflect the specific activities during instruction
target_learners: introductory physics and astronomy college students
target_learning_goals: characterizing instructional practices in active learning courses
examples: Instructors in the long groupwork activities type predominantly guide one or a few long groupwork activities such as worksheets and follow up with real-time writing or demonstrations/videos
key_sources: Meagan Sundstrom, Justin Gambrell, Colin Green, Adrienne L. Traxler, and Eric Brewe. (2025). Beyond named methods: A typology of active learning based on classroom observation networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01124

article_title: Enabling Blind and Visually Impaired Individuals to Pursue Careers in Science
citation: L. Petitdemange and S. Nashed. (2025). ENABLING BLIND AND VISUALLY IMPAIRED INDIVIDUALS TO PURSUE CAREERS IN SCIENCE. SF2A 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17620
title: AccesSciencesDV accessible website collecting adapted academic resources and good practices for BVI science education
description: AccesSciencesDV (accessciencesdv.fr) is the article's project to nationalize and generalize its support approach. The article states "This accessible website will collect adapted resources in academic topics as: Mathematics, Biology, Physics" and provide the good practices for making science more accessible. Its collaborative e-learning platform gives teachers and BVI students access to methods for making science more accessible, addressing the documented scarcity of adapted materials and teacher training.
requirements: collaborative contribution from teachers and BVI students to keep resources evolving
target_learners: BVI students in academic topics including Mathematics, Biology, Physics
target_learning_goals: independent access to adapted academic resources
teacher mastery of accessibility good practices
examples: Figure 2 shows the website accessciencesdv.fr, described as a collaborative e-learning platform for teachers and BVI students

article_title: Quantum Readiness in Latin American High Schools: Curriculum Compatibility and Enabling Conditions
citation: Alvarado León, A. C., Herrera Cueva, O. D., Morales Orvezo, R. M., Vargas Saldaña, D. A. C., & Herrera Cueva, F. (2025). Quantum Readiness in Latin American High Schools: Curriculum Compatibility and Enabling Conditions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16257
title: Academic readiness framework for pre-university quantum education
description: The framework defines academic readiness as "the degree of development of the academic, institutional, and contextual competences required to integrate quantum computing into high school curricula". It comprises two main components—academic coursework (curricular coverage of linear algebra, complex numbers, probability, modern physics, programming, plus alternative pathways such as IB/AP) and enablers (teacher training, technology infrastructure, institutions and public policies, socioeconomic factors, and student culture)—operationalized as eight indicators scored on a 1–5 ordinal scale. The article applies it to produce a cross-country diagnosis of Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and Colombia.
requirements: Official curricula, policy documents, national statistics, and educational reports as evidence sources for coding
constraints: Qualitative and comparative; scores are assigned by research-team agreement on documentary evidence rather than direct assessment of student performance
target_learners: High school students in Latin America
target_learning_goals: Quantum computing foundations including complex numbers, linear algebra, probability, modern physics, and programming
examples: Applied to six countries using documentary analysis, coding, and comparative matrices presented as radar charts and heat maps
key_sources: Alvarado León, A. C., Herrera Cueva, O. D., Morales Orvezo, R. M., Vargas Saldaña, D. A. C., & Herrera Cueva, F. (2025). Quantum Readiness in Latin American High Schools: Curriculum Compatibility and Enabling Conditions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16257

article_title: Access Timing as Scaffolding: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to GenAI in Education
citation: Janne Rotter, Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Access Timing as Scaffolding: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to GenAI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15850
title: Treat GenAI access timing itself as implicit scaffolding rather than adding explicit prompts
description: The article proposes that when learners may access GenAI is itself a pedagogical lever: strategically delaying access preserves productive struggle while mitigating over-reliance, without explicit metacognitive prompts or structured scaffolds. The authors state that "simply timing the access to GenAI can already enhance learning" and that this "also works on unscaffolded naive tools like for instance off-the-shelf LLMs like Mistral or Claude", keeping adoption barriers low for educators and human-AI learning system designers.
requirements: A mechanism (human or automated) that decides when access is granted during a task
Learners engage with the task before access is granted
constraints: Final learning outcomes partly depend on the quality of the underlying LLM; low-quality or misleading responses may weaken the pedagogical benefit
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
metacognitive engagement
responsible AI use
examples: In the study, the RL agent granted access after failed attempts on a question, and participants reported it was helpful to have the AI assistant after failing a few times to avoid frustration
key_sources: Janne Rotter, Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Access Timing as Scaffolding: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to GenAI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15850

article_title: Computer-generated QIS tutorial feedback is valued by students, but does not replicate in-class collaboration
citation: Josephine C. Meyer, Steven J. Pollock, Bethany R. Wilcox, and Gina Passante. (2026). Computer-generated QIS tutorial feedback is valued by students, but does not replicate in-class collaboration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15444
title: AcePhysics: an online platform delivering pencil-and-paper QIS tutorials with computer-generated Socratic-style feedback
description: AcePhysics is an online platform using computerized feedback to mimic the Socratic style of questioning students may receive from instructors or peers, allowing instructors to assign tutorials as a "plug-and-play" out-of-class task. Each tutorial is based on a pencil-and-paper tutorial developed by the group, adhering closely to its structure with adaptations for the virtual medium. The platform intentionally does not rely on AI, because available AI models could not replicate Socratic dialogue. Students receive real-time feedback on closed-form answers, and some problems offer optional hints.
requirements: Students must have a personal device and internet access to complete the online tutorial as assigned homework.
constraints: The article concludes AcePhysics is not a substitute for in-person tutorials, even though it duplicates several aspects of them; the sociocultural experience of the tutorial setting likely cannot be replicated solo.
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate physics and quantum information science students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and fluency with tensor products and other QIS skills
examples: In this study, students completed an AcePhysics tutorial on tensor products solo on their personal device, while peers completed the same tutorial on paper in groups of 3 with a facilitator simulating a TA.
key_sources: Josephine C. Meyer, Steven J. Pollock, Bethany R. Wilcox, and Gina Passante. (2026). Computer-generated QIS tutorial feedback is valued by students, but does not replicate in-class collaboration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15444

article_title: A Theoretical Framework for Physics Education Research: Modeling Student Thinking
citation: Edward F. Redish. (2004). A Theoretical Framework for Physics Education Research: Modeling Student Thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0411140
title: Account for knowledge compilation when presenting arguments: instructors' compiled blocks may exceed students' working memory
description: Because experts work with large blocks of compiled knowledge, arguments that seem simple to instructors can exceed students' working memory. "When a group of knowledge elements – facts and processes – is easily available and can easily be used as a single unit in working memory, we say the knowledge is compiled." If students have not compiled the knowledge, an argument the instructor does in a few operations may require students a long series of manipulations with intermediate storage.
requirements: Students need substantial repetition and practice to compile knowledge
constraints: Compilation is knowledge- and individual-dependent; uncompiled knowledge forces step-by-step processing
target_learning_goals: making multi-step reasoning tractable in working memory
developing functional physics knowledge
examples: Physics instructors work with many large blocks of compiled knowledge, so their few-operation arguments may require students to carry out long manipulations
key_sources: Edward F. Redish. (2004). A Theoretical Framework for Physics Education Research: Modeling Student Thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0411149

article_title: Impact of uncorrected hyperopia on visual function and academic performance in preschool and school-age children.
citation: Kulp MT, Ciner EB, Candy TR, Ying G-s, Hall C, Quinn G, Moore B. (2026). Impact of uncorrected hyperopia on visual function and academic performance in preschool and school-age children. Optometry and Vision Science. https://doi.org/10.1002/ovs2.70018
title: Accommodative effort and instability mechanism linking moderate hyperopia to near-task visual deficits
description: The review proposes that because a moderately hyperopic eye is underpowered for its length, the child "must exert and sustain greater accommodation than a child with age-typical refractive error to achieve clear vision at all distances." Increased accommodative demand produces less accurate and more variable responses (accommodative lag) and, through accommodative-vergence coupling, excessive convergence. The result is greater and more variable blur plus unstable eye alignment during near tasks, a trade-off between strained near vision and greater defocus, which the review links to impaired print-based literacy tasks and sustained visual attention.
requirements: Assessment requires objective measures of accommodation, since subjective testing methods overestimate children's accommodation levels
constraints: The review states the impact of and need for hyperopic correction remains uncertain
target_learners: preschool and school-age children with moderate uncorrected hyperopia
target_learning_goals: near visual function supporting print-based early literacy tasks and sustained visual attention during learning activities
examples: The review cites that a child with >=1.5 D hyperopia may exhibit a 2 D accommodative lag when viewing a near target at 25 cm, and that objective testing shows children's accommodation levels around 7 D rather than the historically assumed high levels.
key_sources: Kulp MT, Ciner EB, Candy TR, Ying G-s, Hall C, Quinn G, Moore B. (2026). Impact of uncorrected hyperopia on visual function and academic performance in preschool and school-age children. Optometry and Vision Science. https://doi.org/10.1002/ovs2.70018

article_title: The relationship between the burnout syndrome and academic success of medical students: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Ilić IM, Ilić MD. (2023). The relationship between the burnout syndrome and academic success of medical students: a cross-sectional study. Archives of Industrial Hygiene and Toxicology. https://doi.org/10.2478/aiht-2023-74-3719
title: Three-component model of academic burnout (emotional exhaustion, cynicism, reduced academic efficacy)
description: The article describes academic burnout as recognisable by "a high level of cynicism, high level of exhaustion, and low performance". It defines emotional exhaustion as severe fatigue caused by educational demands, cynicism as a student's mental detachment from studies, and reduced academic efficacy as the feeling of declining competence and reduced achievement. This three-component structure underpins the MBI-SS instrument used to classify students at high burnout risk in the study.
requirements: Measured with an instrument capturing all three components, such as the MBI-SS with its three subscales
constraints: The article applies the model to medical students in a single Serbian faculty; cutoffs are those validated for the student version of the instrument
target_learning_goals: recognising and monitoring academic burnout as a factor affecting academic achievement
examples: The study classified students as high burnout risk using MBI-SS cutoffs: emotional exhaustion >14, cynicism >6, academic efficacy <23 on 7-point items
key_sources: Ilić IM, Ilić MD. (2023). The relationship between the burnout syndrome and academic success of medical students: a cross-sectional study. Archives of Industrial Hygiene and Toxicology. https://doi.org/10.2478/aiht-2023-74-3719

article_title: Testing for SES differences in the responsiveness of educational expectations in a twin design.
citation: Mirko Ruks. (2023). SES differences in the responsiveness of educational expectations in a twin design. PLoS ONE 18(8): e0290454. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0290454
title: ACE-beta twin models as a design for estimating responsiveness while controlling for unobserved genetic and social confounding
description: The ACE-beta twin model is a biometric structural equation approach that decomposes variance into additive genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and non-shared environmental (E) components estimated as latent factors, and additionally estimates phenotypic pathways of interest. The article uses it to estimate the responsiveness of educational expectations to performance "by estimating these confounders as latent variables within the model, providing an direct estimate of social and genetic confounding". It is conceptually comparable to the MZ fixed-effects model but explicitly models the unobserved confounders.
requirements: Twin data comparing monozygotic and dizygotic twins, with the ACE model chosen after inspecting twin correlations
Exogeneity with respect to non-shared environmental influences, as with the MZ-FE model
constraints: The equal environment assumption, no assortative mating, and no gene-environment interactions or correlations are assumed; assortative mating is likely violated for educational outcomes, underestimating genetic effects
SES may not be exogenous; estimating passive gene-environment correlation would require other designs such as a nuclear twin family design
target_learners: adolescent students aged 10–14 in German secondary schools
target_learning_goals: formation of educational expectations in response to academic performance signals
examples: The article estimates univariate, multivariate and moderated ACE-beta models (M1a–M3b) on TwinLife data using the R package twinflex, a wrapper for OpenMx
key_sources: Mirko Ruks. (2023). SES differences in the responsiveness of educational expectations in a twin design. PLoS ONE 18(8): e0290454. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0290454

article_title: Awareness of Practice and Comparison with Best Evidence in Surgical Site Infection Prevention in Colorectal Surgery.
citation: Badia Josep M., Casey Anna L., Rubio-Pérez Inés, Arroyo-García Nares, Espin Eloy, Biondo Sebastiano, Balibrea José M. (2020). Awareness of Practice and Comparison with Best Evidence in Surgical Site Infection Prevention in Colorectal Surgery. Surgical Infections. https://doi.org/10.1089/sur.2019.203
title: Active diffusion of high-evidence SSI prevention recommendations, targeting both professionals and their practice settings, to close the evidence-practice gap
description: The article concludes that passive dissemination of guidelines is insufficient and recommends active implementation. It states that "The active diffusion of homogenous SSI prophylactic recommendations with a high rate of scientific evidence ought to decrease taxes of SSI consistently" and that "Implementation policies must concentrate not only on the professionals, but also on the settings in which they practice." It also cites surveillance of SSI with confidential feedback to surgeons as reducing SSI risk in colorectal operations.
requirements: Understanding the level of implementation of preventative measures and providers' awareness of the available scientific evidence.
constraints: Self-reported practice may overrate actual performance, as the article notes self-reporting has been shown to overrate performance.
target_learners: practicing colorectal surgeons and surgical trainees
target_learning_goals: adoption of evidence-based surgical site infection prevention practices
examples: The survey identified checklists, standardized orders, surveillance, feedback of SSI rates, and educational programs as the strategies surgeons rated most highly for implementing guidelines.
key_sources: Badia Josep M., Casey Anna L., Rubio-Pérez Inés, Arroyo-García Nares, Espin Eloy, Biondo Sebastiano, Balibrea José M. (2020). article_title: Clinical Competencies for the Care of Hospitalized Patients with Alcohol Use Disorders.
citation: Phillips Thomas, Porter Amy, Sinclair Julia. (2020). Clinical Competencies for the Care of Hospitalized Patients with Alcohol Use Disorders. Alcohol and Alcoholism. https://doi.org/10.1093/alcalc/agaa024
title: Eight core service components framework for multidisciplinary alcohol care teams
description: The article organizes ACT clinical competencies around eight core service components identified by NHS England and Improvement as essential roles of the ACT: the article states "Eight core clinical components have been identified as essential roles of the ACT". The components span case identification and brief advice, triage and comprehensive alcohol assessment, specialist nursing and medical care planning, management of medically-assisted alcohol withdrawal, psychosocial interventions, safe discharge and community referral, clinical leadership with dedicated time, and trust-wide education and training. The 72 competencies are mapped onto these components in Table 1, each phrased as what the ACT "possesses the specialist knowledge, skills and behaviours to" do.
requirements: A suitably qualified multidisciplinary workforce drawn from different professional groups is required to deliver the eight components and related competencies
constraints: Implementation of ACTs within the UK NHS has been variable with models of services differing significantly
target_learners: non-specialist hospital workforce trained by ACTs
target_learning_goals: assessment and management of alcohol use disorders in acute hospital settings
delivery of medically-assisted alcohol withdrawal care and psychosocial interventions
examples: Table 1 maps the 72 competencies to the eight components, e.g. component 4 covering medically-assisted alcohol withdrawal spans statements 33-50

article_title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of pediatricians on infantile colic in the Middle East and North Africa region.
citation: Indrio F, Miqdady M, Al Aql F, Haddad J, Berkouk K, Khatami K, Mouane N, Rahmani A, Alsaad S, Salah M, Samy G, Tafuri S. (2017). Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of pediatricians on infantile colic in the Middle East and North Africa region. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-017-0939-0
title: ACT Infantile Colic Survey questionnaire
description: A 15-item anonymous questionnaire developed by the Allied Against Infantile Functional GI Disorders (ACT) Working Group with reference to existing research literature, covering respondent characteristics and closed questions on colic diagnosis, risk factors, symptoms, parental attitudes, treatment measures and perceived prophylaxis. It was validated by a group of 15 pediatricians and distributed to 1800 practicing healthcare professionals, with 1628 completed responses. The instrument is provided as Additional file 1.

Ethics committee approval in all countries and written informed consent prior to study initiation
constraints: Convenience sampling at national and regional pediatric meetings; non-random participant selection
Collects only self-reported management practices; no attempts were made to determine actual local clinical practice

article_title: Motivational Climate in Sport Is Associated with Life Stress Levels, Academic Performance and Physical Activity Engagement of Adolescents.
citation: Castro-Sánchez M., Zurita-Ortega F., García-Marmol E., Chacón-Cuberos R. (2019). Motivational Climate in Sport Is Associated with Life Stress Levels, Academic Performance and Physical Activity Engagement of Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16071198
title: Achievement goal theory distinguishes task-oriented and ego-oriented motivational climates created by explicit and implicit signals
description: The article frames its study with achievement goal theory, under which perceived ability is judged either against personal progress or against others. The motivational climate is defined as "a set of signals, as much explicit as implicit (use of feedback, grouping systems, type of evaluation, and task design), which predispose individuals to achieve success". Coaches and physical education teachers promote climates oriented towards task or ego, steering learners towards mastery or towards demonstrating ability over rivals.
requirements: Agents such as coaches or physical education teachers create the prevailing climate through feedback, grouping systems, evaluation type and task design
target_learners: adolescents in obligatory secondary education who play sport outside school
target_learning_goals: motivation towards sport and physical activity
adaptive responses to success and failure

article_title: The Effect of Task Ordering in Continual Learning
citation: Samuel J. Bell and Neil D. Lawrence. (2022). The Effect of Task Ordering in Continual Learning. Preprint. Under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13323
title: Continual learning evaluations should specify and account for task ordering as a source of performance variance
description: The paper argues that because reordering tasks significantly changes forgetting and accuracy, benchmark results that omit the precise task sequence are incomplete. Its stated contribution is "to demonstrate that task ordering is a signiﬁcant source of variance in continual learning performance that must be properly accounted for by future work." Evaluations should therefore report orderings and treat ordering as an experimental factor.
requirements: Reporting the precise order of the task sequence in continual learning benchmark results
constraints: Evidence comes from single-headed supervised binary classification settings; impact on multi-headed models remains open
target_learners: researchers designing and evaluating continual learning methods
target_learning_goals: valid and reproducible evaluation of sequential learning methods
examples: The paper's experiments used power analysis, Bonferroni correction, and seed-controlled permutation conditions to isolate ordering effects
key_sources: Samuel J. Bell and Neil D. Lawrence. (2022). The Effect of Task Ordering in Continual Learning. Preprint. Under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13323

article_title: From Amateur to Master: Infusing Knowledge into LLMs via Automated Curriculum Learning
citation: Nishit Neema, Srinjoy Mukherjee, Sapan Shah, Gokul Ramakrishnan & Ganesh Venkatesh. (2025). From Amateur to Master: Infusing Knowledge into LLMs via Automated Curriculum Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26336
title: ACER: a multi-stage pipeline for synthesizing curriculum-aligned textbook corpora and Bloom's-taxonomy-guided QA pairs for domain knowledge infusion
description: ACER (Automated Curriculum-Enhanced Regimen) is "a multi-stage pipeline designed to transform high-level learning goals into a structured synthetic training corpus". It proceeds through domain detailing (domain name, intent, and target-audience metadata yielding a domain description, core subtopics, and 6-8 key questions aligned with Bloom's taxonomy), outline generation of a hierarchical table of contents, section-level synthetic textbook content generation, and two-stage QA generation whose difficulty "gradually escalates, following a cognitive progression from comprehension to interpretation, analysis, and application". Four persona versions (high school, undergraduate, graduate, researcher) of each textbook encode educational progression.
requirements: A strong content-generation model (the article uses Gemini 2.0 Flash) prompted as a domain author
Domain name, intent statement, and target-audience metadata as inputs
Decontamination against benchmark content (cosine similarity threshold 0.9 to MMLU)
constraints: The article did not ablate between different models for content generation
Evaluation was limited to 1B and 3B scale models
target_learners: Large language models being continually pretrained for domain specialization
target_learning_goals: Deep, principled domain knowledge in underrepresented domains such as microeconomics, statistics, econometrics, mathematics, and psychology
examples: For the five target domains ACER generates on average 6.4M tokens per domain, totaling about 32M tokens overall
A generated microeconomics book included a dedicated section on Supply Curve and Elasticity, after which the ACER-trained model answered an elasticity question the baseline missed
key_sources: Nishit Neema, Srinjoy Mukherjee, Sapan Shah, Gokul Ramakrishnan & Ganesh Venkatesh. (2025). From Amateur to Master: Infusing Knowledge into LLMs via Automated Curriculum Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26336

article_title: From Amateur to Master: Infusing Knowledge into LLMs via Automated Curriculum Learning
citation: Nishit Neema, Srinjoy Mukherjee, Sapan Shah, Gokul Ramakrishnan & Ganesh Venkatesh. (2025). From Amateur to Master: Infusing Knowledge into LLMs via Automated Curriculum Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26336
title: Four curriculum schedules for incorporating synthetic book corpora into continual pretraining: Flat, Cognitive, Cognitive+Content, and Interleaved
description: The article experiments with "four curriculum schedules for incorporating synthetic book corpus into continual pretraining": Flat (all books, easy QA, and hard QA presented together without ordering), Cognitive (books then easy QA then hard QA, with domains and personas mixed randomly within stages), Cognitive+Content (which "extends the cognitive schedule by introducing content-based ordering: High school, Undergraduate, Graduate, Researcher"), and Interleaved (chapter-section-level interleaving across domains while preserving persona order within each category). This taxonomy aligns learning along both a cognitive-difficulty dimension and a content/persona dimension, and the schedules are ablated against a Flat baseline to test whether structured ordering improves domain knowledge infusion.
requirements: A synthetic corpus divided into books, easy QA, and hard QA subsets, generated across multiple persona levels
A general replay data source mixed with the in-domain corpus
constraints: The Interleaved schedule underperformed in this continual-pretraining setting, with large drops in mathematics and statistics
target_learners: Large language models undergoing continual pretraining
target_learning_goals: Progressive acquisition of domain knowledge along cognitive difficulty and audience-level dimensions
examples: The Cog schedule progresses from textbooks to easy QA to hard QA, with corpora from different domains and personas mixed randomly within each section

article_title: A meta-analytic review of achievement goal measures: Different labels for the same constructs or different constructs with similar labels?
citation: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947
title: Constrained working definition of achievement goals as future-focused cognitive representations of competence-related end states
description: The article adopts a deliberately constrained definition of achievement goals, excluding affect, attributions, self-beliefs, and interests. Its working definition is "a future-focused cognitive representation that guides behavior to a competence-related end state that the individual is committed to either approach or avoid." This definition, drawn from Elliot and Fryer's five basic features of goals, distinguishes mastery (developing competence) from performance (demonstrating competence) definitions, each crossed with approach or avoidance valence. The authors argue this constraint affords greater conceptual clarity when examining goal effects.
requirements: Goal measures must use goal-relevant language assessing goal-directed reasons or standards, rather than goal-related affect or interest
constraints: The authors acknowledge the constrained definition may not mirror the real-life experience of goal pursuit, which may be an inseparable blend of theoretically unique components
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of achievement motivation constructs
construct validity in motivation research
examples: Items coded as goal-relevant included stems such as "My goal is to . . ." and "It is important to me to . . .", while items like "I feel successful when . . ." were coded as no goal
key_sources: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947

article_title: A meta-analytic review of achievement goal measures: Different labels for the same constructs or different constructs with similar labels?
citation: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947
title: Component taxonomy of achievement goal constructs: appearance, normative, and evaluative components for performance goals and five components for mastery-approach goals
description: From a conceptual review of the literature, the article derives a taxonomy of the components actually operationalized under each achievement goal label. As the authors summarize: "We identified three components of performance-approach goals (appearance, normative, evaluative), four components of performance-avoidance goals (appearance, normative, evaluative, and fear of negative outcomes), five components of mastery-approach goals (interest, task-mastery, improvement, potential attainment, and challenge seeking), and four components of mastery-avoidance goals." Avoidance versions mirror approach versions but tend to also include fear of negative outcomes. This taxonomy grounds the item-level coding used as moderators in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Individual scale items must be coded by the component each item most strongly represents to connect theoretical components with operational definitions
constraints: The taxonomy reflects the components found in the literature through December 2006 and the authors' own conceptual grouping of constructs
target_learning_goals: construct-valid measurement of achievement goals
comparability of findings across achievement goal research programs
examples: Tables 1 through 4 list authors' labels under each component, e.g., ability validation (appearance), performance-approach (normative), and mastery-challenge (challenge seeking)
key_sources: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947

article_title: A meta-analytic review of achievement goal measures: Different labels for the same constructs or different constructs with similar labels?
citation: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947
title: Item-level coding system for achievement goal scale items
description: The article developed a coding system classifying every individual item in each achievement goal scale. Items were first coded for goal-relevant language matching the article's three-part goal definition, then coded as general goal or into component categories such as performance-normative, performance-appearance, performance-evaluative, mastery-potential, mastery-improve, mastery-task, mastery-interest, and mastery-learning, with fear/negative-affect codes for avoidance scales. Three coders "agreed on 81% of the items (␬ ⫽ .79)", with disagreements resolved by consensus. This coding operationalized the item-content moderators tested in the meta-analysis.
requirements: At least two independent coders rating every scale item, with disagreements resolved through consensus
constraints: Items that did not reflect language explicitly corresponding to the article's three-part definition of a goal were coded as no goal
target_learning_goals: reliable classification of achievement goal scale items
construct-valid measurement of achievement goals
examples: Performance-normative example item: "My goal this semester is to get a better grade than other students"; mastery-potential example item: "I want to learn as much as possible in this course"
key_sources: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2010). A Meta-Analytic Review of Achievement Goal Measures: Different Labels for the Same Constructs or Different Constructs With Similar Labels? Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018947

article_title: Modeling the distinct phases of skill acquisition.
citation: Tenison, C., & Anderson, J. R. (2015). Modeling the distinct phases of skill acquisition. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/xlm0000204
title: ACT-R operationalization of Fitts and Posner's three phases of skill acquisition
description: The article uses ACT-R, a cognitive architecture representing declarative facts and procedural production rules, to operationalize Fitts and Posner's (1967) three phases. In the cognitive phase "The participant must perform a sequence of calculations to produce the answer"; in the associative phase the learner retrieves a declarative fact; and "With enough practice the learner can acquire a production that simply produces the answer 15 in response to the problem without querying declarative memory." Speedup within the first two stages is attributed to knowledge compilation and declarative strengthening. The study's three HMM states are interpreted as parallels to these phases.
requirements: Practice opportunities on the same problems so that declarative facts can be strengthened and productions compiled
constraints: Once the autonomous phase is reached, ACT-R has no further basis for speedup apart from hypothetical new motor programs
target_learners: University students learning novel arithmetic operations
target_learning_goals: Mathematical fluency: fast and accurate problem solving
Transition from calculation to retrieval to automatic recognition of answers
examples: The study taught participants the Pyramid operation (e.g., 8$4 = 8+7+6+5) and modeled their 36 practice opportunities per problem with a three-state HMM
key_sources: Tenison, C., & Anderson, J. R. (2015). Modeling the distinct phases of skill acquisition. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/xlm0000204

article_title: Degradation of validity over time: A test and extension of Ackerman's model.
citation: Keil, C. T., & Cortina, J. M. (2001). Degradation of validity over time: A test and extension of Ackerman's model. Psychological Bulletin, 127(5), 673-697. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.127.5.673
title: Ackerman's skill acquisition model: resource allocation across cognitive, perceptual speed, and psychomotor abilities for consistent and inconsistent tasks
description: Ackerman's (1987, 1988) model is a resource allocation account in which "the relative importance of certain abilities to task performance changes during skill acquisition." It distinguishes three abilities (cognitive, perceptual speed, psychomotor) and two task types: consistent tasks that can "become automatic, fast, effortless" and become resource-insensitive, versus inconsistent tasks that "will continuously be resource dependent." The model predicts cognitive ability predicts early performance, perceptual speed waxes next, and psychomotor ability rises latest, with these shifts developing more slowly for inconsistent tasks. Keil and Cortina test its propositions using expert-rated longitudinal data.
requirements: Expert coding of predictors into cognitive, perceptual speed, and psychomotor ability categories and criteria into consistent versus inconsistent tasks
Longitudinal data spanning the interval between predictor and criterion measurement
constraints: The distinction between consistent and inconsistent tasks is often fuzzy (Langan-Fox, Waycott, & Galna, 1997)
Prior tests used short time spans, limiting generalizability to training, selection, and validity degradation over time
target_learners: adults acquiring job and task skills
target_learning_goals: predicting performance over the course of skill acquisition
key_sources: Keil, C. T., & Cortina, J. M. (2001). Degradation of validity over time: A test and extension of Ackerman's model. Psychological Bulletin, 127(5), 673-697. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.127.5.673

article_title: The high heritability of educational achievement reflects many genetically influenced traits, not just intelligence
citation: Krapohl, E., Rimfeld, K., Shakeshaft, N. G., Trzaskowski, M., McMillan, A., Pingault, J.-B., Asbury, K., Harlaar, N., Kovas, Y., Dale, P. S., & Plomin, R. (2014). The high heritability of educational achievement reflects many genetically influenced traits, not just intelligence. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1408777111
title: Active genotype–environment correlation model of education: children as active participants selecting and creating experiences correlated with genetic propensities
description: The article proposes moving from a passive model of schooling as instruction ('to build in') to an active model of education ('to bring out'), in which "children are active participants in selecting, modifying, and creating their experiences that are correlated with their genetic propensities, known in genetics as genotype–environment correlation". The authors present this as a new model for education suggested by the pervasive role of genetics in educational achievement, and link it to personalized learning.
requirements: Recognition that genetic influences pervade educational achievement and its correlates, not just intelligence
constraints: The authors state no policy implications necessarily follow, because policy depends on values and knowledge
target_learning_goals: educational achievement across academic subjects
examples: The authors state the active genotype–environment correlation model of education adds support for the trend toward personalized learning, made more practical by advances in educational technology and software
